title: Roots, Rational Powers, and Classical Inequalities: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Rational powers of rational bases computed from the definition
items.statement: In $\mathbb{R}$, with the rational powers of [[def-rational-power]]: $(4/9)^{1/2} = 2/3$; $(8/27)^{1/3} = 2/3$; $(4/9)^{3/2} = 8/27$; $(27/8)^{-2/3} = 4/9$; and $8^{2/6} = 8^{1/3} = 2$, one value produced from either representative of the rational $1/3 = 2/6$. Every base occurring is a positive rational and every exponent a rational with numerator an integer and denominator a natural $\ge 1$, so the definition applies in each case; the last display is the instance of [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] that [[def-rational-power]] records in its `justified_by`. The item also checks the negative-exponent and non-coprime-representative cases, the two places where the definition is most easily misread.
items.strategy: (i) $2/3$ is the nonnegative square root of $4/9$ and the nonnegative cube root of $8/27$, since $(2/3)^{2} = 4/9$ and $(2/3)^{3} = 8/27$ by field arithmetic; uniqueness in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] therefore gives $(4/9)^{1/2} = 2/3$ and $(8/27)^{1/3} = 2/3$, using the representatives $1/2$ and $1/3$, whose denominators are $2$ and $3$ respectively. (ii) At the representative $3/2$ the definition gives $(4/9)^{3/2} = \big((4/9)^{1/2}\big)^{3} = (2/3)^{3} = 8/27$. (iii) At the representative $-2/3$ it gives $(27/8)^{-2/3} = \big((27/8)^{1/3}\big)^{-2} = (3/2)^{-2} = \big((3/2)^{2}\big)^{-1} = (9/4)^{-1} = 4/9$, the negative exponent being the clause of [[def-integer-power]] and the last step the uniqueness of inverses. (iv) $8^{1/3} = 2$ because $2^{3} = 8$ and $2 \ge 0$; since $2/6 = 1/3$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] gives $8^{2/6} = 8^{1/3}$. Every step stays inside the hypotheses of [[def-rational-power]]; no value is assigned to a negative base.

items.title: Odd powers are bijections of $\mathbb{R}$: $x^{3} = -8$ has the unique solution $x = -2$
items.statement: Let $n \ge 1$ be odd. Then $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$ onto $\mathbb{R}$: every real number has exactly one real $n$-th root. Explicitly, $x^{3} = -8$ has the unique solution $x = -2$, and $x^{5} = -32$ has the unique solution $x = -2$. For a negative right-hand side this is a statement about the solution of $x^{n} = a$; it does not extend the symbol $a^{1/n}$, since [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] produces that symbol only for $a \ge 0$ and [[def-rational-power]] does not define rational powers of negative bases (its separate zero-base clause concerns nonnegative bases only). This is the claim the A-page prose records when it says that odd roots of negatives do exist while [[fs-negative-has-square-root]] shows that even ones do not.
items.strategy: Existence: let $a \in \mathbb{R}$. If $a \ge 0$, take $y := a^{1/n}$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. If $a < 0$, put $b := -a > 0$ and $y := b^{1/n} \ge 0$, and set $x := -y$; then $x^{n} = (-y)^{n} = (-1)^{n}y^{n} = -y^{n} = -b = a$, where $(-y)^{n} = (-1)^{n}y^{n}$ is the product law of [[lem-power-laws]], $(-1)^{n} = -1$ for odd $n$ is an induction from that same law, and $(-1)(-1) = 1$ is [[lem-of-mult-neg]]. Injectivity: suppose $x \ne y$. If $0 \le x < y$ then $x^{n} < y^{n}$ by [[lem-power-monotone]]. If $x < y \le 0$ then $0 \le -y < -x$, so $(-y)^{n} < (-x)^{n}$ by monotonicity, that is $-y^{n} < -x^{n}$ by the odd-power identity, equivalently $x^{n} < y^{n}$ by the sign rules of [[lem-of-sign-rules]]. If $x < 0 \le y$ then $x^{n} < 0 \le y^{n}$ by the odd-power identity and $u^{n} > 0$ for $u > 0$. So $x \mapsto x^{n}$ is injective, hence bijective by the existence argument. The displayed solutions follow from $(-2)^{3} = -8$ and $(-2)^{5} = -32$ by [[def-integer-power]], uniqueness being the injectivity proved. No continuity and no completeness beyond [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] is used, so the argument is choice-free.

items.title: The two-term AM-GM inequality, its equality case, and $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$
items.statement: (a) For all $a, b \ge 0$, $\dfrac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$, equivalently $ab \le \Big(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\Big)^{2}$, with equality in either form exactly when $a = b$. (b) Consequently, for every $x > 0$, $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$, with equality exactly when $x = 1$.
items.strategy: (a) is [[thm-am-gm]] at $n = 2$ with $a_0 := a$, $a_1 := b$: the geometric mean is $(ab)^{1/2}$, which is $\sqrt{ab}$ by [[def-rational-power]] and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]; the equality clause is the theorem's; and the equivalence of the two displays is the strict monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives, that is $ab \le A^{2} \iff (ab)^{1/2} \le A$ for $A \ge 0$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]). (b) Apply (a) to $a_0 := x$ and $a_1 := x^{-1}$ (the negative integer power of [[def-integer-power]]): the product is $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$, so the geometric mean is $1^{1/2} = 1$ by [[lem-rational-power-laws]], and the arithmetic mean is $(x + x^{-1})/2$. Equality in (a) means $x = x^{-1}$, equivalently $x^{2} = 1$; for $x > 0$ this holds exactly at $x = 1$, since $0 < x < 1$ gives $x^{2} < 1^{2} = 1$ and $x > 1$ gives $x^{2} > 1^{2} = 1$ by [[lem-power-monotone]].

items.title: Comparing rational powers: $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$
items.statement: (i) $2^{1/2} > 2^{1/3}$; (ii) $3^{1/2} > 2^{1/2}$; (iii) $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$; hence $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$. All bases are positive and all exponents rational, so [[def-rational-power]] applies. Clauses (i) and (ii) are instances of the two monotonicity statements of [[lem-rational-power-monotone]], but (iii) is not: it compares bases $2 < 3$ against exponents in the opposite order $1/2 > 1/3$, and neither monotonicity clause decides it.
items.strategy: (i) $2 > 1$ and $1/3 < 1/2$, so exponent monotonicity gives $2^{1/3} < 2^{1/2}$. (ii) $1/2 > 0$ and $2 < 3$, so base monotonicity gives $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/2}$. (iii) Raise both sides of the desired comparison to the sixth power: $\big(2^{1/2}\big)^{6} = 2^{(1/2)\cdot 6} = 2^{3} = 8$ and $\big(3^{1/3}\big)^{6} = 3^{(1/3)\cdot 6} = 3^{2} = 9$ by the iterated-power law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] together with [[def-integer-power]]; since $8 < 9$, the strict monotonicity of $t \mapsto t^{6}$ on $[0,\infty)$ ([[lem-power-monotone]], using $2^{1/2} \ge 0$ and $3^{1/3} \ge 0$ from [[def-rational-power]]) gives $2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}$. Chaining (i) and (iii) gives the displayed order. The route in (iii) is the standard one for comparisons that no single monotonicity clause reaches.

items.title: A weighted AM-GM computation: $8^{2/3}\,1^{1/3} \le \frac{2}{3}\cdot 8 + \frac{1}{3}\cdot 1$
items.statement: Take $n := 2$, $x_0 := 8$, $x_1 := 1$ and the rational weights $w_0 := 2/3$, $w_1 := 1/3$, so that $\iota(w_0) + \iota(w_1) = 1$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Then [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] gives $$8^{2/3}\cdot 1^{1/3} \;\le\; \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 8 + \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot 1,$$ where the left-hand side is $4$ and the right-hand side is $17/3$; so $4 < 17/3$ and the inequality is strict here. With $x_0 := x_1 := 8$ instead, both sides equal $8$, so the bound is attained by a constant list.
items.strategy: $8^{1/3} = 2$ since $2^{3} = 8$ and $2 \ge 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]), so $8^{2/3} = \big(8^{1/3}\big)^{2} = 4$ by the definition at the representative $2/3$; and $1^{1/3} = 1$ since $1^{3} = 1$. The right-hand side is $(2/3)\cdot 8 + (1/3)\cdot 1 = 16/3 + 1/3 = 17/3$ by the scaling and addition laws of finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $4 = 12/3 < 17/3$. For the constant list $x_0 = x_1 = 8$, the addition law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives $8^{2/3}\,8^{1/3} = 8^{2/3 + 1/3} = 8^{1} = 8$, which equals $(2/3)\cdot 8 + (1/3)\cdot 8$ by scaling. No equality characterization of weighted AM-GM is claimed — [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] records the inequality only — which is why the second display is verified by direct computation.

items.title: Young's inequality at $p = q = 2$ and at $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$
items.statement: (i) At the conjugate pair $p = q = 2$, [[thm-young-inequality]] reads $ab \le \frac{a^{2}}{2} + \frac{b^{2}}{2}$ for all $a, b \ge 0$, with equality exactly when $a = b$; the instance $a := 4$, $b := 9$ gives $36 \le 97/2$. (ii) At $p := 3$ and $q := 3/2$, conjugate since $\frac13 + \frac23 = 1$, it reads $ab \le \frac{a^{3}}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\,b^{3/2}$; the instance $a := 2$, $b := 4$ gives $8$ on both sides.
items.strategy: (i) The inequality is [[thm-young-inequality]] at $p = q = 2$. For the equality clause, apply [[thm-am-gm]] at $n = 2$ to the nonnegative list $(a^{2}, b^{2})$ — exactly the weighted-AM-GM step of [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] at the weights $1/2, 1/2$. Its geometric mean is $(a^{2}b^{2})^{1/2} = ab$, since $ab \ge 0$ and $(ab)^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$ by [[lem-power-laws]] make $ab$ the nonnegative square root of $a^{2}b^{2}$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]); and its equality clause says that equality holds exactly when $a^{2} = b^{2}$, which for $a, b \ge 0$ means $a = b$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The instance is arithmetic: $(4^{2} + 9^{2})/2 = 97/2 \ge 36 = 4\cdot 9$. (ii) $1/3 + 2/3 = 1$ by rational arithmetic, so the theorem applies; the instance evaluates $a^{3}/3 = 8/3$ and $(2/3)\,b^{3/2} = (2/3)\big(4^{1/2}\big)^{3} = (2/3)\cdot 8 = 16/3$, whose sum is $8 = ab$.

items.title: The two-term Lagrange identity and Cauchy-Schwarz
items.statement: For all reals $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$, $$(a_0^{2} + a_1^{2})(b_0^{2} + b_1^{2}) - (a_0b_0 + a_1b_1)^{2} = (a_0b_1 - a_1b_0)^{2};$$ consequently $(a_0b_0 + a_1b_1)^{2} \le (a_0^{2} + a_1^{2})(b_0^{2} + b_1^{2})$, with equality exactly when $a_0b_1 = a_1b_0$ — the two-entry form of the proportionality clause of [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]. The instance $a_0 := 1$, $a_1 := 2$, $b_0 := 3$, $b_1 := 4$ reads $5\cdot 25 - 121 = 4 = (-2)^{2}$.
items.strategy: Expand the left-hand difference with distributivity over the two-entry sums ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]): $a_0^{2}b_0^{2} + a_0^{2}b_1^{2} + a_1^{2}b_0^{2} + a_1^{2}b_1^{2} - \big(a_0^{2}b_0^{2} + 2a_0b_0a_1b_1 + a_1^{2}b_1^{2}\big)$ cancels to $a_0^{2}b_1^{2} - 2(a_0b_1)(a_1b_0) + a_1^{2}b_0^{2} = (a_0b_1 - a_1b_0)^{2}$, using $(-c)^{2} = c^{2}$ and $(-1)^{2} = 1$ from [[lem-power-laws]] and [[lem-of-mult-neg]]. The difference is a square: if its base is zero then the square is $0$ by [[def-integer-power]], while a nonzero base has a positive square by [[lem-of-square-positive]]. Thus the difference is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when $a_0b_1 - a_1b_0 = 0$; rearranging gives the inequality and its equality case. The instance is a direct evaluation. This derivation uses no root and reproduces, in the two-entry case, the expansion route by which [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] is proved; the root form of that theorem needs [[thm-of-square-roots]] and is not used here.

items.title: Hölder at the conjugate pair $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$: an exact equality instance and a strict instance
items.statement: $p := 3$ and $q := 3/2$ are conjugate rationals, $\frac13 + \frac23 = 1$. For the two-entry lists $a_0 = a_1 = b_0 = b_1 = 1$, [[thm-holder-finite]] reads $$\sum_{k<2}|a_kb_k| = 2 \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<2}|a_k|^{3}\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum_{k<2}|b_k|^{3/2}\Big)^{2/3} = 2^{1/3}\,2^{2/3} = 2,$$ so both sides are equal here. For $a = (2,0)$ and $b = (0,3)$ the inequality is strict: the left-hand side is $0$ and the right-hand side is $2\cdot 3 = 6$.
items.strategy: Compute the finite sums at $k = 0, 1$ from [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; $1^{r} = 1$ for each positive rational $r$; and $2^{1/3}\,2^{2/3} = 2^{1/3 + 2/3} = 2^{1} = 2$ by the addition law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]]. In the strict instance, $(8)^{1/3} = 2$ and $\big(3^{3/2}\big)^{2/3} = 3^{(3/2)(2/3)} = 3^{1} = 3$ by the iterated-power law, with $0 < 6$. Only the inequality is claimed: [[thm-holder-finite]] records no equality characterization, and none is asserted here.

items.title: Minkowski for two-entry vectors: equality and strict cases
items.statement: For all reals $x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1$, $$\big((x_0+y_0)^{2} + (x_1+y_1)^{2}\big)^{1/2} \;\le\; \big(x_0^{2} + x_1^{2}\big)^{1/2} + \big(y_0^{2} + y_1^{2}\big)^{1/2},$$ and equality holds exactly when $x_0y_1 = x_1y_0$ and $x_0y_0 + x_1y_1 \ge 0$. Two instances: for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (6,8)$ both sides are $15$; for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (4,-3)$ the left-hand side is $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$ and the right-hand side is $10$, so the inequality is strict.
items.strategy: The inequality is [[thm-minkowski-finite]] at $p = 2$, with $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]). Equality analysis: write $A := x_0^{2}+x_1^{2}$, $B := y_0^{2}+y_1^{2}$ and $C := x_0y_0 + x_1y_1$; expanding gives $A + 2C + B$ for the squared left side and $A + B + 2\sqrt{A}\sqrt{B} = A + B + 2\sqrt{AB}$ for the squared right side, the last step by the product law of [[lem-rational-power-laws]]. Both sides are nonnegative, so equality holds exactly when the squares agree ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]), that is exactly when $C = \sqrt{AB}$; and $C = \sqrt{AB}$ holds exactly when $C \ge 0$ and $C^{2} = AB$. The exact identity and equality clause of the already derived [[ex-cauchy-schwarz-lagrange-identity-two-terms]] give $AB-C^{2}=(x_0y_1-x_1y_0)^{2}\ge0$, with equality exactly when $x_0y_1=x_1y_0$. This is the stated condition and handles zero vectors as well as nonzero vectors. The two instances are direct computations: for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (6,8)$, $x+y = (9,12)$ has $9^{2}+12^{2} = 225 = 15^{2}$ while $5 + 10 = 15$; for $x = (3,4)$ and $y = (4,-3)$, $x+y = (7,1)$ has squared length $50$, so the left side is $\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25}\,\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}$ by the product law, and $5\sqrt{2} < 10$ because $0 \le \sqrt{2} < 2$ (from $2 < 4 = 2^{2}$ by [[lem-of-square-monotone]]) and $5 > 0$. Here $x_0y_1 - x_1y_0 = 3(-3) - 4\cdot 4 = -25 \ne 0$, consistent with the equality criterion.

items.title: AM-GM fails for negative entries: $(-1,-4)$ has geometric mean $2$ and arithmetic mean $-5/2$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the conclusion $\sqrt{ab} \le \dfrac{a+b}{2}$ of the two-term arithmetic-geometric mean inequality holds for arbitrary real $a, b$. Witness: $a := -1$, $b := -4$. The product is $ab = 4$, so the geometric mean is $4^{1/2} = 2$, while the arithmetic mean is $(-1-4)/2 = -5/2$; thus $G = 2 > -5/2 = A$ and the inequality fails. The failure is not an accident of the witness: for any two negative entries $a, b < 0$ the product is positive, so $G > 0$, while $A < 0$, giving $G > A$. A second failure mode is non-existence: for $a := -1$, $b := 1$ the product is $-1$, which has no real square root ([[fs-negative-has-square-root]]), so $G$ is not defined at all. By contrast the equivalent squared form $ab \le A^{2}$ of [[thm-am-gm]] survives for all real $a, b$, since $A^{2} - ab = (a-b)^{2}/4 \ge 0$; the hypothesis $a, b \ge 0$ is spent exactly on passing from that squared form to the geometric-mean form, which needs a nonnegative arithmetic mean and a real geometric mean.
items.strategy: Evaluate $ab = 4$ and $A = -5/2$ by field arithmetic, and $G = 4^{1/2} = 2$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] since $2 \ge 0$ and $2^{2} = 4$; then $2 > -5/2$ because $-5/2 < 0 < 2$ by [[cor-of-one-positive]] and [[lem-of-sign-rules]]. For the general negative-pair statement, $a, b < 0$ give $ab > 0$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]), so $G = (ab)^{1/2} > 0$, while $A = (a+b)/2 < 0$; the comparison follows from trichotomy. The non-existence clause is [[fs-negative-has-square-root]]. For the closing observation, $4A^{2} - 4ab = (a+b)^{2} - 4ab = (a-b)^{2} \ge 0$ by [[lem-of-square-positive]], so $ab \le A^{2}$; this displays precisely what the nonnegativity hypothesis is needed for, namely that $A$ is itself a mean of nonnegative entries and $(ab)^{1/2}$ a real number. For the square argument, a zero difference gives square $0$ by field multiplication, while a nonzero difference has positive square by the actual hypothesis of [[lem-of-square-positive]]; this verifies nonnegativity including equality rather than misapplying its strict clause at zero.

items.title: Weighted AM-GM needs nonnegative weights summing to $1$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the inequality $\prod_{k<n} x_k^{w_k} \le \sum_{k<n} w_k x_k$ of [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] holds for all positive $x_k$ and all rational weights $w_k$ of sum $1$, or for all rational weights whatsoever. Two witnesses. (i) For $x_0 := x_1 := 4$ and $w_0 := w_1 := 1$, whose sum is $2 \ne 1$: the left-hand side is $4^{1}\cdot 4^{1} = 16$ and the right-hand side is $1\cdot 4 + 1\cdot 4 = 8$, so $16 > 8$. (ii) For $x_0 := 4$, $x_1 := 1/4$, $w_0 := 2$ and $w_1 := -1$, whose sum is $1$ but which contains a negative weight: the left-hand side is $4^{2}\cdot(1/4)^{-1} = 16\cdot 4 = 64$ and the right-hand side is $2\cdot 4 + (-1)\cdot(1/4) = 8 - 1/4 = 31/4$, so $64 > 31/4$. Both hypotheses on the weights — nonnegativity and total mass $1$ — are therefore load-bearing.
items.strategy: Verify each power by [[def-rational-power]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]: $4^{1} = 4$; $(1/4)^{-1} = \big((1/4)^{1}\big)^{-1} = 4$ via the negative-exponent clause of [[def-integer-power]]; and the sums are field computations in $\mathbb{R}$ with the weights read through the embedding $\iota$ of [[lem-of-q-embeds]]. The comparisons $16 > 8$ and $64 > 31/4$ follow from [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules ($64 = 256/4 > 31/4$). In (ii) the weight $-1$ is a legitimate rational by [[def-rationals]]; the point is that [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] requires $w_k \ge 0$, and the example shows the conclusion fails without it even when $\sum_k \iota(w_k) = 1$.

items.title: Minkowski fails for $p = 1/2$: the hypothesis $p \ge 1$ is load-bearing
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the inequality of [[thm-minkowski-finite]] holds for every positive rational $p$. Witness: $p := 1/2$, with the two-entry lists $x_0 := 1$, $x_1 := 0$ and $y_0 := 0$, $y_1 := 1$. The left-hand side $\big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k+y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{1/(1/2)} = \big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k+y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2}$ is $(1+1)^{2} = 4$, while the right-hand side $\big(\sum_{k<2}|x_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2} + \big(\sum_{k<2}|y_k|^{1/2}\big)^{2}$ is $1 + 1 = 2$; so the inequality fails. Every expression is defined: $1/2$ is a positive rational, $|z|^{1/2} = \sqrt{|z|}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] with its supplementary clause $0^{1/2} = 0$, and the outer exponent $1/p = 2$ is an integer power.
items.strategy: Compute: $|1|^{1/2} = 1^{1/2} = 1$ since $1 \ge 0$ and $1^{2} = 1$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-rational-power]]); $|0|^{1/2} = 0$ by the supplementary clause; the two-term sums are $1 + 1 = 2$ by [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]; the outer squares are [[def-integer-power]]. Then $4 > 2$ by [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules, since $4 = 2 + 2 > 2$. The example shows that the conclusion of [[thm-minkowski-finite]] is genuinely false outside its hypothesis $p \ge 1$ and cannot be read as an artefact of undefined powers.

references.locator: Chapter 13 §13.7, Theorem 13.96 and its standing hypothesis 1 < p < ∞, printed pp. 298-299

items.title: Bernoulli fails for $x < -1$: $x = -4$, $n = 3$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** $(1+x)^{n} \ge 1 + nx$ holds for every real $x$ and every natural $n$. Witness: $x := -4$, $n := 3$. Then $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ while $1 + 3x = -11$, so $(1+x)^{3} < 1 + 3x$ and the inequality fails. Two boundary remarks sharpen the failure: at $n = 1$ the two sides agree for every $x$, so the failure needs $n \ge 2$; and at $x = -3$, $n = 3$ the two sides happen to agree ($-8 = -8$), so a witness must be chosen rather than assumed. The hypothesis $x \ge -1$ of [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]] is therefore load-bearing.
items.strategy: Evaluate $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ and $1 + 3x = -11$ by [[def-integer-power]] and field arithmetic; the comparison $-27 < -11$ is equivalent to $0 < 16$, which is [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules of [[lem-of-sign-rules]] and [[lem-of-add-order]]. The two boundary remarks are direct evaluations: $(1+x)^{1} = 1 + x = 1 + 1\cdot x$ by the recursion clause; and $(1-3)^{3} = (-2)^{3} = -8 = 1 + 3(-3)$.

items.title: The iterated rational-power law fails without a positive base: $\big((-3)^{2}\big)^{1/2} = 3 \ne -3$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** the identity $(a^{r})^{s} = a^{rs}$ of [[lem-rational-power-laws]] holds for every real $a$ and all rationals $r, s$ for which both sides are defined. Witness: $a := -3$, $r := 2$, $s := 1/2$. Here $a^{r}$ is the integer power $(-3)^{2} = 9$, so $(a^{r})^{s} = 9^{1/2} = 3$ by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], while $a^{rs} = (-3)^{1} = -3$ is again an integer power; the two sides differ. Both displayed expressions are defined by the library's definitions — only the rational-power step, on the positive base $9$, uses [[def-rational-power]] — so the positivity hypothesis $a > 0$ in [[lem-rational-power-laws]] cannot be dropped. The correct general statement in this case is that $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2} = |a|$ for every real $a$.
items.strategy: $(-3)^{2} = 9$ and $(-3)^{1} = -3$ are [[def-integer-power]] evaluations; $9^{1/2} = 3$ since $3 \ge 0$ and $3^{2} = 9$, by uniqueness in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. The two values differ because $3 \ne -3$. For the closing statement: $a^{2} \ge 0$ so $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2}$ exists, and $|a| \ge 0$ with $|a|^{2} = a^{2}$ by [[lem-of-abs-value]]; uniqueness of the nonnegative square root therefore gives $\big(a^{2}\big)^{1/2} = |a|$, which is precisely the failure of $(a^{r})^{s} = a^{rs}$ when $a < 0$: the left side is $|a|$, not $a$. No integer-power law is being denied — [[lem-power-laws]] permits zero bases for its natural-exponent identities and requires nonzero bases for its extension to all integer exponents — and the counterexample isolates the rational-power hypothesis.

items.title: Five finite proofs of Bernoulli, with rational exponents and the quadratic refinement
items.statement: Five proof routes verify the same integer statement: for $x\ge-1$ and a natural $n$, $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$, with equality exactly when $n\le1$ or $x=0$. The routes are ordinary induction, geometric-sum comparison, an exact nonnegative supporting-line remainder, AM-GM, and a finite binomial/positive-weight expansion. They cover $-1\le x<0$ as well as $x\ge0$; $0^0=1$ is the integer-power convention. In addition, with rational $r$ and $x\ge-1$ (requiring $x>-1$ when $r<0$), $(1+x)^r\ge1+rx$ for $r\ge1$ or $r\le0$, and $(1+x)^r\le1+rx$ for $0\le r\le1$. Equality is exactly $x=0$ or $r\in\{0,1\}$. For rational $r\ge2$, the promised quadratic refinement follows in the stronger form $(1+x)^r\ge1+rx+(r/2)x^2$; hence it holds with any natural coefficient $m$ satisfying $2m\le r$, including the coefficient customarily written $\lfloor r/2\rfloor$. For $1\le r<2$ that floor coefficient is zero and the ordinary bound applies. The stronger refinement has equality exactly when $x=0$ or $r=2$. At $x=-1$, the supplementary clause of [[def-rational-power]] supplies $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$, and [[def-integer-power]] supplies $0^0=1$; negative powers of zero remain undefined. No irrational exponent or exponential/general convexity theorem is asserted.
items.strategy:
Write $y=1+x\ge0$, and use the canonical natural/rational embeddings in every real-field formula. Finite sums below are sums in $\mathbb R$, and all powers in the first five routes have natural exponents. Separate $n=0,1$ and $x=0$ first: these give equality immediately. The remaining case is $n\ge2$, $y\ge0$, $y\ne1$.

Route 1, ordinary induction: use the proved induction argument and equality clause of [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]], not a newly minted duplicate supplier. Its step is $y^{n+1}\ge(1+nx)y=1+(n+1)x+nx^2$, since $y\ge0$ licenses multiplication and $nx^2\ge0$. To see strictness without losing the $y=0$ endpoint, start from $y^2-(1+2x)=x^2>0$. If $y>0$, multiply the strict inequality at $n$ by $y$ and discard $nx^2\ge0$; if $y=0$, the right side $1-n$ is strictly negative for $n\ge2$.

Route 2, geometric-sum comparison: [[lem-power-difference-factorisation]] at bases $1,y$ gives $y^n-1=(y-1)\sum_{k<n}y^k$. If $y>1$, every term is at least $1$ and the $k=1$ term is strictly greater for $n\ge2$, so the sum is $>n$ and multiplication by $y-1>0$ gives the strict Bernoulli bound. If $0\le y<1$, every term is at most $1$ and the $k=1$ term is strictly smaller, including $y=0$; thus the sum is $<n$, and multiplication by the negative $y-1$ reverses the inequality. This proves the full negative-$x$ range, not just the positive range.

Route 3, exact supporting-line remainder: for $n\ge2$, finite distributivity and telescoping give $y^n-1-n(y-1)=(y-1)^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}(n-1-j)y^j$. Derive the identity locally: multiplying the last sum by $y-1$ cancels adjacent coefficients and gives $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}y^k-(n-1)$; multiplying once more gives $y^n-ny+(n-1)$. Each term in the original sum is nonnegative for $y\ge0$ and its constant term is the positive real image of $n-1$. Hence the remainder is positive unless $y=1$. This supplies the power function's supporting line at $1$ directly, without an unproved convexity lemma.

Route 4, AM-GM: apply the existing [[thm-am-gm]] to the $n$ nonnegative entries $y^n,1,\ldots,1$. Their product is $y^n$ and its unique nonnegative $n$th root is $y$. Thus $ny\le y^n+n-1$, precisely Bernoulli. For $n\ge2$, equality forces $y^n=1$ by the theorem's equality clause, and then $y=1$ by [[lem-power-monotone]]. At $y=0$, the theorem still applies to nonnegative entries.

Route 5, finite binomial expansion on both signs: construct real coefficients $b_{0,0}=1$, $b_{0,k}=0$ outside $k=0$, and $b_{n+1,k}=b_{n,k}+b_{n,k-1}$, extending each finite row by zero outside $0\le k\le n$. The existence of successive finite rows is recursion; no combinatorial counting theorem is assumed. Induction gives $b_{n,0}=b_{n,n}=1$, $b_{n,1}=n$, and $b_{n,k}\ge0$, as well as $(u+v)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_{n,k}u^kv^{n-k}$: multiply the preceding finite expansion by $u+v$, shift the index in one sum and use the row recursion. It also gives $k b_{n,k}=n b_{n-1,k-1}$ for $1\le k\le n$: apply the preceding-row identities to $k(b_{n-1,k}+b_{n-1,k-1})$, rewrite the second part as $(k-1)b_{n-1,k-1}+b_{n-1,k-1}$, and combine with the Pascal recursion to obtain $n b_{n-1,k-1}$; handle $k=1,n$ by the endpoint identities. These are identities in the real field after embedding the natural indices. For $x>0$, use $(u,v)=(x,1)$; subtracting the $k=0,1$ terms leaves only nonnegative terms and the $k=n$ term $x^n>0$. For $-1\le x<0$, put $t=-x\in(0,1]$, $y=1-t\ge0$. The same expansion and the coefficient identity give $1=(t+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}$ and $nt=\sum_{k=1}^{n} k b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}$. Subtracting yields $nt-(1-y^n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(k-1)b_{n,k}t^ky^{n-k}\ge0$, strictly so from the $k=n$ term $(n-1)t^n>0$. Thus $y^n>1-nt=1+nx$. This proves the negative range by positive weights, not by illegally dropping alternating-sign terms in the expansion of $(1+x)^n$.

Rational extension: now require $y=1+x>0$. Apply the existing two-term [[thm-weighted-am-gm-rational]] only with positive bases and nonnegative rational weights summing to one. For $r>1$, bases $y^r,1$ and weights $1/r,1-1/r$ give $y\le y^r/r+1-1/r$. For $r<0$, bases $y,y^r$ and weights $-r/(1-r),1/(1-r)$ have geometric product $1$ by [[lem-rational-power-laws]], so $1\le(-ry+y^r)/(1-r)$. For $0<r<1$, bases $y,1$ and weights $r,1-r$ give $y^r\le ry+1-r$. Rearrange each inequality by multiplying positive denominators. Handle $r=0,1$ separately. The weighted supplier does not state an equality clause, so prove the needed strictness: write the two positive rational weights with a common positive natural denominator, repeat each base according to its positive numerator, and apply the strict equality clause of [[thm-am-gm]] to this finite list. If the bases differ the list is not constant and the inequality is strict; clearing the root preserves strictness. The existing proof of the weighted supplier supplies this finite-repetition construction; rational representations and embeddings are recorded in [[lem-rat-positive-denominator]], [[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]] and the rational power laws. In the three cases above the bases differ whenever $y\ne1$ (for negative $r$, equality $y=y^r$ would give $y^{1-r}=1$, contradicting positive-exponent monotonicity). Therefore the asserted equality conditions follow without inventing an equality clause in the supplier. Finally for $r\ge2$ put $s=r/2\ge1$ and $z=y^2>0$, and apply the just-proved rational Bernoulli bound to $z$: $y^r=z^s\ge1+s(z-1)=1+rx+(r/2)x^2$. This uses $z-1>-1$ even when $-1<x<0$, so the full stated $x$ domain is valid. Equality is $s=1$ or $z=1$; because $y>0$, the latter is $y=1$. Replacing $r/2$ by a natural $m\le r/2$ only decreases the nonnegative quadratic term. The floor notation is explanatory, not an invocation of a later floor supplier.

Rational endpoint $x=-1$: the supplementary clause of [[def-rational-power]] sets $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$. Thus for $r\ge1$ the lower inequality is $0\ge1-r$, with equality exactly at $r=1$, and for $0<r\le1$ the reversed inequality is $0\le1-r$, again with equality exactly at $r=1$. At $r=0$ use the existing integer-power convention $0^0=1$, yielding equality. Negative $r$ are excluded here because zero has no inverse. For $r\ge2$ the quadratic bound reduces to $0\ge1-r/2$, equal exactly at $r=2$. This handles the endpoint directly; it does not apply the positive-base weighted theorem at a zero base or silently extend its hypotheses.

references.title: Jim Belk, Convexity, Inequalities, and Norms (Cornell University)
references.locator: Theorem 5, pp. 5-6, weighted AM-GM statement and convexity/exponential proof. Only the statement is corroborating context here: the published rational-weight supplier supplies a complete finite proof, and the Bernoulli consequences below are derived locally. items.title: Five finite AM-GM proofs, with the same sharp equality case
items.statement: For a natural $n\ge1$ and nonnegative reals $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$, put $A=(\sum_{k<n}a_k)/n$ and $G=(\prod_{k<n}a_k)^{1/n}$, using the unique nonnegative root. Five finite routes verify $\prod_{k<n}a_k\le A^n$, equivalently $G\le A$, with equality exactly when every entry is the same. They are Cauchy's forward-backward induction, ordinary induction by sum-preserving replacement, ordinary induction by product-preserving replacement, ordinary induction from the independently proved integer Bernoulli inequality, and binary averaging with geometric-mean padding. The last route stops after one padding argument, rather than the backward descent used by the first. No route invokes a derivative, logarithm, exponential, convergence or an unproved optimization theorem.
items.strategy:
Use [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] for sums and products in $\mathbb R$, and embed natural lengths before field operations. By [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] and [[lem-power-monotone]], proving $\prod a_k\le A^n$ is equivalent to $G\le A$ because $A,G\ge0$. Handle $n=1$ first. If some entry is zero, the product and $G$ are zero, so the inequality is immediate; equality is $A=0$, which by nonnegativity of the summands means every entry is zero. Hence every nontrivial proof route may assume all entries positive, so $A,G>0$ and every division below is legal.

Route 1, Cauchy forward-backward induction: use the existing full proof and equality clause of [[thm-am-gm]], not a duplicate supplier. Its two-entry base is $((u+v)/2)^2-uv=(u-v)^2/4\ge0$, strict when $u\ne v$. Write the doubling lengths as natural numbers $N_0=1$, $N_{j+1}=N_j+N_j$ via [[thm-recursion]]; do not use real-field powers as list lengths. The two-entry bound combines two equal-sized blocks, so $P(N)$ implies $P(N+N)$ with equality only when each half is constant and both half-means agree. The backward step $P(m+1)\Rightarrow P(m)$ appends the $m$-entry arithmetic mean $A$; the augmented mean is still $A$, and cancellation of the positive $A$ from $P_m A\le A^{m+1}$ gives $P_m\le A^m$. Induction gives $N_j\ge j+1$, so $N_n>n$; descent from $N_n$ to $n$ is a finite natural induction on the missing length, exactly as in the published supplier. Appended means do not change whether the original entries are all equal.

Route 2, sum-preserving finite replacement: prove by ordinary induction on $n$ that any positive $n$ entries of sum $n$ have product at most $1$, with equality only for the constant list $1$. The $n=1$ case is immediate. For a nonconstant normalized list, there are entries $u<1<v$: otherwise a list entirely on one side of $1$, with a strict entry, would have sum strictly below or above $n$. Replace these two entries by $1,w$ with $w=u+v-1>0$. The sum stays fixed and the product of the pair strictly increases, since $w-uv=(1-u)(v-1)>0$. Remove the newly fixed $1$; the remaining $n-1$ positive entries have sum $n-1$, so by the induction hypothesis their product is at most $1$. The original product is strictly smaller than the replacement product, hence $<1$. The constant list gives equality. Apply this result to $a_k/A$, whose sum is $n$, and multiply by $A^n$. The replacement is a proof step on a finite list, not an infinite smoothing process or an invocation of existence of a maximum.

Route 3, product-preserving finite replacement: prove by ordinary induction on $n$ that positive $n$ entries of product $1$ have sum at least $n$, with equality only for the constant list $1$. Again the base is immediate. In a nonconstant product-one list there must be $u<1<v$; products of entries all on one side of $1$ are strictly on that side unless they all equal $1$. Replace $u,v$ by $1,uv$, preserving the product while strictly decreasing the sum because $u+v-1-uv=(1-u)(v-1)>0$. Remove the $1$ and apply the $(n-1)$-entry induction hypothesis, proving the original sum is strictly greater than $n$. For the given list, divide every entry by $G$: the product is $1$ since $G^n=\prod a_k$, so $\sum a_k/G\ge n$, giving $A\ge G$, with the stated strict/equality alternatives. This finite induction differs from Route 2 by fixing the product and decreasing the sum.

Route 4, integer Bernoulli induction: this route uses only [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]], whose actual published proof is ordinary induction from order arithmetic; it does not use the AM-GM-derived rational extension in the other new example. Suppose the AM-GM claim and equality clause hold at length $n-1$ with $n\ge2$. Let $B=(\sum_{k<n-1}a_k)/(n-1)>0$, $c=a_{n-1}>0$, $t=c/B>0$, and $h=(t-1)/n>-1$. The induction hypothesis gives $\prod_{k<n}a_k\le B^{n-1}c=B^n t$. The full integer Bernoulli bound at $h,n$ gives $(A/B)^n=(1+h)^n\ge1+nh=t$, so $\prod a_k\le A^n$. Equality forces equality both in the $(n-1)$-entry hypothesis and in Bernoulli. Since $n\ge2$, Bernoulli equality implies $h=0$, thus $c=B$; the former equality makes all remaining entries equal to $B$. Conversely a constant list gives equality. This proves the ordinary inductive step from $1$ to every natural length without circular use of AM-GM in the Bernoulli supplier.

Route 5, binary averaging and geometric-mean padding: derive $P(N_j)$ directly from the square identity in Route 1 by induction on the doubling natural lengths $N_j$, with the full equality clause. In the step split a positive list of length $N+N$ into two length-$N$ halves with means $U,V$. The induction hypothesis bounds the product by $U^N V^N=(UV)^N$, and $UV\le((U+V)/2)^2$ bounds this by the $N+N$ power of the whole mean. Equality implies both halves are constant and $U=V$, hence the whole list is constant. Now choose $N=N_n\ge n$ and append $N-n$ copies of the *geometric* mean $G$ of the original list. The padded product is $G^n G^{N-n}=G^N$. The binary-length inequality gives $G\le(\sum_{k<n}a_k+(N-n)G)/N$, so subtracting $(N-n)G$ yields $nG\le\sum a_k$. Equality in the final inequality is exactly equality for the padded list, so all original entries equal $G$; this remains true if no entries needed appending. There is no backward descent: this uses one finite padding by $G$, in contrast with Route 1's arithmetic-mean descent. The natural length difference and all shifted finite sums are justified by natural-order/discrete arithmetic and the finite-sum laws.

Unpack the definition and record what the data are. items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]. Choose a factorization $Q_{ij}(u,v)=P_{ij}(u,v)P_{ji}(v,u)$ with $P_{ij}\in k[u,v]$ nonzero for all $i
e j$; with (Q1) one may order the pairs and take $P_{ij}=Q_{ij}$, $P_{ji}=1$. On the graded space $\mathrm{Pol}_n:= igoplus_{
u\in I^n}k[x_1,\dots,x_n]e(

u_a=
u_{a+1}$ set $	au_a(f e(
u)):=\dfrac{f-s_a(f)}{x_a-x_{a+1}}e(
u)$, the divided difference operator of the sign convention fixed in relation (6) of [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] (the quotient lies in $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ because $f-s_af$ vanishes at $x_a=x_{a+1}$). Give $\mathrm{Pol}_n$ the grading of [[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]] with $\deg x_ae(
u):=2d_{
u_a}$, together with the summand shifts that make each $	au_a$ homogeneous of degree $-b_{
u_a
u_{a+1}}$ (they exist by the antisymmetry of the increments $-b_{ij}-\deg P_{ij}$ and are unique up to one constant on each fixed-weight sequence orbit). Then every generator acts homogeneously of its degree, the operators satisfy relations (1)-(7), and they define a homomorphism of graded algebras $ho:R_n(Q)	o\mathrm{End}_k^{\mathrm{gr}}(\mathrm{Pol}_n)$, the graded algebra of homogeneous endomorphisms, with $ho(R_n(Q)_m)\,\mathrm{Pol}_{n,d}\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}_{n,d+m}$. **For nonzero $P_{ij}$ this homomorphism is injective.** After localizing at the nonzero polynomials $P_{ij}(x_a,x_b)$ ($
u_a
e
u_b$) and the differences $x_a-x_b$ ($

items.strategy:
Work weightwise, with finitely many sequences. For each unordered pair choose one orientation and set P_ij=Q_ij, P_ji=1. The other factorizations are homogeneous too: in a positively weighted polynomial domain, the extreme weighted degrees of a product cannot cancel, so a homogeneous nonzero product has homogeneous factors. Define the shift of a sequence by a sum over its ordered unequal-colour pairs; exchanging neighboring i,j changes that sum by Delta_ij=-b_ij-deg P_ij. The factorization gives Delta_ji=-Delta_ij, so assigning one half of this pair function in either orientation integrates the increments (without dividing by 2). Equal-colour increments vanish. This proves the claimed homogeneous action and uniqueness on each weight orbit.
For relations, multiplication and permutations verify (1)-(3), far crossings verify (5), and partial_a=(1-s_a)/(x_a-x_(a+1)) satisfies partial_a x_a-x_(a+1)partial_a=1, partial_a x_(a+1)-x_a partial_a=-1 and partial_a^2=0 by applying both sides to an arbitrary polynomial. On an unequal-colour component the two consecutive crossings multiply by P_ji(x_(a+1),x_a)P_ij(x_a,x_(a+1))=Q_ij(x_a,x_(a+1)), proving (4). For (7), three distinct colours give the same product of the three pair factors times the longest permutation. Three equal colours give the common operator sum_(w in S3)sgn(w)w divided by (x_a-x_(a+1))(x_a-x_(a+2))(x_(a+1)-x_(a+2)). The cases with only the first or last two colours equal follow from partial_a(fg)=partial_a(f)g+s_a(f)partial_a(g); the case (i,j,i) gives exactly (Q_ij(x_a,x_(a+1))-Q_ij(x_(a+2),x_(a+1)))/(x_(a+2)-x_a). Thus all relations hold with the already fixed native sign.
For independence, pass only for this argument to the direct sum of rational function fields. Each chosen reduced crossing word has a nonzero coefficient times its permutation, plus terms of strictly smaller permutation length: unequal crossings contribute their nonzero P-factor and equal crossings contribute the nonzero reflection coefficient of partial_a. Distinct field automorphisms are linearly independent over the field: from a shortest purported relation sum c_w w=0, evaluate on fg and subtract one selected w(g) times its evaluation on f; choosing g separated by two different permutations produces a shorter relation, a contradiction. The same argument in each source/destination idempotent block separates its permutation operators. Hence the PBW spanning monomials are independent under this action and the representation is faithful; this is not inferred merely from surjectivity after localization. Once the P-factors and equal-colour differences are inverted, unequal crossings give s_a and equal crossings give s_a=1-(x_a-x_(a+1))partial_a. These generate the skew group algebra, proving precisely the localized isomorphism. Finiteness of each homogeneous component is weightwise and follows from the PBW finite crossing words and positive dot degrees, not from a finite total-dimensional algebra. No AC is used.

items.title: The PBW (monomial) basis theorem for KLR algebras
items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] and fix a reduced-expression system: for each $w\in S_n$ one reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$, and for $
u\in I^n$ put $	au_w:=	au_{i_1}\cdots	au_{i_r}\in R_n(Q)$. Then the monomials $	au_wx_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}e(
u)$, over all $w\in S_n$, $a_1,\dots,a_n\ge0$ and $
u\in I^n$, form a $k$-basis of $R_n(Q)$; equivalently $R_n(Q)$ is a free $k$-module on these monomials, and $R( eta)$ has the corresponding basis. Moreover each $R( eta)$ has finite-dimensional homogeneous components, and the graded dimension of the summand $e(
u)R_n(Q)e(
u')$ is the formal Laurent Hilbert series counting the monomials (bounded below, equivalently the finite sum of the corresponding rational geometric series), so the graded ranks are independent of the parameters $Q$: for each fixed $ eta$, $\dim_kR( eta)_m<\infty$ for all $m$ and $R( eta)_m=0$ for $m\ll0$; if $I$ is finite the same holds for $R_n(Q)$. In particular $R( eta)$ is a locally finite graded algebra ; its degree-zero part need not be one-dimensional (already $x_1	au_1\in R(2\alpha_i)_0$ is a nontrivial idempotent).
items.strategy: Move dots to the right using (6); each correction removes a crossing. Use far commutations and braid moves to turn a nonreduced permutation word into one with an adjacent repeated simple reflection, then use (4) to remove that pair. The correction in (7) also removes crossings. Induction on the number of crossings therefore spans by reduced words followed by dot monomials. Two reduced words for the same permutation are connected by braid/far moves; all their differences have fewer crossings, so they reduce to the fixed chosen word. This Coxeter reduction can be proved for S_n by moving n successively to its destination with adjacent swaps and inducting on n; the inversion number decreases exactly at a deletion and each alternative neighboring sorting choice is a far or three-term braid move. The leading-permutation independence argument proved in the polynomial-representation supplier makes these spanning monomials a basis over k. Their degree is fixed by their labelled crossings and dots, independent of Q. For a fixed weight there are finitely many sequences and permutations, so their crossing degrees have a finite lower bound; the dot degrees are positive. For any fixed total degree only finitely many nonnegative exponent tuples occur. This proves local finiteness and boundedness below, without claiming R(beta)_0=k or comparing the infinite algebra dimension with the quantum half dimension. No AC is used.

items.title: Induction and restriction bimodules for KLR algebras
items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]. For $ eta,\gamma\in Q_+$ put $e( eta,\gamma):=\sum_{
u\in I^{ eta},
u'\in I^{\gamma}}e(
u\ast
u')\in R( eta+\gamma)$, where $
u\ast
u'$ is concatenation; this is an idempotent. The block inclusions $R( eta)\hookrightarrow R( eta+\gamma)$, $r\mapsto r\otimes1$ and $R(\gamma)\hookrightarrow R( eta+\gamma)$, $s\mapsto1\otimes s$ combine into an injective $k$-algebra map $R( eta)\otimes_kR(\gamma)	o R( eta+\gamma)$ whose image is the separated-block subalgebra of the corner $e( eta,\gamma)R( eta+\gamma)e( eta,\gamma)$; the inclusion generally is proper; in the diagram calculus it is horizontal concatenation of diagrams. **Induction** and **restriction** are the functors on graded left modules
$$\mathrm{Ind}_{ eta,\gamma}(M oxtimes N):=R( eta+\gamma)e( eta,\gamma)\otimes_{R( eta)\otimes_kR(\gamma)}(M\otimes_kN),\qquad \mathrm{Res}_{ eta,\gamma}L:=e( eta,\gamma)L,$$
where $\otimes_{R( eta)\otimes_kR(\gamma)}$ is the graded balanced tensor product of [[def-graded-balanced-tensor-product-and-homogeneous-hom]] (total-degree grading) and $M\otimes_kN$ carries the graded tensor product structure. Both functors are additive and degree-zero on degree-zero maps and extend to the direct sums over weights; the $R( eta+\gamma)e( eta,\gamma)$-side is a graded $(R( eta+\gamma),R( eta)\otimes_kR(\gamma))$-bimodule and $e( eta,\gamma)R( eta+\gamma)$ is its right-module counterpart, so the two tensor functors are of the two HA-18 sidedness types. Shifts satisfy $\mathrm{Ind}_{ eta,\gamma}(M\{r\} oxtimes N\{s\})\cong\mathrm{Ind}_{ eta,\gamma}(M oxtimes N)\{r+s\}$ and $\mathrm{Res}_{ eta,\gamma}(L\{r\})\cong(\mathrm{Res}_{ eta,\gamma}L)\{r\}$ ([[lem-graded-balanced-tensor-and-shift-isomorphisms]]). For a partial flag $ eta= eta_1+\cdots+ eta_r$ the iterated functors are defined by iteration, and the parenthesization-independent identification is the one consumed below.
items.strategy: Concatenation sends the two tensor-factor identities to e(beta,gamma), so this is a unital map into that corner, not a unital map into all of R(beta+gamma) unless e=1. Relations within each block are preserved and separated generators commute; this defines the homomorphism. The PBW monomials with permutations contained in S_|beta| x S_|gamma| and arbitrary dots are exactly the images of tensor products of the two PBW bases, so they are independent. Hence the map is injective. Its image need not equal the corner: for beta=gamma=alpha_i the corner is NH_2 while its image is k[x_1,x_2], excluding tau_1. Balanced tensor and idempotent multiplication now give the displayed functors. Each balance relation and outer action preserves degree, and moving shifts through the total tensor grading gives the two stated shift isomorphisms. Iterating block concatenation gives the same idempotent and multiplication map in every parenthesization; the map a tensor (b tensor m) -> ab tensor m and its inverse on balanced tensors prove the associativity identification. No AC is used.

items.title: Nil-Hecke idempotents and divided-power KLR projectives
items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]. For $i\in I$ and $n\ge1$ the subalgebra $R(n\alpha_i)$ is generated by the polynomial subalgebra $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and the crossings $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_{n-1}$ with $\tau_a^2=0$ (because $Q_{ii}=0$), the braid and far commutation relations, and the nil-Hecke dot moves, i.e. it is the nil Hecke algebra of rank $n$; its PBW basis is $\{x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}\tau_w\}_{a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n,w\in S_n}$. Fix a reduced expression $w_0=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{\binom n2}}$ of the longest element and put $\partial_{w_0}:=\tau_{i_1}\cdots\tau_{i_{\binom n2}}$ (independent of the reduced expression). The **divided-power idempotent** is
$$e_{i,n}:=x_1^{n-1}x_2^{n-2}\cdots x_{n-1}\,\partial_{w_0}\in R(n\alpha_i),$$
and its horizontal reflection is $\psi(e_{i,n}):=\partial_{w_0}x_1^{n-1}\cdots x_{n-1}$. Both are nonzero idempotents of degree $0$, and $e_{i,n}\ne0$ because the PBW basis separates the monomials involved. The **divided-power projective** is
$$P_{i,n}:=R(n\alpha_i)\,\psi(e_{i,n})\{-d_i\tbinom n2\},$$
where the shift is the one fixed by the source normalization: as a graded left module $R(n\alpha_i)\psi(e_{i,n})$ is the polynomial representation, it is indecomposable projective, and with this shift one has $R(n\alpha_i)\cong P_{i,n}^{\oplus[n]_{q_i}!}$ with $[n]_{q_i}!=\prod_{a=1}^n\frac{q_i^a-q_i^{-a}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}}$, so $P_{i,n}$ is the unique indecomposable projective summand up to shift and $\mathrm{End}_{R(n\alpha_i)}(P_{i,n})_0=k$. For a divided-power sequence $\theta=i_1^{(n_1)}\cdots i_r^{(n_r)}$ put $\beta=\sum_an_a\alpha_{i_a}$ and $P_\theta:=\mathrm{Ind}(P_{i_1,n_1}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes P_{i_r,n_r})$ along the ordered concatenation of the blocks; then $[P_\theta]$ represents the ordered product of these divided powers; one may reorder only by the proved commuting/Serre relations, and adjacent colours need not commute, and for a single colour $\theta=i^{(n)}$ one has the indecomposability above.
items.strategy: Well-definedness. (i) $R(n\alpha_i)$ is the nil-Hecke algebra by the relations of [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] specialized to $Q_{ii}=0$; the PBW basis of [[thm-klr-pbw-basis-theorem]] is $\{x^a\tau_w\}$, so the span of $\{x^a\tau_w\}$ is everything. (ii) $\partial_{w_0}$ is independent of the reduced expression by the braid relations, and $e_{i,n}^2=e_{i,n}$ is the standard nil-Hecke idempotent computation: $\partial_{w_0}x_1^{n-1}\cdots x_{n-1}$ is the image of the symmetrizing operator, and the divided-difference identities move the $x$'s through the crossings; the same computation gives $\psi(e_{i,n})^2=\psi(e_{i,n})$. (iii) Nonvanishing: in the PBW basis the monomial $x_1^{n-1}\cdots x_{n-1}\tau_{w_0}$ has leading coefficient $1$ and cannot cancel. (iv) The module $R(n\alpha_i)\psi(e_{i,n})$ is the polynomial representation of the nil-Hecke algebra (KL I §2.2), hence projective and indecomposable; the displayed decomposition into $[n]_{q_i}!$ copies after the shift is KL's example computation, and $\mathrm{End}_0=k$ is the degree-0 part of that computation because the full endomorphism algebra of the polynomial column is the symmetric polynomial ring, whose degree-zero part is k. (v) For several colours, $P_\theta$ is defined by induction along the block embedding of [[def-klr-induction-and-restriction-bimodules]]; the class is the ordered induction product; no commuting relation for adjacent colours is used. The nonadjacent commuting and the full Serre relations are proved later in the Serre supplier. The construction is choice-free; no AC is used. For the projective duality used later, P#=HOM_R(P,R)^psi is defined by taking ordinary homogeneous degrees. Evaluation proves (P#)#=P for a finite shifted free module, and restriction to an idempotent summand proves it for every finite projective. It reverses shifts. In one color the polynomial nil-Hecke representation has symmetric-variable endomorphism ring, whose degree-zero part is k. The trace partial_(w0) on the polynomial ring is a symmetric-variable-linear perfect pairing: its matrix on the Artin basis and the complementary monomials is triangular with leading coefficients1, so successive elimination supplies a dual basis. This identifies the left polynomial module with its # dual shifted by 2d_i binom(n,2); the declared shift -d_i binom(n,2) centers it and makes P_(i,n)#=P_(i,n). The same dual-basis calculation decomposes NH_n=End_(symmetric polynomials)(polynomials) into the stated shifted polynomial columns, giving precisely [n]_(q_i)! and the indecomposable-projective assertions. Order of colors is never suppressed. Explicitly, with delta=(n-1,n-2,...,0), partial_(w0)(x^delta)=1: the alternating numerator determinant det(x_r^(n-s)) is the Vandermonde product dividing it, with the fixed native divided-difference sign. Hence e=x^delta partial_(w0) and e'=partial_(w0)x^delta square to themselves; nonzero follows by applying the corresponding operators to x^delta and1. The map NH_n e' -> k[x_1,...,x_n], a e' -> a·1, is the polynomial-column identification because e' projects to symmetric polynomials and e'1=1. Multiplications and divided differences realize all symmetric-linear matrix units using the dual Artin trace basis, so NH_n=End_C(polynomials); this proves injectivity/surjectivity of that identification and End_NH(polynomials)=C in every characteristic. The Artin trace is perfect integrally because triangular coefficient elimination uses diagonal ±1, never division by n!.

items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] and $\beta\in Q_+$.
(i) Every finitely generated graded left $R(\beta)$-module has a decomposition into finitely many indecomposable graded modules, unique as a finite multiset of degree-zero graded isomorphism classes, including the actual shifts of their summands; in particular the category $\mathrm{GrMod}_0R(\beta)$ of finitely generated graded modules has the Krull-Schmidt property.
(ii) Every simple graded $R(\beta)$-module is finite-dimensional, killed by the augmentation ideal $\mathrm{Sym}^+(\beta)$ of the CENTRAL color-symmetric polynomial subalgebra C_beta; up to isomorphism and shift there are finitely many, and each has a projective cover which is finitely generated.
(iii) The split Grothendieck group $K_0(R(\beta))$ of finite graded projective modules is a free $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-module: the classes of the indecomposable finitely generated graded projectives, modulo grading shifts, form a basis with the shift action $q[P]=[P\{1\}]$; equivalently the classes of all finitely generated indecomposable graded projectives form a shift-orbit basis. Similarly $G_0(R(\beta))$ is free on the shift orbits of simple modules, and the Hom pairing of projective covers and simples has diagonal entries dim_k End^0(S_b), with the selected cover/simple shifts, under the Hom convention of [[def-projective-simple-hom-pairing-on-grothendieck-groups]].
items.strategy:
Let C_beta be the color-symmetric polynomial subalgebra: in each sequence corner it is the polynomial ring in elementary symmetric functions of the dots of each color. It is central because unequal crossings permute the dot positions and equal-color divided differences commute with symmetric polynomials. In each color block the polynomial ring is free over its symmetric subring on the Artin monomials x_1^a1 ... x_m^am, 0<=a_r<m-r+1. To prove this, successively adjoin roots of the universal monic polynomial T^m-e_1T^(m-1)+...+(-1)^m e_m: adjoining the first root gives a free rank-m module, division by T-x_1 gives the monic degree-(m-1) polynomial for the next root, and iteration yields precisely these monomials. The resulting root algebra is the polynomial ring in the ordered roots, since its elementary symmetric coefficients recover the e_r; this proves both spanning and independence. Combining these bases with PBW gives R(beta) finite free over C_beta, of rank (|beta|!)^2. Only centrality and this freeness, not an unproved assertion about all projective centers, are needed here.
Every finite graded module is bounded below and locally finite by PBW. Choose finitely many homogeneous generators of degrees d_j; End^0(M) injects into product_j M_(d_j) by evaluation, so is finite-dimensional. Split a nontrivial homogeneous idempotent whenever present; each split lowers the finite dimension of the endomorphism algebra, giving termination. For an indecomposable, every endomorphism has a polynomial minimal equation because its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is finite-dimensional. Factor that equation as T^r g(T) with g(0) nonzero; Bezout yields a polynomial projector separating the nilpotent and invertible parts. Indecomposability forces either nilpotence or invertibility. Thus every f or 1-f is invertible; the nonunits form the unique maximal ideal (if a,b are nonunits and a+b were a unit, multiply by its inverse to contradict this criterion). The usual decomposition comparison sum_j p i_j p_j i=1 then gives a matching invertible summand and cancellation, proving uniqueness in the degree-zero category. No noetherian-ungraded Fitting theorem is substituted for this argument.
For a graded simple S, a positive-degree central c has kernel and image graded submodules; if it acted nontrivially it would be bijective, contradicting the least nonzero degree of the cyclic bounded-below module S. Hence C_beta^+ kills S, and Abar=R(beta)/C_beta^+R(beta) is finite-dimensional. It has finitely many graded simple shift orbits. Projective covers lift genuinely to R, rather than just existing in Abar: take a finite shifted free F surjecting to a projective cover Qbar of S over Abar. In End^0_R(F) the reduction kernel is nilpotent: its entries have positive central degree, and a sufficiently long product has degree exceeding every fixed generator-degree difference minus the lower degree bound of R. Homogeneous lifts of each matrix entry give a surjective reduction map to End^0_Abar(Fbar). A finite nilpotent ideal lifts idempotents: if e^2-e lies in I, replacing e by e-(2e-1)(e^2-e) squares the error ideal; iterate until I^(2^r)=0. Lift the projector onto Qbar; its image Q is projective. The kernel of Q->S is graded superfluous: after reducing by C^+, this is true for Qbar, and a bounded-below graded quotient X=C^+X is zero by its least nonzero degree. Therefore Q is an indecomposable projective cover. Every indecomposable projective is one of these covers up to shift, by reducing and lifting the corresponding split projector and using the same graded Nakayama argument.
Finite decompositions give the free K_0 shift-orbit basis; finite length of finite-dimensional modules gives the G_0 basis. For a projective cover P_b and simple S_c, Hom(P_b,S_c) is zero unless b=c at its selected shift, and then equals End(S_b). The unscaled dual-basis conclusion follows after the separate locally proved maximal-tail supplier establishes absolute simplicity; it is not inferred from finite-dimensional algebra alone. The Krull-Schmidt, cover, basis and weighted Hom clauses above are complete and do not use AC.

items.title: Generic KLR induction and restriction adjunctions preserve projectives
items.statement:
Let Q be the KLR datum above and beta,gamma in Q_+. Put A=R(beta+gamma), B=R(beta) tensor_k R(gamma), e=e(beta,gamma), and c=(beta|gamma). The bimodules eA and Ae are ungraded free respectively as left and right B-modules, of rank binomial(|beta|+|gamma|,|beta|). As GRADED modules they are finite projective direct sums of the appropriate principal idempotent B-modules with labelled shuffle shifts: for each concatenated word xi=nu*eta the right-module summand e(xi)B has shift delta_R(w,xi)=deg(tau_w e(xi)); the left-module summand B e(xi) has shift delta_L(w,xi)=deg(e(xi)tau_w)=delta_R(w,w^-1 xi), using respectively the corresponding right/left minimal shuffle representatives. These degrees depend on the labels; no common shift for an entire B copy is asserted. Ind=Ae tensor_B - and Res=e(-) are exact, commute with internal shifts, and preserve finitely generated graded projectives. Ind is left adjoint to Res. The right adjoint of Res is Coind=HOM_B(eA,-), with (a f)(t)=f(ta), and the exact generic second-adjunction formula is
Coind_(beta,gamma)(M boxtimes N) ~= Ind_(gamma,beta)(N boxtimes M){c}.
Thus the second adjunction reverses the two blocks and has the displayed shift; same-ordered unshifted biadjunction is not asserted. The formula is an isomorphism of functors and holds on arbitrary graded B-modules after interpreting the right side with the block-flip equivalence. This is distinct from the cyclotomic E_i/F_i biadjunction theorem. Moreover, e_(beta,gamma) R(beta+gamma) e_(beta',gamma') has a finite Mackey filtration indexed by nonnegative four-block weight matrices ((a,b),(c,d)) with row sums beta,gamma and column sums beta',gamma'. Its subquotient is the corresponding composite four-block restriction, flip of the middle blocks and induction bimodule, shifted by -(b|c). The same statement holds for arbitrary numbers of blocks.
items.strategy:
Choose minimal shuffle representatives and fixed reduced words. Every permutation has a unique parabolic-times-minimal-shuffle decomposition with additive length, so the PBW basis identifies eA as the sum over words (nu,eta) and minimal shuffles of its appropriate shifted left principal modules B e(nu*eta), and horizontal reflection gives the right principal modules e(nu*eta)B for Ae. Each shuffle crossing degree is computed on its actual labelled word. Their ungraded sums combine to binomial many copies of B; their graded sums are finite projective, generally not shifted-free copies of B. Idempotent multiplication is exact and tensor with a projective right module is exact; projective summands of finite shifted free modules stay projective under restriction by the first freeness claim and under induction because Ae is a projective left A-module. The balanced map a tensor m -> (l -> appropriate image) or directly the universal property of tensor gives Hom_A(Ae tensor_B X,L)=Hom_B(X,eL). The right-adjoint bijection is Hom_B(eL,X)=Hom_A(L,HOM_B(eA,X)), with maps f -> (l -> (t -> f(tl))) and g -> (el -> g(l)(e)); these are inverse and preserve degree.
For the second-adjunction bimodule, let y be the longest block shuffle, of degree -c, and e'=e(gamma,beta). Use PBW to project eAe' to its y coefficient, interpreted in B by identifying the reversed blocks. Denote this B-balanced coefficient map by t. Dot slides and block crossing slides preserve the longest-shuffle coefficient; all dot/braid correction terms have shorter shuffle length and vanish under t. Thus t is balanced for the block-flip equivalence. The map Ae' -> HOM_B(eA,B), z -> (u -> t(uz)), has degree c. Pair the left and right shuffle bases by complementary shuffles. Ordered by shuffle length, their coefficient matrix is triangular with diagonal units 1 (equal-colour signs are absorbed in the reflected chosen words); to see this, a complementary pair is the reduced longest shuffle and every noncomplementary pair either misses its permutation or reduces by a quadratic/braid correction to smaller length. Finite triangular elimination gives an inverse over B, without localization or a central Frobenius trace. Hence HOM_B(eA,B) ~= Ae'{c} with the right B action transported by block flip. Since eA is finite projective over B, evaluation identifies HOM_B(eA,B) tensor_B X with HOM_B(eA,X). This proves the functorial formula on all graded modules. The longest-shuffle functional and the triangular basis calculation are the local content of Lauda-Vazirani Theorem2.2/§2.3, read on the full source, translated to the fixed native sign and the actual homogeneous-Hom convention. No cyclotomic trace is imported and no AC is used. For Mackey, choose reduced double-coset representatives for the row and column block permutation groups. Partition the PBW monomials of the corner by their four intersection blocks, and filter by crossing length of these representatives. The span of preceding double cosets is a bimodule: moving a row/column block generator across a representative either remains in its double coset with an internal block permutation, or uses a quadratic/braid correction removing crossings and hence lies earlier. In the associated quotient these lower terms vanish. The remaining monomials are exactly tensor products of the PBW bases for the four blocks, the balanced row/column induced bimodules, and the unique minimal crossing of the two middle blocks. This basis bijection defines inverse maps from the composite four-block bimodule to the quotient, so it proves the filtration formula, not only a character identity. The crossed colors are precisely b and c, giving degree -(b|c). Iterating the same permutation argument gives the multi-block version. This local Mackey supplier is the one used by the maximal-tail proof and the twisted bialgebra proof.

items.title: The KLR Cartan (graded Hom) pairing on the projective Grothendieck group
items.statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] and let $\psi$ be the horizontal-reflection anti-involution of $R(\beta)$ (reflection of diagrams about a horizontal axis, which reverses the order of crossings); for a finite graded left module $P$ let $P^{\psi}$ be the right module with $p\cdot r:=\psi(r)p$. For $\beta\in Q_+$ define the **Cartan pairing**
$$(\ [P],[Q]\ )_\beta:=\mathrm{gdim}_k\bigl(P^{\psi}\otimes_{R(\beta)}Q\bigr)\in\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\cdot(\beta)_q,\qquad (\beta)_q:=\prod_i\prod_{a=1}^{\beta_i}\frac1{1-q^{2d_i a}},$$
for finite graded projective modules $P,Q$, where $\mathrm{gdim}_kM=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}q^m\dim_kM_m$; the tensor is over the graded algebra with the total-degree grading ([[def-graded-balanced-tensor-product-and-homogeneous-hom]]). Equivalently define the **hom pairing** $([P],[Q])'_\beta:=\mathrm{gdim}_k\operatorname{HOM}_{R(\beta)}(P,Q)$ ([[thm-projective-hom-pairing-is-additive-and-graded-sesquilinear]]); then $([P],[Q])'_\beta=([P^\#],[Q])_\beta$ for the graded left projective $P^\#:=\operatorname{HOM}_{R(\beta)}(P,R(\beta))^\psi$. Thus the tensor form is symmetric and bilinear; the Hom form is conjugate-linear in its first variable and linear in its second. For the tensor form $([P],q[Q])=q([P],[Q])$ and $(q[P],[Q])=q([P],[Q])$, while the Hom form obeys $h(q^r[P],q^s[Q])=q^{s-r}h([P],[Q])$. Both are additive, vanish on different-weight components, and descend to $K_0(R)=\bigoplus_\beta K_0(R(\beta))$: the tensor form is A-bilinear and the Hom form is A-sesquilinear (first variable conjugate-linear), with values in $\mathbb Q(q)$, more precisely the localization adjoining all $(1-q_i^{2a})^{-1}$; the values lie in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\cdot(\beta)_q$ because $P^\psi\otimes_{R(\beta)}Q$ is a finite free graded module over the central color-symmetric polynomial subalgebra C_beta. Normalization: $([P_i],[P_i])=(1-q^{2d_i})^{-1}=(1-q_i^2)^{-1}$ and $([P_i],[P_j])=0$ for $i\ne j$.
items.strategy: Well-definedness: $P^\psi\otimes_{R(\beta)}Q$ is a graded vector space of finite dimension in each degree and bounded below, so $\mathrm{gdim}$ is a well-defined element of $\mathbb Z((q))$; freeness over the polynomial/center subalgebra (KL I §2.5, using the basis [[thm-klr-pbw-basis-theorem]]) upgrades it to $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\cdot(\beta)_q$. Symmetry of the first pairing is the commutativity $P^\psi\otimes_{R}Q\cong Q^\psi\otimes_RP$ of the balanced tensor, and the exact comparison is the evaluation isomorphism $\operatorname{HOM}_R(P,R)\otimes_RQ\to\operatorname{HOM}_R(P,Q)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto(p\mapsto f(p)v)$. It is an isomorphism for a shifted free P by direct computation and hence for every finite graded projective summand. Twisting by psi makes its first tensor factor $(P^\#)^\psi$, proving $h(P,Q)=T(P^\#,Q)$. The total Hom degree convention here is HA-18's actual degree d, so h(P{r},Q{s})=q^(s-r)h(P,Q); no scalar conjugation of the tensor value is valid. In rank one h(R,R)=T(R,R)=1/(1-q_i^2), already disproving that false comparison; the additive and sesquilinear properties are HA-19's pairing theorems transported along the identifications of [[lem-klr-module-categories-are-krull-schmidt-with-shift-orbit-bases]]. The generator values follow from $P_i=R(\alpha_i)=k[x_1]$, $P_i^\psi\otimes_{R(\alpha_i)}P_i\cong k[x_1]$ as a graded vector space with $\deg x_1=2d_i$ (KL I Proposition 3.3 and the computation $([P_i],[P_i])=\mathrm{gdim}(k[x])=(1-q^2)^{-1}$ in the simply-laced normalization). The convention for $\psi$ is recorded explicitly because it fixes the sign of the shift of the hom form; no AC is used. For the stated rational denominator, the central polynomial-freeness calculation in the local Krull-Schmidt supplier shows R is finite free over C_beta. Tensoring corner projectives produces the corner eR f, a direct summand of this finite C_beta-free module; general finite projectives give another finite graded C_beta-projective summand. Every such summand is graded free: lift a homogeneous k-basis of V/C_beta^+V to obtain a surjection from a finite shifted free C_beta-module (the cokernel vanishes by the least-degree argument); its projective splitting has kernel K with K/C_beta^+K=0, which also vanishes by that argument. Its Hilbert series is therefore a finite Laurent polynomial times gdim C_beta=product_(i,a)(1-q_i^(2a))^-1. This proves the denominator and local finiteness without using the finite-dimensional HA19 theorem on an infinite algebra.

items.title: Maximal KLR tails give a unique induction head and absolute simple modules
items.statement: Let R be any graded KLR datum in this page over any field k. For a finite-dimensional graded module M of weight beta set epsilon_i(M)=max{r:e(beta-r alpha_i,r alpha_i)M!=0}. If S is simple and r=epsilon_i(S)>0, there is a simple graded R(beta-r alpha_i)-module N with epsilon_i(N)=0 such that Delta_i^r S=N boxtimes L(i^r), where L(i^r) is the unique nil-Hecke simple up to shift. Conversely, for any such N, Ind(N boxtimes L(i^r)) has a unique simple graded head S, appearing once as a composition factor, with epsilon_i(S)=r and Delta_i^r S=N boxtimes L(i^r). Every other composition factor has smaller i-tail. The graded simples of every R(beta) remain simple without grading and are absolutely simple; all ordinary endomorphisms are k and nonzero homogeneous endomorphisms have degree0. The classes of normalized simples and their projective covers are therefore unscaled dual shift-orbit bases for the projective/simple Hom pairing. For each beta there is a finite family of ordered divided-power words Y_b whose normalized projective classes pair triangularly with the simple classes, with diagonal entries1 after choosing the simple grading shifts. Thus the selected [P(Y_b)] form an A-basis of K_0(R(beta)); arbitrary divided words span, but need not be a basis. The identical statements hold for maximal FIRST-color blocks, with epsilon_i^L(M)=max{r:e(r alpha_i,beta-r alpha_i)M!=0}, restriction Delta_i^(L,r), and induction Ind(L(i^r) boxtimes N).
items.strategy:
First the nil-Hecke central quotient is a graded matrix algebra Mat_(r!) k, proved by the explicit Artin polynomial/trace matrix units. Its defining simple L(i^r) is absolutely simple and its divided-projective idempotent has a one-dimensional image. A finite-dimensional simple module over R(mu) tensor NH_r is killed by the positive symmetric tail center (a nonzero central positive map would be bijective, contradicting its least degree), so the matrix units write it uniquely as N boxtimes L(i^r), with N a graded simple R(mu)-module, up to shift. This matrix description works over every field and needs no prior absolute-simplicity claim about N.
Let r be the maximal tail of a graded simple S. Choose a simple submodule N boxtimes L(i^r) of the finite-dimensional Delta_i^r S. If N supported a word ending in i, concatenating any nil-Hecke tail word would give a word of S ending in i^(r+1), a contradiction. Hence epsilon_i(N)=0. Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map M=Ind(N boxtimes L(i^r))->S, necessarily surjective. In the Mackey filtration of Delta_i^r M, any shuffle bringing a positive number t of i-colors from the first factor into the final tail contains Delta_i^t N and is zero. The only surviving filtration quotient keeps the whole last block; it is N boxtimes L(i^r), with zero crossing shift. Consequently Delta_i^r M is precisely this simple B-module and M has no tail greater than r. This is an actual one-surviving-quotient calculation, not a semisimplicity assumption on restrictions.
Every nonzero quotient Q of M has nonzero defining corner: if eQ=0, the composite map Ae tensor_B (N boxtimes L)->Q is zero by the tensor/Res adjunction; hence Q=0. The finite graded semisimple head of M therefore has only one simple summand, once, because its exact e-restriction is a quotient of the simple eM. Its unique simple head is S. The surjective map eM->eS between nonzero simple B-modules is an isomorphism. Exactness gives e ker(M->S)=0, so every other composition factor has smaller tail; in particular S occurs only once. This proves both implications and the maximal-restriction formula in the fixed grading. No reverse-block second adjunction is required.
Prove underlying and absolute simplicity by induction on root height. The rank-zero module is k. For S of positive height choose i with nonzero last-color support, so r>0 and N has smaller height. By induction N and L(i^r) are absolutely simple, hence eS=N boxtimes L(i^r) is an ordinary simple module with endomorphism ring k. The ordinary tensor simplicity can be seen from the full k-matrix action of each factor: tensoring their matrix units gives every matrix unit on the tensor product. If U is any ungraded R-submodule of S, eU is either0 or eS. In the second case U=S because S is generated by eS. In the first case the R-submodule generated by the homogeneous components u_d of vectors u in U is a nonzero graded submodule killed by e: for every homogeneous a, a u lies in U and e a u=0; comparing its degrees gives e a u_d=0 for every d; graded simplicity would make it S, contradicting eS!=0. Thus S is simple ungraded. Any R-endomorphism is determined by its action on eS, so End_R(S) injects into End_B(eS)=k and equals k.
For completeness this implies absolute simplicity without assuming k algebraically closed: if a unital algebra acts simply on a finite-dimensional k-space V with commutant k, it realizes every k-linear matrix. Prove by induction on m that any m linearly independent vectors u_1,...,u_m can be sent to arbitrary target vectors by one algebra element. The image in V^m projects surjectively onto V^(m-1) by induction. Its kernel in the last coordinate is either0 or V by simplicity. If V, the image is all V^m. If0, the image is the graph of an algebra-linear map V^(m-1)->V, necessarily sum_j lambda_j v_j since the commutant is k; applying the identity algebra element forces u_m=sum_j lambda_j u_j, a contradiction. Taking a basis proves the full matrix image, which remains simple after every field extension. Finite support also makes an invertible homogeneous endomorphism of nonzero degree impossible.
Choose a cyclic order of the finite color support and recursively strip maximal tails, producing a finite tuple Y_b for each simple. Two simples with the same tuple agree by the just-proved unique-head recursion. Form P(Y_b) from the reverse ordered normalized divided blocks. Its homogeneous Hom to S_c is the corresponding product of divided idempotents acting on S_c. Compare the tuples lexicographically: if Y_b>Y_c, at the first different entry the required tail is larger than the maximal tail of the successively stripped simple S_c, so the corner is zero. When they agree, every maximal restriction is the simple tensor just proved and each nil-Hecke divided idempotent reduces its tail to one dimension; induction reaches k. Thus the diagonal Hom is a single Laurent monomial with coefficient1. Shift each S_b to make its diagonal1. The finite matrix is triangular over A=Z[q,q^-1] with diagonal1. Krull-Schmidt expresses P(Y_b) in projective-cover classes, and the perfect cover/simple Hom pairing (now End(S)=k) identifies this with that triangular matrix. Successive integral triangular elimination proves the selected classes are an A-basis. This completes integral surjectivity independently of PBW ranks and parameter-flatness. The source-linked KL I3.6–3.20 argument is expanded here in full, including its omitted maximal-tail and arbitrary-field steps; the Mackey/PBW and nil-Hecke calculations are the earlier local suppliers. No AC is used. For the first-color version use the defining idempotent e(r alpha_i,mu) and M=Ind(L(i^r) boxtimes N), with epsilon_i^L(N)=0. A simple submodule of the maximal first-block restriction has this form by the same nil-Hecke matrix units; any first-color support of N would extend the maximal first block, so it vanishes. In its Mackey restriction every nontrivial shuffle bringing a positive number of i-colors from N into the first block contains Delta_i^(L,t)N and is zero. The sole uncrossed quotient is L(i^r) boxtimes N, with shift0. The defining-corner generation and exact-head proof are unchanged. Thus all first-block assertions are proved directly; no unsigned star-crystal preservation is assumed.
