## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A PID $R$ with prime $\pi$, residue field $F$, $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ with $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$, the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)$ and its Weyl modules with Jantzen filtrations ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and the virtual Weyl and Specht symbols ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).

[F1] ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]]) The Gram determinant of $W^{\lambda}$ on its $\nu$-weight space equals $q^{N}$ times the hook-ratio product $\prod_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],b<c}([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}/[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})^{d_{\mu}(\dots)}$; under $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ every factor is nonzero in the domain $R$.

[F2] ([[lem-jantzen-layer-dimensions-equal-the-gram-determinant-valuation]]) The total dimension of the positive Jantzen layers on a non-degenerate form equals the $\pi$-adic valuation of its Gram determinant.

[F3] ([[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]) Equality of all semistandard weight-space dimensions forces equality in the Grothendieck group of $S_F(d,n)$-modules.

[F4] The balanced displacement removes the $h_{ac}$-strip and adds the same number of boxes, preserving degree; its sign is the beta sorting sign ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

[F5] The exact Schur functor has integral corner isomorphism and exact restricted form factor $1$, with $e^*=e$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]). Filtration transport is proved below, rather than assumed from exactness.

[F6] Source results (Mathas, Theorem 5.31 and Corollary 5.32, printed pp. 58-60): the Jantzen sum formula for the q-Schur algebra and its transport to the Hecke side, with the coefficient $\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})$ and the virtual symbols.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work on a fixed weight space of the lifted free Weyl module. Every hook quantum integer is nonzero because its index is at most $n$ and $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in the domain. The balanced Gram formula [F1] gives its determinant, and the unit power of $\hat q$ has valuation zero. The Jantzen Gram-valuation lemma [F2] thus gives the sum of positive filtration-submodule dimensions as $$\sum_{(a,b),(a,c),\ b<c}  (\nu_\pi([h_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h_{ac}]_{\hat q}))  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c).$$ The signed number is exactly the weight dimension of the corresponding balanced virtual Weyl symbol, including zero and cutoff cases. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to every weight. The Weyl weight-character matrix is unitriangular, so [F3] detects equality of Grothendieck classes and proves part 1. These are classes of the filtration submodules $W_F^\lambda(i)$, not their successive quotients and not simply the radical class. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Establish filtration transport before applying the exact functor. On the lifted Weyl module $W$, the identity $e^*=e$ makes $We\perp W(1-e)$. For $x\in We$ and every $i\ge0$, pairing $x$ with all of $W$ is divisible by $\pi^i$ exactly when its pairing with $We$ is. Thus $W(i)e=(We)(i)$. Reducing modulo $\pi$ commutes with the direct summand projection, giving $W_F(i)e=(We)_F(i)$. The actual corner isomorphism and factor-$1$ form identity [F5] identify the latter with the Murphy Specht filtration. Applying the exact functor to the proved Weyl-class identity therefore transports each submodule and every signed term, proving part 2 even when a reduced cell form is identically zero. For the ordinary convention, apply the same $\theta$ to both modules and conjugate the labels; the independently proved Laurent-unit form factor preserves these divisibility filtrations as well. [F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Explain the valid multiplicity information. The Weyl form has nonzero simple head, $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}W_F$, and $W_F(i)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}W_F$ for $i>0$. Consequently for $\nu\ne\lambda$ its actual multiplicity in $W_F$ is its radical multiplicity, bounded above by its multiplicity in the whole positive sum. This whole-sum multiplicity is positive if and only if that factor occurs in the radical, since the first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it. No such conclusion is drawn from an individual positive or negative Weyl coefficient before cancellation. All claims follow from steps 1.1-3.1 and this submodule inclusion. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: General type-A decomposition numbers remain unsolved
items.statement:
The two preceding constraints on the decomposition matrix of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are real but limited, and neither solves the general problem.

(i) Dominance unitriangularity ([[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]]) determines only the diagonal entries $d_{\mu\mu}=1$ and the vanishing region $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$; it gives no value for an off-diagonal entry.

(ii) The q-Schaper/Jantzen sum formula ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]]) is an identity for the sum of the positive Jantzen filtration submodules. Its individual signed hook terms are not multiplicity bounds. After the whole virtual sum is expanded in simple classes and all cancellations are performed, its nonnegative simple coefficients bound the corresponding radical composition multiplicities from above; it neither determines a general multiplicity nor produces a positive combinatorial rule.

Special coefficient regimes and low-rank calculations determine additional entries (canonically based, weight-one, and small-$n$ cases), but the classification of irreducible Specht modules in arbitrary positive characteristic is a known open problem, and no general closed formula for the decomposition numbers of $S_n$ in a fixed positive characteristic is claimed anywhere on this page. This remark records the boundary; it carries no proof obligation and no choice principle.
items.strategy: Prose Remark; no argument phase or proof claim. Correct boundary: signed hook terms are not bounds; only complete simple-class positive-submodule coefficients bound radical multiplicity.

items.title: Residue sequences need not separate when e is at most n
items.statement: The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and the extended quantum-integer identity gives $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$, since $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$. Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. The difference of the two putative separating eigenvalues at $k=2$ is $[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$. Thus interpolation cannot distinguish the two tableaux: a formula that excludes equal values may still define a polynomial, but it is not a separating projector for these two labels. The attempted generator formula has axial distance $\rho=2$ and $[\rho]_{-1}=0$. In fact $L_2$ has a nontrivial Jordan block on this cell, so this cell has no simultaneous JM-eigenbasis. This explicit example shows that the uniform separation hypothesis $e>n$ cannot be dropped; it does not claim that every individual cell at every parameter with $e\le n$ lacks a seminormal basis.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb C$, $q=-1\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, $n=3$, the standard tableaux $s,t$ of shape $(2,1)$ above, and the q-integers of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

[F1] ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) $e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$: the least $m\ge1$ with $[m]_{-1}=0$ is $m=2$, since $[2]_{-1}=1+q=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=1\ne0$.

[F2] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) The q-content value of an entry is $[\operatorname{content}]_q$ with $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$ and $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$; at $q=-1$ one has $[1]_{-1}=1$ and $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$.

[F3] ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]) Under the hypothesis $e>n$ the q-content sequence determines the standard tableau, and the denominators of the spectral projectors are nonzero.




## Counterexample

1.1 Contents of the two tableaux: for $s$ with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,1,-1$; for $t$ with rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,-1,1$. [given]

2.1 Collision: by [F1] and [F2], $[2]_{-1}=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1$; hence $[\operatorname{content}_s(1)]_{q}=0=[\operatorname{content}_t(1)]_q$, $[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q$ and $[\operatorname{content}_s(3)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(3)]_q$, so the two q-content sequences coincide even though $s\ne t$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Interpolation and axial distance. The eigenvalue difference that would be needed to distinguish $s$ and $t$ at $k=2$ is $1-1=0$. Equal-value exclusion in a polynomial product does not make its literal denominators zero; it instead loses the factor that could distinguish these tuples. No polynomial in the JM operators can provide the two distinct joint-eigenvalue labels used in the separated-range construction. For the swap of $2$ and $3$, $\rho=1-(-1)=2$ and $[2]_{-1}=0$, so the displayed separated-range generator formula is undefined here. [step 2.1, F1, F3]

4.1 Verify the failure of a JM-eigenbasis on this cell directly. Put $m_s=1+T_1$ and $m_t=(1+T_1)T_2$ modulo the higher row-shape ideal. The quadratic relation gives $m_sT_1=q m_s$. The higher row symmetrizer is $1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$, so its vanishing in this cell gives $m_tT_1=-m_s-m_t$. At $q=-1$, since $L_2=q^{-1}T_1=-T_1$, it follows that $m_sL_2=m_s$ and $m_tL_2=m_s+m_t$. Thus $L_2-I$ is nonzero and $(L_2-I)^2=0$ on this two-dimensional cell. It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, so a simultaneous JM-eigenbasis cannot exist on this cell. Together with step 2.1 this supplies the claimed concrete boundary counterexample, without making a universal claim about all cells outside the separated range. [given, F2, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: The Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements through rank four
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. In $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) for $n\ge4$ are $$L_1=0,\quad L_2=q^{-1}T_{(1,2)},\quad L_3=q^{-1}T_{(2,3)}+q^{-2}T_{(1,3)},\quad L_4=q^{-1}T_{(3,4)}+q^{-2}T_{(2,4)}+q^{-3}T_{(1,4)},$$ and in general $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$. For the standard tableau $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3&4\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ of shape $(3,1)$ the contents of the entries $k=1,2,3,4$ are $0,-1,1,2$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), so the diagonal eigenvalues of $L_1,\dots,L_4$ on the Murphy vector $m_t$ are $[0]_q=0$, $[-1]_q=-q^{-1}$, $[1]_q=1$ and $[2]_q=1+q$; the triangular correction terms $\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ are present in general ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) in the Murphy basis, even in the semisimple range. In the separated range, replacing $m_t$ by the seminormal vector $f_t$ removes these correction terms, as proved in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]. At $q=1$ the four elements specialize to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy elements $X_1=0$, $X_2=(1\,2)$, $X_3=(1\,3)+(2\,3)$, $X_4=(1\,4)+(2\,4)+(3\,4)$ and the eigenvalues to $0,-1,1,2$, the standard contents of $t$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^{\times}$, the Hecke algebra $H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]), the content vector of a standard tableau ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), and the q=1 specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

[F1] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$; $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$, $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, and $[m]_1=m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$.

[F2] ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) $m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ on the Murphy cell module, so the displayed values are the diagonal entries and the correction terms are as stated.



## Verification

1.1 Substitution: in [F1], for $k=1$ the sum is empty, giving $L_1=0$; for $k=2$ it has the single term $q^{1-2}T_{(1,2)}=q^{-1}T_{(1,2)}$; for $k=3$ it has $q^{-1}T_{(2,3)}+q^{-2}T_{(1,3)}$; and for $k=4$ it has $q^{-1}T_{(3,4)}+q^{-2}T_{(2,4)}+q^{-3}T_{(1,4)}$, matching the displayed list. [given, F1]

1.2 Contents: reading the tableau $t$ with rows $(1,3,4)$ and $(2)$, the node of $1$ is $(1,1)$ with content $1-1=0$, the node of $2$ is $(2,1)$ with content $1-2=-1$, the node of $3$ is $(1,2)$ with content $2-1=1$ and the node of $4$ is $(1,3)$ with content $3-1=2$; by definition $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ is the q-integer of these contents. [given, F1]

2.1 Eigenvalues: by [F1], $[0]_q=0$, $[-1]_q=-q^{-1}[1]_q=-q^{-1}$, $[1]_q=1$ and $[2]_q=1+q$; substituting into the triangularity formula [F2] gives the stated diagonal eigenvalues $0,-1,1,2$ up to the q-powers $-q^{-1},1,1+q$. The correction terms are exactly the sum $\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ of [F2] and are not asserted to vanish outside the semisimple range. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2]

3.1 Specialization: setting $q=1$ in the displayed formulas turns $L_k$ into $\sum_{j<k}(j\,k)=X_k$ by the specialization isomorphism of [[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]] and [F1], giving $X_1=0$, $X_2=(1\,2)$, $X_3=(1\,3)+(2\,3)$ and $X_4=(1\,4)+(2\,4)+(3\,4)$; the eigenvalues $[m]_1=m$ become $0,-1,1,2$, the contents of $t$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1] ∎

items.title: The Murphy cellular basis of H(S_3)
items.statement: Work over any commutative ring $R$ with $q\in R^{\times}$ and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_3)$ with generators $T_1,T_2$, the braid relation $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ and quadratics $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The Murphy cellular basis ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]) is indexed by the partitions $(3),(2,1),(1^3)$ ordered by dominance. Explicitly, with $*$ the antiautomorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]): (a) for $\lambda=(3)$, $\mathrm{Std}(3)=\{s\}$ and $m_{ss}=m_{(3)}=1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$; (b) for $\lambda=(2,1)$, $\mathrm{Std}(2,1)=\{t,u\}$ with $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$, $u=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$, and $m_{(2,1)}=1+T_1$ (the row symmetrizer of $S_{(2,1)}=\langle(1\,2)\rangle$), so that $m_{tt}=1+T_1$, $m_{tu}=(1+T_1)T_2$, $m_{ut}=T_2(1+T_1)$ and $m_{uu}=T_2(1+T_1)T_2$; (c) for $\lambda=(1^3)$, $\mathrm{Std}(1^3)=\{v\}$ and $m_{vv}=m_{(1^3)}=1$. In total $1+4+1=6=3!=|S_3|$ elements; the middle cell carries $|\mathrm{Std}(2,1)|^2=4$ basis elements, its two off-diagonal elements satisfy $m_{tu}^*=m_{ut}$, and the largest cell is spanned by $m_{ss}$, illustrating the cellular anti-involution. At $q=1$ this is the Murphy basis of the group algebra $\mathbb Z[S_3]$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).
items.strategy: Read the elements off the definitions: $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ (so $m_{(3)}$ has six terms, $m_{(2,1)}=1+T_1$ has two, $m_{(1^3)}=1$ has one) and $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ with the distinguished representatives $d(t)=1$, $d(u)=s_2$. The products are then computed directly from $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$ and the braid relation, and they match Mathas's Example 2.2(ii). No choice is used.

items.title: The q-Schaper calculation for (3,2) at e = 2
items.statement:
Take $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]_{(1+\hat q)}$, the prime element $\pi=1+\hat q$ (so that $F=\mathbb C$ and $q:=\hat q+\pi R$ specialises to $-1$, giving $e=2$), and $\lambda=(3,2)$, $n=5$. Evaluating the q-Schaper virtual sums ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula, thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product, thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules, lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form, lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening, thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) with the hook valuations $
u_\pi([2]_{\hat q})=
u_\pi([4]_{\hat q})=1$, $
u_\pi([3]_{\hat q})=
u_\pi([1]_{\hat q})=0$ gives, in the source's normalisation, $$\sum_{i>0} igl[W^{(3,2)}_F(i) igr]= igl[W^{(3,1^2)}_F igr]+ igl[W^{(2^2,1)}_F igr]- igl[W^{(1^5)}_F igr],\qquad \sum_{i>0} igl[S^{(3,2)}_F(i) igr]=2 igl[D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}} igr].$$ Further Jantzen calculations give $W^{(1^5)}_F=L^{(1^5)}_F$, $W^{(2^2,1)}_F=L^{(2^2,1)}_F$ and $W^{(3,1^2)}_F\sim L^{(3,1^2)}_F+L^{(2^2,1)}_F+L^{(1^5)}_F$, so at the level of the sum formula alone one gets $d_{(3,2),(3,1^2)}=1$ and only the bound $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}\in\{1,2\}$. The extra dimension/filtration argument on the Specht side gives $S^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{M}}\cong D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}}$ (both sides have dimension $5$), whence $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}=1$: the virtual sum alone did not determine the entry. Translated to the Dipper-James convention of this page by conjugating and applying the same $	heta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), this reads $S^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong D^{(3,2)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$, while the partition $(2,2,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so its own labelled cell-form quotient vanishes, $D^{(2,2,1)}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=0$. The computed entry is consistent with the dominance bound $d_{\lambda\mu}
e0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$ of [[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The DVR $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]_{(1+\hat q)}$, unit $\hat q$, uniformizer $\pi=1+\hat q$, residue field $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, $e=2$, and $d\ge5$. All displayed Weyl modules are for this $S_F(d,5)$.

[F1] The corrected **balanced** sum formula and its signs are [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The weight Gram product is [[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]].

[F2] $v([h]_{\hat q})$ is $1$ for $h=2,4$ and $0$ for $h=1,3,5$; the even roots are simple over $\mathbb C$. The Weyl forms have nonzero simple heads and their first reduced Jantzen submodule is the radical.

[F3] The exact integral corner identifies each Weyl corner and its form with the Murphy cell and form, and identifies each simple image with its Murphy form quotient, including zero images ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], steps 1.1–5.1). Nonzero images are pairwise distinct absolutely simple modules by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. The specific zero forms needed here are proved below from the actual integral row symmetrizers and straightening ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]); no general finite-$e$ restricted nonzero criterion is used.



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Check the lift. Localization makes $\hat q$ a unit since its residue is $-1$, so the exact PID hypotheses of [F1] hold; the generic factorial is nonzero. The identities $[2]=1+\hat q$, $[4]=(1+\hat q)(1+\hat q^2)$ and evaluation of the odd quantum integers at $-1$ prove [F2]. These values refer to this lift, not an arbitrary field or lift with quantum characteristic $2$. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 Compute the balanced symbols explicitly. For $(3,2)$, $\beta=(6,5,3,1,0)$ and its hook array is $\begin{smallmatrix}4&3&1\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}$. The pair $(1,1),(1,2)$ gives $(9,2,3,1,0)$, which sorts to the beta sequence of $(1^5)$ with sign $-1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(3)=1$. The pair $(1,1),(1,3)$ gives $(7,5,2,1,0)$, shape $(2,2,1)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(1)=1$. The pair $(2,1),(2,2)$ gives $(7,4,3,1,0)$, shape $(3,1^2)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(2)-v(1)=1$. The remaining pair has repeated beta entries and vanishes. Thus the first displayed Weyl identity follows by direct substitution. [F1, F2]

1.3 Verify the two zero forms locally. Over $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, the row-symmetrizer calculation in the integral Murphy cell gives the following explicit common divisor. For a shape $\eta$, put $\delta^j=(\eta_j-\eta_{j+1},\ldots,\eta_k)$, a row-difference composition of $\eta_j$, and let $g_j$ be the gcd of $[\gamma]!_Q$ over partitions $\gamma$ dominating that composition. To check the divisor, sort the entries of the first canonical row in a row-standard tableau, obtaining an additive-length permutation $w$. Multiplication by its row symmetrizer gives $Q^{\ell(w)}[\beta]!_Q$ times a row-standard vector and a parabolic word, where $\beta$ counts these entries in each row. Any surviving contribution modulo higher shapes has its residual row composition dominated by $\eta$, so its partial sums give $\beta\unrhd\delta^1$. Therefore $g_1$ divides its scalar. Straighten while fixing that canonical row and repeat on the remaining rows; after all rows only the canonical tableau remains and its coefficient has divisor $\prod_j g_j$. The independent cell product reads this coefficient as each Gram entry. All operations are the integral length-additive parabolic and fixed-row straightening identities of [F3], so the divisibility is proved before specialization. For $\eta=(3,2)$ the last-row composition is $(2)$, so $g_2=[2]!_Q=1+Q$. For $\eta=(3,1,1)$ its first-row composition is $(2,0,1)$; the dominating partitions are $(3)$ and $(2,1)$, and both factorials are divisible by $1+Q$, so $g_1$ is too. Thus every Gram entry of both cells vanishes at $Q=-1$. Their simple Schur images are zero by the exact radical-corner identity, rather than an appeal to the exhausted classifier. [F3, algebra]

2.1 Compute the smaller rows rather than assuming them. The same calculation for $(3,1^2)$ gives $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,1^2)}(i)]=[W^{(2,2,1)}]+[W^{(1^5)}]$: the pairs with hook lengths $(5,2)$ and $(2,1)$ give those two terms, while the $(5,1)$ coefficient is zero. For $(2,2,1)$, the only nonzero symbols arise from pairs $(4,2)$ and $(3,1)$, both of valuation difference zero. For $(2,1^3)$ the sole pair is $(5,1)$, also zero; $(1^5)$ has no pair. Hence these three Weyl modules have zero positive sums and zero radicals, so they equal their simple heads. For $(3,1^2)$ each displayed simple occurs once in the positive sum; because its first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it, both radical multiplicities are exactly $1$. Its class is consequently $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+[L^{(2,2,1)}]+[L^{(1^5)}]$. Substitution into step 1.2 now gives $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]$, proving the stated preliminary multiplicity conclusions without reading a signed individual Weyl coefficient as a simple multiplicity. [F1, F2, step 1.2]



3.1 Supply the actual dimension argument. The regular-weight Gram product for the Murphy cell $(2,2,1)$ is $$\hat q^7\frac{[4]_{\hat q}}{[2]_{\hat q}}[3]_{\hat q}^4   =\hat q^7(1+\hat q^2)[3]_{\hat q}^4,$$ since its two signed symbols have shapes $(1^5)$ and $(2,1^3)$ with standard-tableau counts $1$ and $4$. The five standardizations have lengths $0,1,1,2,3$, giving exponent $7$. At $\hat q=-1$ this determinant is $-2\ne0$. Thus $S_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}=D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}$ is simple of dimension $5$, counted by its five standard tableaux. Both Schur simples $L^{(3,1^2)}$ and $L^{(3,2)}$ are killed by the local zero-form calculation of step 1.3 and the exact corner/form identity [F3]. Applying the functor to the positive sum of step 2.1 therefore gives $\sum_{i>0}[S_{\mathrm M}^{(3,2)}(i)]=2[D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}]$. The form of $(3,2)$ is identically zero by step 1.3, so its first submodule is the whole five-dimensional cell. Every composition factor of that cell must appear in the positive sum, hence must be this five-dimensional simple. Dimension forces exactly one factor, proving $S_{\mathrm M}^{(3,2)}\cong D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,2,1)}$. Exact projection of a composition series, with distinct nonzero simple images as in [F3], gives $d_{(3,2),(2,2,1)}=1$. [F1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 A further consistency check is the regular-weight Gram product $\hat q^8[3]_{\hat q}[4]_{\hat q}^4[2]_{\hat q}^6$ for $(3,2)$, whose valuation is $10$, agreeing with two five-dimensional positive Specht submodules. This is a check of the complete balanced formula; it is not the unsupported full-hook product used in the former classification proof. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 Translate simultaneously by $\theta$ and conjugation. The actual ordinary/Murphy module-and-form comparison sends the isomorphism of step 3.1 to $S_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(2,2,1)}\cong D_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(3,2)}$. The partition $(2,2,1)$ is not regular, so its own **cell-form quotient** is zero; this does not say its actual head is zero, since the module itself is simple. The dominance inequality $(3,2)\unrhd(2,2,1)$ agrees with the ordinary-convention unitriangular bound. This proves every claimed numeric conclusion. [F3, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Cellularity does not make every cell module simple
items.statement:
A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled cell-form quotient $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero.

(a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{2\rhd1\}$ ordered so that $2\rhd1$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $a+bx\in A$ one has $1(a+bx)\equiv a\cdot1\pmod{(x)}$ and $x(a+bx)=ax$, so the triangular axiom holds, and $A^{\rhd1}=(x)$, $A^{\rhd2}=0$. The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while both $C^{1}$ and $C^{2}$ are one-dimensional simple modules: on either, $a+bx$ acts as the scalar $a$. In particular the Jacobson radical of $C^{2}$ is zero and its actual head is $C^{2}$, even though its cell-form radical is all of $C^{2}$ and its cell-form quotient is zero: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$.

(b) Hecke instance: let $F$ be a field of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)=2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); for $n=3$ and $\lambda=(1,1,1)$ the partition $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]), so $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while the page's Specht module $S^{(1,1,1)}\cong D^{(3)}$ is the nonzero trivial module (in characteristic $2$ the sign module is trivial) ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

(c) Reducible cell module: in the $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, $e=2$ specialization of the example the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three settings above: the algebra $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, the Hecke algebra $H_{F,q}(S_3)$ in characteristic $2$ at $q=1$, and the q-Schur Weyl module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ over $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, at $e=2$.

[F1] ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) For a cellular basis, products of two elements of the smaller cell vanish modulo the larger cell exactly when the corresponding form entry vanishes; $D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is zero if and only if the cell form is identically zero, and only in the nonzero case is $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ the module-theoretic Jacobson radical and the head quotient.

[F2] ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) For $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the quantum characteristic is $e=2$, $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, and $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\lambda$.

[F3] ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]) For the specified $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ lift with $e=2$, the positive Jantzen submodule sum for $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is $[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$.




## Counterexample

1.1 The abstract instance: in $A=F[x]/(x^2)$ with $c_{11}=1$, $c_{22}=x$ and $2\rhd1$, the product $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$ is congruent to $0\cdot c_{22}$ modulo $A^{\rhd2}=0$, so the axiom holds with zero form value; the products $c_{11}(a+bx)=a+bx\equiv a\,c_{11}\pmod{(x)}$ and $c_{22}(a+bx)=ax=a\,c_{22}$ confirm the triangularity. Hence $C^{2}$ has identically zero form, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$; the module $C^{2}$ itself is one-dimensional with $a+bx$ acting as $a$, hence simple with zero Jacobson radical and head $C^{2}\ne0$. Moreover $x\in A$ is a nonzero nilpotent, so $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)\ne0$ and $A$ is not semisimple. [given, F1]

1.2 The Hecke instance: for $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the sign module is the trivial module, so the Murphy cell module $S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M}$ and its theta-pullback $S^{(1,1,1)}=(S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ are the trivial module; the label $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so by [F2] $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while $S^{(1,1,1)}\ne0$. [given, F2]

1.3 The reducible Weyl module. In the precise lift of [F3], the sum of the positive filtration-submodule classes is $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]\ne0$. At least one of these submodules is nonzero. Since all are contained in the first reduced submodule $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}W_F$, that radical is nonzero. The Schur cell form has nonzero simple head, so its form radical is its unique maximal proper submodule. Consequently $W_F^{(3,2)}$ is reducible, despite having simple head $L^{(3,2)}$. The reduced form radical is not identified with $F\otimes_R$ the generic radical: specialization need not commute with this kernel, and the lifted generic form here is nondegenerate. [given, F1, F3]

2.1 Conclusion: the three instances refute the claims that cellularity forces semisimplicity, forces every cell module to be simple, or forces every labelled cell-form quotient to be nonzero; each is an application of the classification of cell-form quotients [F1] together with the explicit degenerate data. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F1] ∎

title: Cores, Quotients, and Blocks of Symmetric Groups

items.title: Beta-sets, the shift, and the e-runner abacus of a partition
items.statement: Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with $m=\ell(\lambda)$ parts and put $b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i$ for $1\le i\le m$, so that $X_\lambda=\{b_1>\cdots>b_m\}$ is the set of first-column hook lengths of $\lambda$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]], [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]). A **$\beta$-set** is any finite strictly decreasing subset $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$; its **$l$-shift** is $X+l=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$ for $l\ge0$, and its partition is $P(X)=(h_1-(m-1),h_2-(m-2),\dots,h_m-0)$ with trailing zeros deleted. Then $P(X_\lambda)=\lambda$, and $X$ is a $\beta$-set *for* $\lambda$ (that is, $P(X)=\lambda$) if and only if $X=X_\lambda+l$ for some $l\in\mathbb N_0$. For $e\ge2$ the **$e$-abacus** has runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ (left to right) with the position in row $a\ge0$ of runner $i$ labelled $ae+i$; the **configuration $A_X$** carries a bead in the positions of $X$, and $X\mapsto A_X$ is a bijection onto the finite bead configurations, with inverse $A\mapsto X_A$ and $P(A):=P(X_A)$. Shifting $l$ only changes the row labels of the beads, so every shifted $\beta$-set represents the same partition.
items.strategy: A definition item fixing the computational model and its inverse formulas. The identity $P(X_\lambda)=\lambda$ and the 'if and only if' form of the source's Lemma 4.2 are checked by unwinding $P$: solving $h_j-(m-j)=\lambda_j$ for $j\le\ell(\lambda)$ and $h_j-(m-j)=0$ for $j>\ell(\lambda)$ gives $m\ge\ell(\lambda)$ and $X=X_\lambda+(m-\ell(\lambda))$. The runner/residue convention is the printed one (position $ae+i$ on runner $i$). No choice principle is used. Source: Tomczak §4.1, the definition of a $\beta$-set with Lemma 4.2 and the definition of James's $e$-abacus, printed pp. 54-55.

items.title: Hooks are bead-gap pairs on the abacus
items.statement: Let $e\ge2$, $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$ ([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). (i) For $h\ge0$ and $i\in[m]$, $h$ is a hook length in row $i$ of $\lambda$ if and only if $h\le h_i$ and $h_i-h\notin X$; equivalently the hooks of $\lambda$ correspond bijectively to the *bead-gap pairs* $(b,g)$ with $b\in X$, $g\notin X$ and $0\le g<b$, the hook $H_{i,j}(\lambda)$ corresponding to $(b,g)$ having length $b-g$ ([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]). (ii) Removing that hook replaces $X$ by $X'=(X\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$, which is a $\beta$-set for $\lambda\setminus H_{i,j}$, and the hook $H_{i,j}$ is the removable border strip of the corresponding rim hook of $\lambda$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). (iii) Hence $e\mid|H_{i,j}|$ if and only if $b\equiv g\pmod e$, that is, if and only if the bead $b$ and the gap $g$ lie on the same runner of the $e$-abacus; and a hook of length $e$ in row $i$ exists if and only if some bead of $X$ has an empty position immediately below it on its own runner.
items.strategy: Trace the southeast boundary of $[\lambda]$: the beads and gaps of $X$ in increasing order encode the vertical and horizontal steps, so each bead-gap pair $(b,g)$ with $b>g$ cuts out a hook of length $b-g$, and the interval $\{g+1,\dots,b\}$ splits at $g$ exactly when $g$ is a step. This gives the bijection in (i), as in the source's Lemma 4.1, Lemma 4.4 and Corollary 4.5. The removal formula is the source's Proposition 4.7: $Z=(X\setminus\{h_i\})\cup\{h_i-h_{i,j}(\lambda)\}$ is a $\beta$-set for $\lambda\setminus H_{i,j}$, proved by reducing to $X=X_\lambda$ and computing $Z'$. The same-runner criterion and the bead-slide description of an $e$-hook removal are Corollary 4.8, and the identification of the hook with a removable border strip is the published correspondence [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]. No choice principle is used. Source: Tomczak §4.1, Lemmas 4.1/4.4 and Corollaries 4.5/4.8 with Proposition 4.7, printed pp. 53-59.

items.title: The e-core, the e-quotient, and the e-weight
items.statement: Let $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ with $\beta$-set $X$ ([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]], hooks as in [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]). $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when $e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when $\lambda$ has no hook of length $e$. For a $\beta$-set $X$ let $X^{(e)}_i=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$ be the set of row labels of the beads on runner $i$; set $X^{(e)}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\}$ (the *top-packed* $\beta$-set) and define the **$e$-core** $C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)})$. Choose the $\beta$-set so that $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$, and define the **$e$-quotient** $Q_e(\lambda)=(\lambda^{(0)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)})$ by $\lambda^{(i)}=P(X^{(e)}_i)$ and the **$e$-weight** by $w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|=\sum_i|\lambda^{(i)}|$. Every $e$-core is $e$-regular and $e$-restricted. The definitions are independent of the chosen $\beta$-set: shifting by $1$ permutes the runners and changes the quotient only by a cyclic shift of the components, which the normalisation $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$ removes (proved below in the core-independence theorem of this page).
items.strategy: A definition item recording the printed conventions; the well-definedness statements are deferred to the core theorem, which proves that $X\mapsto X+1$ cyclically shifts the runners and preserves $X^{(e)}$ up to a shift. The $e$-regularity of an $e$-core is the one-line argument that $e$ equal parts $\lambda_i=\cdots=\lambda_{i+e-1}$ create the hook of length $e$ at $(i,\lambda_{i+e-1})$, and $e$-restrictedness is the conjugate statement. No choice principle is used. Source: Tomczak §4.1, the definitions of an $e$-core, of $X^{(e)}_i$, of $Q_e(\lambda)$, of $X^{(e)}$ and of $C_e(\lambda)$, with the remark on the normalising shift before the worked example, printed pp. 58-60.

items.title: Virtual Weyl combinations detect q-Schur block separation
items.statement: Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S=S(d,n)$ be the $q$-Schur algebra with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$, $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional right $S$-module all of whose composition factors lie in a single block $B$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and let integers $a_\lambda$ satisfy $[M]=\sum_\lambda a_\lambda[W^{\lambda}]$ in $G_0(S\text{-mod})$ ([[def-grothendieck-group-of-an-essentially-small-abelian-category]]). Then $W^{\lambda}$ lies in $B$ whenever $a_\lambda\ne0$. In particular no nonzero virtual combination of Weyl classes all of whose terms lie outside $B$ can equal the class of a module in $B$.

items.title: The e-core is independent of the rim hook removal order
items.statement: Let $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$. The top-packed $\beta$-set $X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]] does not depend on the chosen $\beta$-set of $\lambda$ up to a shift that leaves $P$ unchanged, so the $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition; it is exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing rim $e$-hooks (removable border strips of size $e$, [[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]) until none is left. In particular every removal order gives the same terminal partition $C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal partition contains no hook of length $e$.
items.strategy: Fix a $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$. By [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) an $e$-hook corresponds exactly to a bead with a gap directly below it on its own runner, and removing it is the bead slide one row up; hence iterated $e$-hook removal is exactly the process of sliding beads up until every runner is packed at the top, and that terminal configuration is unique, namely $X^{(e)}$. The remaining point is independence of the shift: replacing $X$ by $X+1$ moves the beads of each runner to the next runner cyclically and adds one row to runner $0$, so it permutes the runners and $P(X^{(e)})$ is unchanged (the source's Lemma 4.9 and its remark); by Lemma 4.2 every $\beta$-set of $\lambda$ is a shift of $X_\lambda$, so the terminal partition is well defined. No choice principle is used. Sources: Tomczak Lemma 4.9 and Theorem 4.10 with proof, printed pp. 59-60; Mathas Lemma 5.34 with its printed proof (printed p. 60), which is exactly this abacus argument.

items.title: The e-quotient controls the hooks of e-divisible length
items.statement: Let $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-quotient $Q_e(\lambda)$ and $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There is a bijection $f$ from the hooks of $\lambda$ of $e$-divisible length onto the hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$, that is, onto $\bigsqcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{\text{hooks of }\lambda^{(i)}\}$, such that $|H|=e\,|f(H)|$ and $Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$, where the right-hand side means that the corresponding hook of the single component containing it is removed. On the abacus $f$ is the rescaling $b=b'e+i$, $g=g'e+i$ of a bead-gap pair lying on runner $i$ ([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).
items.strategy: Restrict the bead-gap bijection of the hook lemma to pairs on a common runner, using part (iii). A bead-gap pair $(b,g)$ with $b\equiv g\equiv i\pmod e$ on runner $i$ has $b=b'e+i$, $g=g'e+i$ with $b'>g'$; passing to the row labels $X^{(e)}_i$ turns it into a bead-gap pair $(b',g')$ of the partition $\lambda^{(i)}$. The length identity $b-g=e(b'-g')$ and the removal identity $Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$ follow from the $\beta$-set removal formula of the hook lemma together with the normalisation $e\mid|X|$. This is the printed bijection of Theorem 4.11 with its proof. No choice principle is used. Source: Tomczak Theorem 4.11, printed pp. 60-61.

items.title: The core-quotient size formula defines the weight
items.statement: Let $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and $e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then $n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$, so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every sequence of rim $e$-hook removals from $\lambda$ down to its $e$-core ([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly $w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of [[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of $\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.
items.strategy: Induct on $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$. If it is zero the abacus is already top-packed, so $\lambda=C_e(\lambda)$ and there is no bead with a gap below it on its runner, hence no hook of length divisible by $e$ by the same-runner criterion and every term of the claimed identity vanishes. Otherwise some runner has a bead with a gap below it, so $\lambda$ has a removable $e$-hook $H$ by the hook lemma; by the quotient theorem $Q_e(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_e(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$, so $w_e(\lambda\setminus H)=w_e(\lambda)-1$, while $|\lambda\setminus H|=|\lambda|-e$. The induction hypothesis applied to $\lambda\setminus H$, together with $C_e(\lambda\setminus H)=C_e(\lambda)$ from the core theorem, gives the size formula. The final counting statement holds because a partition has one hook per box, so the number of hooks of each component equals its size. No choice principle is used. Source: Tomczak Proposition 4.12, parts (i)-(iii) with proof, printed p. 62.

items.title: q-Schur Weyl modules are in the same block iff their labels have the same e-core
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ every partition is its own core and every Weyl module is its own block, the algebra being semisimple.)

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, parameter $q$, quantum characteristic $e$, integer $d\ge n$, and the Weyl modules in the statement. Write $S=S_F(d,n)$ and $W^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}_F$.

[F1] The semistandard cellular basis has cells $W^{\lambda}$, nonzero absolutely simple heads $L^{\lambda}$, and dominance-unitriangular decomposition multiplicities $d_{\lambda\mu}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The cellular anti-involution induces contragredient duality fixing the simple isomorphism classes, through the nondegenerate cell form on each simple head ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The balanced hook-ratio Jantzen formula and alternating beta symbols ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]) use conjugate beta numbers $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+N-j$, with $N$ sufficiently large, and read $$\sum_{r>0}[W^{\lambda}(r)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(v(h^{\lambda}_{ab})-v(h^{\lambda}_{ac})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}],$$ where $W^{\lambda}(r)$ are filtration submodules, $W^{\lambda}(1)=\operatorname{rad}W^{\lambda}$, and the right hand symbols are zero on repeated or negative entries and otherwise have the sign of sorting the beta sequence. The suppliers must carry this balanced form; the earlier displayed unbalanced manuscript indices do not preserve degree.

[F3] Core abaci are obtained by packing beads upwards on each runner, so their shapes depend only on runner bead counts; rim-hook removal is a bead-to-gap move ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Conjugation reverses dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F4] Primitive central idempotents decompose the identity, and every finite-dimensional module splits into their block summands ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). Weyl classes are linearly independent in the Grothendieck group, so a nonzero accumulated Weyl coefficient in the class of a module supported in one block forces that Weyl module into the block ([[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]], [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Composition-factor cores. An off-head simple occurs in $W^{\lambda}$ exactly when it occurs in its radical, equivalently in the positive Jantzen sum: the first submodule is the radical and every later one is contained in it. Its nonzero multiplicity in that sum implies it occurs in some $W^{\mu}$ with $J_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, since otherwise its coefficient in the sum would be zero. Step 2.1 gives the same core and strict dominance descent. Induction on the finite dominance poset proves that every factor $L^{\nu}$ of $W^{\lambda}$ has $C_e(\nu)=C_e(\lambda)$. No identity equating the radical class with the positive sum is asserted. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical. [F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. Such a system lifts matrix diagonal idempotents from the split semisimple quotient: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ squares the idempotency error, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_\nu$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_\nu=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda\nu}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core. [F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, and set $\rho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=\rho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $\nu$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $\nu$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows. [F3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 The bridge coefficients are nonzero. Write $l=\ell(\mu)=\ell(\sigma)$. If $i>1$, then $\sigma_1=\mu_1$ and the row1 hook pair in $\nu$ at columns $j,\mu_1+1$ has lengths $A=h^{\mu}_{1j}$ and $h$: the first is nondivisible because row1 precedes the first divisible row, and the second is divisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\mu$, so its coefficient is nonzero. If $i=1$, then $\sigma_1=j-1$, and the row1 pair at columns $j,j+1$ has lengths $h,h-1$; its balanced transfer $h-1$ sorts to $\mu$, again giving a nonzero coefficient. For $\eta$, the pair at columns $1,\sigma_1+1$ has lengths $A'=\sigma_1+h+l-1$ and $h$. When $i>1$, $A'-h^{\mu}_{i1}=A$, so $A'$ is nondivisible; when $i=1$, $A'=h^{\mu}_{11}+h-1$, also nondivisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\eta$. Each claimed target has precisely two lost and two gained beta values, so the uniqueness argument in step 2.2 rules out cancellation. Thus both $J_{\nu\mu}$ and $J_{\nu\eta}$ are nonzero. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 6.1] ∎

The connectivity argument follows the corrected dominance-minimum route of Lyle–Mathas Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 4.3, while proving the needed elementary row properties locally. Their final Remark explicitly corrects the earlier first-row-only q-Schur argument; the old direct hook move can have zero coefficient.

items.title: The weight-one block decomposition pattern
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, and put $n=m+e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this weight-one class satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $$[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]\qquad(1\le k<e),$$ so the decomposition matrix of the class is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$. Moreover exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted, while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $$[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}],\qquad [S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]\ (2\le k<e),\qquad [S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}],$$ with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, an $e$-core $\gamma$ of $m$, the integer $n=m+e$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,n)$ for $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, where $d\ge n$.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

[F2] The corrected balanced Jantzen formula sums positive filtration **submodules**, not their successive quotients: $$\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda}_F(i)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}_F].$$ Here $\beta_b=\lambda'_b+N-b$ for a fixed sufficiently long conjugate beta sequence, and the right hand symbols are alternating symbols: sort strictly decreasing, attach the sorting sign, and vanish on repeated or negative entries. The equal transfer preserves total size. Moreover $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$. This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

[F3] Core-quotient and abacus theory: a weight-one partition is obtained from a packed core abacus by moving the bottom bead of one runner down one place. The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Restricted means $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i$ ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F4] The exact Schur functor sends $W^{\lambda}$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $L^{\lambda}$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, whose nonzero labels are precisely the restricted partitions. The ordinary Specht dictionary is the proved generic-$q$ form bridge and uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q\ne1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Type-A Hecke Specht modules are in the same block iff their labels have the same e-core
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ the Hecke algebra is semisimple and each partition is its own core, so the statement is the trivial block decomposition.)

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$, a partition $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\vdash n$, and a fixed integer $d\ge n$.

[F1] For $d\ge n$, the Schur idempotent $e\in S=S_F(d,n)$ satisfies $eSe\cong H$, and $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact. It sends each Weyl module $W^{\lambda}$ to the nonzero Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; its simple images are zero or the Murphy simple modules, with the nonzero images indexed by the $e$-restricted partitions ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Blocks: $1=\sum_D\delta_D$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of a finite-dimensional algebra into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, blocks are the ideals cut out by the $\delta_D$, and every nonzero central idempotent is a sum of some of the $\delta_D$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

[F3] The q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules: $S$ is finite-dimensional, $S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for $M=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\nu}$ with $M^{(1^n)}=H$, and $W^{\lambda}_F$ has head $L^{\lambda}_F$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F4] The q-Schur block theorem [[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]: for $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F,W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S$ if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$; the blocks of $S$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$; and if $e=\infty$ then $S$ is semisimple with each $W^{\lambda}_F$ its own block.

[F5] The accepted ordinary/Murphy dictionary identifies the ordinary Specht module with the fixed $\theta$ pullback of the conjugate-shape Murphy cell module. Conjugation sends $C_e(\lambda)$ to $C_e(\lambda)'$, and sends restricted labels to regular labels. In particular it preserves equality of cores. An algebra automorphism permutes primitive central idempotents and therefore preserves the same-block relation ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Number of q-Schur blocks is at least the number of Hecke blocks. Let $H=\bigoplus_iB_i$ be the block decomposition of $H$ with block identities $b_i$. Since $M=\bigoplus_{\nu}M^{\nu}$ and $H=M^{(1^n)}$ is a direct summand, $M=\bigoplus_iMb_i$ with each $Mb_i\ne0$ (it contains $Hb_i=B_i$), and $\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, because a map $f$ satisfies $f(x)=f(xb_i)=f(x)b_i\in Mb_jb_i=0$. Hence $$S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=\prod_i\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$$ is a product of the nonzero algebras $\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$, and a product of nonzero algebras has at least one block per factor; so $\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Nakayama block classification for symmetric groups
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ with the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, an integer $n\ge0$, and the group algebra $k[S_n]$ with group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$ for $\lambda\vdash n$.

[F1] The algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ sends each ordinary Dipper-James Specht module to the classical group Specht module of the same shape, and the quantum characteristic at $q=1$ in characteristic $p$ equals $p$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]], [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). The module comparison uses the accepted signed conjugate Murphy/ordinary dictionary before specialising; it does not identify the same-shape Murphy cell module with the ordinary Specht module.

[F2] The Hecke block criterion, in the Dipper-James normalisation of the same Specht modules as [F1]: [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]] states that for a field $k$ and $q\in k^{\times}$ of quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, two Specht modules $S^{\lambda},S^{\mu}$ of $H_{k,q}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, and that the blocks are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$.

[F4] The core-quotient size formula [[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]: for every $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ one has $n=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$ with $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|\in\mathbb N_0$, and for an $e$-core $\gamma$ the condition $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$ is exactly the condition that $n-|\gamma|$ be an admissible $e$-weight; conversely every such $\gamma$ occurs as the core of a partition of $n$ ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F5] An algebra isomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ preserves blocks: it maps a central idempotent $z$ to the central idempotent $\varphi(z)$, preserves primitivity, and hence induces a bijection between the block sets ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

## Proof

 **Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$. [F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

items.title: Weight-zero symmetric-group blocks are defect zero
items.statement: Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ a partition of $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)=0$, that is, a $p$-core.
