This constructs a regular matching for $J$ together with one new source in $(r,u)$, contradicting maximality. Thus $J$ is essential. [step 41.1, construct]

43.1 This proves the claim, including uniqueness, without assuming a source theorem or using a representation-theoretic count. Two elementary consequences of the witness definition will be used. **Truncation.** If $M$ is essential in $(r,s]$ and $q\in (r,s]\setminus M$, then $M\cap (r,q-1]$ is essential in $(r,q-1]$. Any forbidden witness for the truncated interval has endpoints $\le q$, also outside $M$, and is a witness in the original interval. **Concatenation.** If $P$ is essential in $(r,v-2]$ and $J$ essential in $(v,s]$, then $P\cup \{v\}\cup J$ is essential in $(r,s]$. A forbidden witness wholly to the left or right gives the corresponding forbidden witness. A witness crossing $v$ contains $v$ as a source; restrict it to $\{v\}\cup (J\cap (v,u))$. Since all such sources and their targets are $\ge v$, this is a forbidden witness for $J$. The virtual case $v=r+1$ uses $P=\varnothing$ and the same restriction argument. [step 42.1, construct]

44.1 Let $M$ be essential. If it is regular it is the unique $P(r,s)$ of the regular-essential matching argument already proved, and $\sigma (r,s)=1$. Otherwise let $v$ be the largest element of $M$ satisfying $v-1\notin M$ and $M\cap (r,v-2]\text{ is regular in } (r,v-2]$. Such $v$ exists: take $\min M$, with empty prefix. The prefix is essential by truncation at $q=v-1$, hence equals the unique $P(r,v-2)$; in particular $\sigma(r,v-2)=1$ (or the virtual value 1). [step 43.1, construct]

45.1 We show $J=M\cap (v,s]$ is essential. If it had a witness $t<u$ with $t>v$, that is already a forbidden witness for $M$. If $t=v$, the witness matches $M\cap (v,u)$ into $(v,u)$; combine it with the regular prefix matching, whose images are $\le v-2$. Because $v-1\notin M$, this makes $M\cap (r,u)$ regular in $(r,u-1]$. If $u=s+1$ or there is no element of $M$ above $u$, it makes $M$ regular, contrary to assumption. Otherwise let $q=\min (M\cap (u,s])$; then $q\ge u+1, q-1\notin M$, and that same matching makes $M\cap (r,q-2]$ regular. This contradicts maximality of $v$. Thus $J$ is essential, and $M=P(r,v-2)\cup \{v\}\cup J$. [step 44.1, construct]

46.1 The decomposition is unique. Indeed, in a concatenated set with essential tail $J$, no larger $m>v$ can meet the same two prefix conditions: a regular matching for its prefix, restricted to $\{v\}\cup (J\cap (v,m-1))$, would be a forbidden witness for $J$ with endpoints $v,m-1$. The regular essential case cannot equal a concatenated case, because a regular matching of the whole set restricted to $\{v\}\cup J$ would make $J$ nonessential with endpoints $v,s+1$. [step 45.1, construct]

47.1 Iterating this unique decomposition gives a bijection between essential subsets and **$\sigma$-cut paths** $Q=\{q_{1}<\cdots <q_{f}\}\subset (r,s]$ satisfying $\sigma (r,q_{1}-2)\sigma (q_{1},q_{2}-2)\cdots \sigma (q_{f-1},q_{f} -2)\sigma (q_{f},s)=1$. For $f=0$ the condition is $\sigma (r,s)=1$. The inverse recursively inserts the unique regular essential prefix $P$ and the cut point, so this is a genuine bijection, not merely equal cardinalities. In particular $\varepsilon (r,s)$ counts these paths. [step 46.1, construct]

48.1 For a fixed $r$, $B(z,m)=B(r,m)-C(r,z)$. For a demand $m$ with $B(r,m)=0$, its eligible compensation positions are exactly $z\in (r,m]$ with $C(r,z)=0$. This is a prefix/Ferrers matching problem. A compensation injection exists iff at every cutoff $x$ the number of demands $\le x$ does not exceed the number of eligible compensation positions $\le x$: necessity follows by counting distinct targets; sufficiency follows by pairing increasing demands with increasing available eligible positions. This is a complete greedy matching proof. [step 47.1, construct]

49.1 If $\lambda _{r}\ne 0$, initialize a stack with $r$. Scan $m=r+1,\cdots ,s$. When $\lambda _{m}\ne 0$, push $m$ if $C(r,m)=0$, pop the last push if $B(r,m)=0$, and otherwise do nothing. These push/pop cases are disjoint, since $B-C=\lambda _{m}$. When $\lambda _{m}=0$ and $B=C=0$, the position supplies and consumes its own compensation slot, so it changes neither the matching inequality nor the stack; all other zero-coordinate positions are likewise neutral. Kill the root walk permanently if its initial push $r$ is popped. The prefix matching inequalities prove that $r$ is normal exactly when the walk is not killed. [step 48.1, construct]

50.1 When it is not killed, its final stack is exactly $N(r,s)$. A pushed position $a$ has $C(r,a)=0$ and $\lambda _{a}\ne 0$. For every $m\ge a$ the $B,C$ identities give $B(a,m)=B(r,m)$ and $C(a,m)=C(r,m)$. Thus $a$ is normal precisely when no suffix after it has excess pops over pushes, equivalently when its push survives the last-in-first-out matching. This proves the claimed exact stack interpretation of $\nu$ and $N$. For a killed root, $N$ is empty by definition. The same proof applies verbatim to every shifted weight. [step 49.1, construct]

51.1 We record two consequences of the stack, with proofs exposing the endpoint shift. **Bridge lemma.** Suppose $x<y, \sigma (x,y-2)=1$ and $\nu '(x,y-1)=0$. If $y$ is normal in $[y,s]$, then $N(x,s)=\{x\} \sqcup N(y,s)$, and $x$ precedes all indices of $N(y,s)$. [step 50.1, construct]

52.1 For $y=x+1$, $\nu'(x,x)=0$ means $\lambda _{x}+1=0$; hence $\lambda _{x}=-1\ne 0$ and $C(x,y)=1+\lambda _{x}=0$. This proves the claim by the stack identities. For $y\ge x+2$, the unshifted walk is alive through $y-2$. Shifting only $\lambda _{y-1}$ cannot affect its earlier steps. To make $\nu '=0$ at its final step, the shifted walk must pop its last surviving root: its prior stack therefore has height 1 and $B(x,y-1)+1=C(x,y)=0$, with $\lambda _{y-1}+1\ne 0$. In the original walk $B(x,y-1)=-1\ne 0$. Also $C(x,y-1)=-1-\lambda _{y-1}\ne 0$ by the last nonzero condition. Thus the original $y-1$ step is neutral, and the stack before $y$ consists only of $x$. Since $C(x,y)=0$ and $y$ is normal, $y$ is a nonzero-coordinate push; for every later position the walks based at $x$ and $y$ have identical events. The stack is consequently $\{x\}$ followed by $N(y,s)$, as claimed. This argument works in $p=2$ as well, since $-1$ is always nonzero. [step 51.1, construct]

53.1 **Consecutive-normal lemma.** In a nonempty $N(r,s)$ let $a<b$ be consecutive final stack entries. Then $\sigma (a,b-2)=1$ and $\nu '(a,b-1)=0$. First normality of $a$ gives prefix normality and hence $\sigma =1$. Both final entries satisfy $C(r,a)=C(r,b)=0$, so $C(a,b)=0$. Before $b$ is pushed, the stack based at $a$ has exactly its initial entry: any additional unmatched push earlier than $b$ would survive whenever $b$ survives (last-in-first-out pops cannot remove it before removing $b$), and would be an intervening final normal entry. The step $b-1$ is neutral in the original walk. Indeed $B(a,b-1)=-1$; if $C(a,b-1)=0$, then $\lambda _{b-1}=-1$, and $b-1$ would be such an intervening surviving push. Therefore $\lambda _{b-1}+1\ne 0$. Increasing $\lambda _{b-1}$ by 1 creates exactly one final pop of the height-one stack, proving $\nu '=0$. The adjacent case is $\lambda _{a}+1=C(a,b)=0$, giving $\nu '(a,a)=0$ directly. These conclusions also apply to normal sets under a shift at some final endpoint $s$: when $a<b\le s$, their bridge intervals end before $s$, so their $B,C$ constants are unchanged by the outer shift. The $\lambda _{b}$ term is absent from $C(a,b)$, which is why this remains true even when $b=s$. [step 52.1, construct]

54.1 For a $\sigma$-cut path $M=\{m_{1}<\cdots <m_{h}\}$, put $m_{0}=r$. Retain exactly the cut points $m_{w}$ for which $\nu '(m_{w-1},m_{w}-1)>0$. Call the retained set $Q=\{q_{1}<\cdots <q_{f}\}$. Partition $M$ into blocks between retained cuts. Every internal removed cut has prime-zero bridge; the next retained cut has prime-positive boundary. Repeated application of the bridge lemma, in the weight shifted at the next retained boundary endpoint, shows that the removed cuts in this block are precisely an initial segment of $N'(q_{v},q_{v+1}-1)$ (excluding its first entry $q_{v}$), where $q_{0}=r$. The final block is similarly an initial segment of $N(q_{f},s)$, excluding $q_{f}$. All these normal sets are nonempty, because the retained boundary has positive $\nu '$ and the last $\sigma$ condition makes the final root normal. [step 53.1, construct]

55.1 More explicitly, the block containing a removed-cut chain $x=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_t$ before a retained endpoint $y$ has $\sigma (a_{j},a_{j+1}-2)=1$ and prime-zero between consecutive removed cuts, while $\nu'(a_t,y-1)>0$. The last root $a_t$ is normal for the weight shifted at $y-1$. Repeated bridge identities therefore make $a_0,\ldots,a_t$ the first $t+1$ entries of $N'(x,y-1)$. This proves the asserted initial-segment property and determines $t$ uniquely. The final block uses the same argument with unshifted $N$. [step 54.1, construct]

56.1 Conversely, for any $Q=\{q_{1}<\cdots <q_{f}\}$ choose integers $1\le a_{v}\le \nu '(q_{v},q_{v+1}-1)$ for $v=0,\cdots ,f-1$, and $1\le a_{f}\le \nu (q_{f},s)$. For every segment insert the first $a_{v}-1$ normal indices after its initial index, and include every retained cut $q_{1},\cdots ,q_{f}$. The consecutive-normal lemma proves each new bridge has the required $\sigma$ condition and prime-zero value. Normality of the last inserted index proves $\sigma$ up to the next retained boundary and a positive $\nu '$ there; the final index is normal in its tail. Thus the result is a $\sigma$-cut path. Its retention operation returns exactly $Q$, and the initial-segment lengths return the chosen $a_{v}$. The two constructions are inverse. [step 55.1, construct]

57.1 Hence there is an explicit bijection from $\sigma$-cut paths onto the disjoint union, over all $Q\subset (r,s]$, of sets of size $\nu '(r,q_{1}-1)\nu '(q_{1},q_{2}-1)\cdots \nu '(q_{f-1},q_{f} -1)\nu (q_{f},s)$, with size $\nu (r,s)$ when $Q=\varnothing$. Together with the essential/path bijection already proved this proves that $\varepsilon$ equals this weighted-cut sum. Grouping its nonempty cuts by their first point gives the complete local recurrence $\varepsilon (r,s)=\nu (r,s)+\sum _{u=r+1}^s \nu '(r,u-1) \varepsilon (u,s)$.  $(A)$ This is the source item five point six, part (iv) seam established by finite injections/bijections, not by an essential-basis or branching citation. [step 56.1, construct]

58.1 Fix $s$ and consider indices $1,\ldots,s$. Let $A$ be the strictly upper triangular integer matrix $A[r,u]=\nu '_\Lambda (r,u-1)$ for $r<u$, and $B$ the strictly upper triangular matrix $B[r,u]=\varepsilon '_\Lambda (r,u-1)$ for $r<u$. Apply $(A)$ to the interval $[r,u-1]$ in the dominant weight $\Lambda +\omega _{u-1}$. Its first primed factor on $[r,v-1], v<u$, does not see the outer endpoint shift, so it is $\nu '_\Lambda (r,v-1)$. The tail is $\varepsilon '_\Lambda (v,u-1)$. Therefore $B=A+AB$. [step 57.1, construct]

59.1 Since $A$ is strictly upper triangular, $I+B=I+A+\cdots +A^{s-1}=(I-A)^{-1}$. Let $E$ and $N$ be column vectors with entries $\varepsilon (r,s)$ and $\nu (r,s)$. Equation $(A)$ is $E=N+AE$, so $N=(I-A)E$. Multiplying by $I+B$ gives $E=(I+B)N$. Component $r$ is precisely $(R)$: $\varepsilon _\Lambda (r,s)=\nu _\Lambda (r,s)+\sum _{u=r+1}^s \varepsilon '_\Lambda (r,u-1)\nu _\Lambda (u,s)$. All entries are ordinary integers; only nilpotence and finite matrix multiplication are used. This is also the finite reverse-character-inversion arithmetic needed by the first-level construction. No division, characteristic-zero argument, or generic dimension count appears. [step 58.1, construct]

60.1 For $r=s$, essential subsets consist only of $\varnothing$ and it is essential exactly when $\lambda _{r}\ne 0$; the normal set is then $\{r\}$. Both sides are 0 or 1 accordingly. All endpoint and zero-coordinate cases are therefore included. Nothing in the proof depends on the prime beyond working in a characteristic-$p$ field for the zero tests and $1\ne 0$. The recurrence is uniform in arbitrary dominant coordinates and every root interval. [step 59.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The operators, coefficient recursions and raising pivots are integral before specialization. The basis and count recurrence retain arbitrary dominant polynomial weights, including the nonrestricted shifted weights used in first-level character inversion.

In the empty-set definition of $\Xi$, the highest coefficient is the product forced by the explicit action. The printed sum in the 1995 definition is not used; neither that misprint nor a source count theorem is a proof premise.

items.title: Kleshchev's first-level branching multiplicity
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ (every field is splitting for
symmetric groups, so no algebraic closedness is needed) and let $\lambda$ be
a $p$-regular partition of $n$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]), so that $D^\lambda$ is the
simple head of the Specht module $S^\lambda_k$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). Let
$A=(j,\lambda_j)$ be a removable node of $\lambda$ whose removal
$\lambda(j)$ is again $p$-regular, and call $A$ **normal** for $\lambda$ when
the transposed node $(\lambda_j,j)$ of the $p$-restricted partition
$\lambda'$ is a normal node in the sense of
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] (this is
Kleshchev's normality; it is computed in the reduced signature of the correct
residue class of $\lambda'$). Then
$$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not normal, and
$$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=1+\#\{B:\ B\ \text{is a normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A\text{ with }\operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$$
if $A$ is normal. Here $\operatorname{res}$ is the residue $c-r\bmod p$ and
"above" means strictly smaller row index. Equivalently, the multiplicity is the piecewise integer
$\gamma(A)=\mathbf1_{A\text{ normal}}\cdot\#\{B:B\text{ normal removable, weakly above }A,\ \operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$.
Thus $A$ is normal precisely when this piecewise multiplicity is nonzero.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$ and a removable $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ whose removal is $p$-regular.

[F1] The actual Schur endomorphism algebra, normalized semistandard maps, weight projections and right corner action are those of [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]] and [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. The complete $q=1$ Weyl-corner, form/radical and first-level comparison required here are proved inline below, without the held general comparison or any finite-e classifier.

[F2] The actual signed-conjugate bridge has unit form factor $q^{N_\lambda-L_\lambda}$, equal to one at $q=1$, and identifies ordinary Specht form quotients with signed conjugate Murphy form quotients. The published group radical criterion gives nonzero ordinary quotients exactly at regular partitions, distinctly labelled by those partitions ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]], [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], [[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).

[F3] The complete local interval-basis/count lemma supplies the integral negative cut words, positive detection, exact essential-subset dimensions, and finite matching recurrence for arbitrary dominant polynomial weights and all root intervals, including the last-coordinate increase of one ([[lem-type-a-modular-root-interval-essential-subset-basis-and-count]]). Its proof supplies these properties over every field, without a characteristic-zero PBW or external count theorem.

[F4] The general cellular rank-one action gives simplicity, absolute simplicity and completeness of the actual nonzero Schur cell quotients ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]). The signature convention is [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]], and restriction has its usual exact group-module meaning ([[def-restriction-induction-and-coinduction-for-group-modules]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Use the actual $q=1$ Schur Weyl-cell simple $L_N(\mu)$, $\mu$ dominant polynomial, converted from right to left by star. Its highest vector $v$ has weight $\mu$ and norm $1$. The local lemma [F3] proves from the tensorword endomorphism realization that negative coefficient operators span each weight space, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector, and integral cut-root words span every grade whose simple-root coefficients are $0$ or $1$. It also proves the complete essential-subset basis and the dimension formula $\dim L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha(r,s)}=\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$. The local lemma [F3] also proves for every dominant $a$ and every interval, by finite matching/path/stack bijections and finite triangular matrix inversion, $\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s)$, where $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$. These are actual proved local inputs, including all zero dimensions and arbitrary nonrestricted auxiliary weights. [F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 We spell out a further modular consequence of the same foundation to close the algebraic support seam. Let $\Gamma$ be a deficit with each simple-root coefficient $0$ or $1$, with disconnected support $\Gamma=\delta+\zeta$ separated by at least one zero coefficient. Take the first component $\delta$ entirely inside the Levi on the first $N-1$ coordinates. Every negative cut word of grade $\Gamma$ factors uniquely into a $\delta$-word and a $\zeta$-word, since no root crossing a missing simple root can occur; the two groups commute. Every positive coefficient word of grade $\Gamma$ similarly factors. All positive/negative cross commutators between the separated groups vanish. Consequently the matrix of highest coefficients at $\Gamma$ is the tensor product of the two separate coefficient matrices at $\delta$ and $\zeta$: for positive tests $e,e'$ and negative words $f,f'$, $\operatorname{highest}(ee'ff'v)=\operatorname{highest}(efv)\operatorname{highest}(e'f'v)$. The rightmost separated test/word leaves the Cartan coordinates of the other interval unchanged, since the intervals are nonadjacent; this verifies the displayed equality even though $f'fv$ has shifted weight. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Choose bases $f_av$ and $f'_bv$ of the separate images. Positive detection yields positive linear-combination tests $e_a$ and $e'_b$ with $e_af_cv=\delta_{ac}v$, $e'_bf'_dv=\delta_{bd}v$, by finite matrix inversion over the field. Thus the products $f_af'_bv$ are independent, since $e_ae'_b$ tests detect their coefficients; they span by the preceding factorization. On the entire weight space at $\Gamma$ the operator $P_\delta=\sum_a f_ae_a$ is the identity: applied to $f_cf'_bv$, its cross commutations give $f_cf'_bv$. Every $e_a$ is a positive Levi coefficient word of nonzero weight $\delta$, and every $f_a$ is a negative Levi coefficient word. This argument proves the identity on arbitrary entangled linear combinations, not only pure products. If a separate image is zero, the full weight space is zero and cannot supply a primitive vector. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Now let $M_0\subset M_1$ be consecutive terms of a finite composition series of the first level, and choose $x\in M_1$ representing the highest vector of a simple factor, of full deficit $\Gamma$. Positive Levi operators of nonzero weight send $x$ into $M_0$, because they annihilate its highest class. If $\Gamma$ had a disconnected initial component $\delta$, the identity $P_\delta x=x$ would put $x$ into $M_0$: $e_ax\in M_0$ and $f_a$ preserve $M_0$. This is impossible. Hence any primitive factor vector of binary deficit ending at the last simple root has support a single terminal interval. This is the disconnected-root primitive exclusion, proved here, without a characteristic-zero PBW theorem or a pure-product assumption for $x$. [step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Suppose $\mu_N=0$ and let $l=N-1$. Define the first level $M$ as the sum of weight spaces of $L_N(\mu)$ whose last diagonal coordinate is $1$. It is a polynomial Schur/$\mathrm{GL}_{N-1}$ module of degree $|\mu|-1$; the Levi preserves that coordinate. Put $\beta_i=\alpha_i+\cdots+\alpha_l$. For any $i$ write $\nu_i=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{N-1})-\epsilon_i$, as a weight, and write $d_i=\dim L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\beta_i}$, $b_u=[M:L_{N-1}(\nu_u)]$ when $\nu_u$ is dominant, and $b_u=0$ otherwise. Dominance of $\nu_u$ is equivalent to $a_u>0$. No modular restriction condition is imposed on a dominant $\nu_u$. In particular non-$p$-restricted factors still contribute to all character equations below. [step 4.1, construct]

6.1 A simple factor contributing to the $\nu_i$ weight must have highest weight $\eta$ dominating $\nu_i$. The standard Schur cell simples have unique highest vector, all other weights dominated by it, and cover all simple Schur modules by the cellular regular-module argument. Thus this statement applies to every factor over every field. Lift $\eta$ by appending the last coordinate $1$, and let $\Gamma=\mu-(\eta,1)$. Since $\eta$ is a weight of the first level, $\Gamma$ is a nonnegative integral combination of simple roots; since $\eta$ dominates $\nu_i$, $\beta_i-\Gamma$ is a nonnegative integral combination of Levi roots. Consequently $\Gamma_j=0$ for $j<i$, $\Gamma_j\in\{0,1\}$ for $i\le j<l$, and $\Gamma_l=1$. The support exclusion just proved forces $\Gamma=\beta_u$ for some $u\ge i$. Thus $\eta=\nu_u$ and $\nu_u$ must be dominant. Only these terminal labels can contribute to this character equation; no stronger assertion about the other first-level factors is needed. [step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Weight-space dimensions are additive on a composition series. Indeed the actual weight idempotents give direct projections, so taking a fixed torus weight is exact. The own highest weight of $L_{N-1}(\nu_i)$, when defined, has dimension $1$. Thus $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u>i}b_ua_{iu}$, $a_{iu}=\dim L_{N-1}(\nu_u)_{\nu_i}$. For an invalid $\nu_u$ its term is omitted. The lower weight deficit is $\nu_u-\nu_i=\epsilon_i-\epsilon_u=\alpha_i+\cdots+\alpha_{u-1}$. The fundamental coordinates of $\nu_u$ on that interval are $a_i,\ldots,a_{u-2},a_{u-1}+1$. Any altered coordinate at $u$ is outside the interval and has no effect on the local formulas. The proved interval-basis theorem therefore gives $d_i=\varepsilon_a(i,l)$, $a_{iu}=\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$. This is valid for every legitimate dominant $\nu_u$, including those not $p$-restricted. When $a_u=0$, $\nu_u$ is nondominant and $b_u=0$; also $\nu_a(u,l)=0$ because its root is not normal. [step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Substitute these dimensions into the character equation and compare it with the local recurrence of [F3] at $(i,l)$: $\varepsilon_a(i,l)=b_i+\sum_{u>i}b_u\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$, $\varepsilon_a(i,l)=\nu_a(i,l)+\sum_{u>i}\nu_a(u,l)\varepsilon'_a(i,u-1)$. Starting at $i=l$ and proceeding downwards proves $b_i=\nu_a(i,l)$ for all $i$. This is finite integer reverse substitution, never reduction of the character multiplicities modulo $p$. The rank is $N-1$, unrelated to the prime except in the $B,C$ zero tests. [step 7.1, construct]

9.1 The local lemma [F3] uses only the infinite purely transcendental extension $K=F(t)$ for polynomial identities and Gaussian elimination. Its scalar-extension argument is reversible: all cut/raising matrices have entries in $F$, hence their finite ranks and kernels preserve extension; its essential labels and pivot tests yield bases over $F$ itself. Schur cell simples remain simple under every field extension by the cellular rank-one action and their nonzero form. Extending a finite Schur composition series thus retains the simple factors and their labels, so the integers $b_i$ computed over $K$ are exactly those over $F$. The first-level weight subspace commutes with extension because it is the image of a finite sum of weight idempotents. Neither an algebraic closure nor an assumption that the original field is infinite is used. All nil/zero-weight cases remain in the equations. [step 8.1, construct]

10.1 Let $\lambda$ be $p$-regular, $\lambda\ne(n)$, put $N=n$, $\mu=\lambda'$, $\mu_N=0$. The index of $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ is $i=\lambda_j$, not $j$, and not $p$. The coordinate $a_u=\mu_u-\mu_{u+1}$ is the multiplicity of the part $u$ in $\lambda$; in particular $a_u<p$, but the preceding algebraic proof did not need that restriction. A removable $A$ is the last row of its width $i$ block, hence $j=\mu_i$. [step 9.1, construct]

11.1 The root normal walk based at $i$ starts with a push for $A$ and scans $u=i+1,\ldots,l$. At coordinates with $a_u=0$ the compensation walk is neutral, even when $B=C=0$: the same position supplies and consumes a compensation slot. At positive coordinates $u$, the last ordinary row $k$ of the width $u$ block gives a removable node, and $C(i,u)=u-i+\sum_{t=i}^{u-1}a_t=u-\lambda_j+j-k$. Thus $C(i,u)=0$ is exactly the removable node's residue equal to $A$'s residue. The first ordinary row $k$ of the width $u$ block has an addable node in column $u+1$, and $B(i,u)=u-i+\sum_{t=i}^{u}a_t=u-\lambda_j+j-k+1$. Thus $B(i,u)=0$ is exactly that addable node's residue equal to $A$'s residue. Since $0<a_u<p$ at a positive coordinate, $B=C+a_u$ shows these two events cannot occur together at that same $u$. Empty widths give only the neutral compensation case. The artificial final zero-width row also has no effect. Scanning positive $u$ in increasing order lists the ordinary corners above $A$ in the order $j-1,\ldots,1$, with a width block contributing its boundary event when the residue matches. The top extra addable node of width $\lambda_1+1$ is already the $B$ event of the width $\lambda_1$ coordinate; no boundary event is omitted. [step 10.1, construct]

12.1 Under transpose a removable ordinary node becomes a removable $\mu$-node of opposite residue, and an addable becomes an addable of opposite residue. The top-to-bottom $\mu$-signature following $A'$ lists exactly these above ordinary nodes in this order. The only possible equal-column lower ordinary addable node lies immediately below $A$ and has residue differing by $1$, so it is absent from this residue class. Consequently the root push/pop walk is exactly the reduced-signature stack after $A'$: push a removable $-$, pop on an addable $+$, implementing cancellation $-+$. [step 11.1, construct]

13.1 Earlier signature signs do not change whether $A'$ or any later push is removed. $A$ survives precisely when no later prefix has more pops than pushes; this is exactly root normality $\sigma(i,l)$. If it survives, the final stack consists of $A$ together with those above ordinary removable nodes in $A$'s residue class whose transposes survive as normal nodes. The stack proof of [F3] identifies this final stack with $N(i,l)$, so $\nu_a(i,l)=0$ if $A$ is not normal, and $\nu_a(i,l)=1+\#\{\text{normal removable nodes strictly above }A\text{ of }A\text{'s residue}\}$ if $A$ is normal. The node count here is piecewise. It is not the unconditioned count of normal nodes weakly above $A$ when $A$ is nonnormal. [step 12.1, construct]

14.1 Work at $q=1$ with right Schur modules, reversing the star conversion used for the algebraic count. The Hecke presentation has $T_i^2=1$ and the symmetric-group braid relations; its standard basis $T_w$ maps bijectively to the group basis $w$, so $H(F,1,S_m)=FS_m$. Let $e$ be the weight projection of type $\omega=(1^m)$, with $\operatorname{End}_H(H)=H$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. The normalized semistandard map $\varphi_{ST}$ is supported from $\operatorname{type}(T)$ to $\operatorname{type}(S)$. Thus $e\varphi_{ST}e$ survives exactly when both types are $\omega$. These tableaux are ordinary standard tableaux, their defining fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ gives $\varphi_{st}\mapsto m_{st}$. The higher Schur ideal corner is exactly the higher Murphy ideal, as equality of the corresponding basis spans. The projection on a Weyl cell fixes $w_T$ exactly for $\operatorname{type}(T)=\omega$. To read its right $H$ action, choose the independent fixed outer index also of type $\omega$; evaluation at $1$ then turns $\varphi_{st}\rho_h$ into $m_{st}h$ modulo the corresponding higher ideal. Hence $W^\xi e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$ by $w_t\mapsto c_t$, with the actual same-shape Murphy action, over every field. [step 13.1, F1, F2, construct]

15.1 Choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of shape $\xi$ and type $\omega$ in the Schur cell product $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\xi(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$. Evaluate every map at $1$ in the corner. The Murphy product is $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\xi(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so its independent cell-product coefficient gives $B_\xi(w_s,w_t)=G_{\mathrm M,\xi}(c_s,c_t)$. The scalar is exactly $1$. Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\xi(xe,y(1-e))=B_\xi(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. Thus the Weyl decomposition $W^\xi=W^\xi e\oplus W^\xi(1-e)$ is orthogonal, and $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\xi e)=\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\xi)e$, including an identically zero corner form. The canonical shape/type $\xi$ diagonal is the projection onto $M^\xi$ and is idempotent, so the same cell-product coefficient gives canonical norm $1$; $L^\xi=W^\xi/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}$ is nonzero simple. Projection by $e$ is exact (lift $ye$ by $xe$, and kernels are intersections fixed by $e$), so $L^\xi e\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$, including zero. At $q=1$ the unit form comparison [F2] gives $D_{\mathrm M}(\xi)\cong D^{\xi'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ when $\xi'$ is regular, and zero otherwise by the published ordinary radical criterion. These nonzero quotients are distinctly labelled group simples. This proves restricted survival locally and uses no general finite-e classification. [step 14.1, F2, F4, construct]

16.1 Take $N=m=n$ and the tensorword realization of $S(N,m)$ already proved in [F3]. Let $p$ be the sum of all actual weight projections with last coordinate $1$. Its tensorwords have exactly one occurrence of $N$. Identify their remaining ordered positions with $(F^{N-1})^{\otimes(m-1)}$. For each lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$, define $\kappa(E_A)=E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$, where the last row and column have only their final entry $1$. On every word with one $N$ this map preserves its position and applies $E_A$ to the other positions. Consequently products are exactly the lower products, $\kappa(1)=p$, and $\kappa$ embeds $S(N-1,m-1)$ as a unital subalgebra of $pS(N,m)p$. This describes the lower Schur action on $Xp$, and for the star-converted left simple it is exactly the block-diagonal $\mathrm{GL}_{N-1}$ action used in the character calculation, because $g^{\otimes(m-1)}$ expands in $E_A$ and $\operatorname{diag}(g,1)$ acts at the unchanged $N$ position. Transpose sends $E_A$ to $E_{A^{\mathsf t}}$, so $\kappa$ respects star. The first level counted above is therefore precisely $L_N(\mu)p$, converted to the right; no source-only definition of first level is being substituted. [step 15.1, F1, F3, construct]

17.1 Let $e'$ be the lower regular-type projection $(1^{N-1})$. In this embedding $\kappa(e')=e$, the full type $(1^N)$ projection. Use the explicit coset-word map $m_\nu T_d\mapsto(\text{row of entry }j\text{ in }t^\nu d)_j$. On the regular type its jth letter is $jd^{-1}$, in right permutation notation. Consequently $\rho_h:d\mapsto hd$ changes a regular word by the corresponding label permutation $h^{-1}$, because $(hd)^{-1}=d^{-1}h^{-1}$. A lower corner element $\rho'_h$ acts by this same label permutation $h^{-1}$ on $1,\ldots,N-1$ and fixes label $N$. The orbit embedding therefore gives exactly $\rho_h$ on the full regular tensorword basis, with no extra inversion or opposite-algebra map. Thus $\kappa(\rho'_h)=\rho_h$, with the subgroup action in the right convention exactly $X\rho_h$. Consequently $(Xp)e'=Xe$ as $FS_{N-1}$-modules, with the latter the ordinary restriction of $Xe$. Apply this to $X=L_N(\mu)$. This is the complete local $q=1$ first-level/corner identity; it is independent of the held generic comparison. [step 16.1, construct]

18.1 Apply the exact lower projection $e'$ to a finite composition series of $L_N(\mu)p$. Each factor $L_{N-1}(\eta)$ becomes $D_{\mathrm M}(\eta)$, proved by the lower-rank form/corner calculation of steps 14.1–15.1; it is a distinctly labelled simple when $\eta$ is restricted, and zero otherwise. Deleting repeated terms leaves a composition series of the group restriction corner. Thus the multiplicity of a restricted $\eta$ agrees exactly with its lower Schur multiplicity. Nonrestricted $\eta$ were retained in the earlier character calculation and are killed only here. For $\mu=\lambda'$, [F2] gives $L_N(\mu)e\cong D^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$. The candidate $\nu_i=(\lambda\setminus A)'$ is restricted by the regular-removal hypothesis, and its image is $D^{\lambda\setminus A}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$. Hence the desired group restriction multiplicity is $b_i$. Twisting both modules by sign preserves multiplicity because sign of $S_n$ restricts to sign of $S_{n-1}$. To match a left-module convention for the ordinary $D$ in the Statement, apply the exact inverse/star equivalence from right group modules to left ones, $g\cdot x=xg^{-1}$. It commutes with restriction and sign twisting and preserves composition series. The ordinary polytabloid quotient is the same partition-labelled quotient in this convention; if the dictionary uses its contragredient realization, the induced nondegenerate invariant quotient form identifies that simple with its contragredient. Explicitly $x\mapsto(y\mapsto\beta(x,y))$ is bijective and equivariant since $\beta(gx,y)=\beta(x,g^{-1}y)$. This uses the form only after passing to the nonzero radical quotient, as in [[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]; no self-duality of a possibly degenerate Specht module is assumed. Together with the algebraic count and signature calculation, this gives both displayed cases of the theorem. [step 17.1, F2, F4, construct]

19.1 For $\lambda=(n)$ the ordinary simple is trivial and restricts trivially, so the unique removable node has multiplicity $1$. Its transposed $\mu=(1^n)$ node is normal: no subsequent same-residue addable can cancel it, and the preceding possible addable gives a $+-$ pair rather than a cancellation. There are no above ordinary removables. For $n=1$ this is the one-dimensional restriction to $S_0$; for $n=0$ the removable-node hypothesis is empty. These cases avoid requiring $\mu_N=0$ where it is false. All primes, all fields of characteristic $p$, all $p$-regular $\lambda$ and all regular removals retain the original stated scope. [step 18.1, construct]

20.1 The piecewise integer $\gamma(A)=\mathbf1_{A\text{ normal}}$ times the number of normal nodes weakly above $A$ has value zero off normality and is at least one on normality, since $A$ itself is counted. The preceding multiplicity and boundary proofs therefore establish both the formula and its stated equivalence over every field of characteristic $p$. [step 19.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The proof supplies the full local first-level count and signature calculation. The source Theorems 9.3 and 1.4 document its origin and are not proof premises. The rank is $n-1$ and the root interval starts at $\lambda_j$; the prime appears only in zero tests. All lower dominant Schur factors, including nonrestricted ones, are retained until the exact corner functor kills their images. The former unconditional above-count equivalence was false: for $p=2$, $\lambda=(5,3,1)$, $A=(3,1)$, $A$ is nonnormal while a normal node of its residue exists above it. The piecewise correction preserves both original displayed cases.

items.title: Normal-node composition multiplicities under residue restriction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $A$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ such that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
is again $p$-restricted; let $D(\mu)$ be the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$ in the dual-Specht (cellular) convention, so that
$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]],
[[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]), and let
$E_i$ be the residue-summand functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not a normal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B:\ B\ \text{normal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly below }A\}$$
(counting $A$ itself) if $A$ is normal. The corresponding
Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion (Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5, equivalently
Kleshchev II Theorem 0.4) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$, a removable $i$-node $A=(r,\mu_r)$ with $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
$p$-restricted, and the residue-summand functor $E_i$.

[F1] $\operatorname{Res}^{S_d}_{S_{d-1}}M=\bigoplus_jE_jM$, and $E_jM$ is the
sum of the generalized eigenspaces of the last Jucys-Murphy element
$L_d=T_d-T_{d-1}$ with eigenvalue $j$, for every finite-dimensional
$kS_d$-module $M$; here $T_m=\sum_{1\le a<b\le m}(a\ b)$ is the
transposition class sum of $S_m$
([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]],
[[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]).

[F2] The central transposition class sum $T_m$ acts on the ordinary integral Specht lattice and every field specialization by the total content $z_\xi=\sum_{(r,c)\in[\xi]}(c-r)$ ([[lem-transposition-class-sum-acts-on-a-specht-module-by-total-content]]). At $m=0,1$, both the class sum and total content are zero directly. The actual same-shape perfect pairing identifies the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$ with the star dual of the ordinary Specht module ([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]). Since $T_m^*=T_m$, the same scalar acts on that dual and its nonzero form quotient $D(\xi)$. This uses the ordinary module itself, not a false ordinary/Murphy equality of form radicals.

[F3] For a $p$-restricted $\nu$, the module $D(\nu)$ is nonzero, simple,
self-dual and absolutely irreducible, so every $kS_{d-1}$-endomorphism of
$D(\nu)$ is a scalar ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).

[F4] The complete locally proved piecewise count is [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]]. For the ordinary regular label $\lambda=\mu'$ and the transposed removable node $A'$, its multiplicity is zero off normality and counts the same-residue normal nodes weakly above $A'$ on normality. The group sign/conjugate dictionary and signature order in [F5] transport this exact count; no bibliographic normal-node theorem is a proof premise.

[F5] The dictionary between the two conventions: transposing exchanges
removable nodes of $\lambda$ with removable nodes of $\lambda'$, exchanges
"strictly above" for the dual order of the same residue class, and negates
residues, $c-r\mapsto r-c$; the normal nodes of $\lambda'$ in the signature
sense are exactly the transposes of the normal nodes of $\lambda$ in
Brundan's sense ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Localization of an occurring factor. On $D(\mu)$ the class sum $T_d$ acts by $z_\mu$ by [F2], hence it acts by that scalar on the whole restriction. The operator $L_d=T_d-T_{d-1}$ on this restriction is therefore $z_\mu-T_{d-1}$, a central $kS_{d-1}$ operator preserving every submodule. If $D(\nu)$ occurs as a composition factor, [F2] gives its $T_{d-1}$ scalar $z_\nu$. Thus $L_d$ acts on this factor by $z_\mu-z_\nu=c(A)-r(A)=i$. The generalized primary projections are exact by [F1]; every occurrence of this factor lies in $E_iD(\mu)$, and none in another summand. Consequently $[E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]=[D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}}:D(\nu)]$, also when both sides are zero. This does not assert that a factor occurs before its multiplicity is computed. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Apply the local count [F4] to $\lambda=\mu'$ and the ordinary node $A'$. The group dictionary is $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ and likewise for $\nu$; sign restricts to sign, so simultaneous twist preserves the restriction multiplicity. Transposing negates residues and reverses the order of corners in a fixed residue class, as [F5] states. The ordinary piecewise formula is therefore zero when $A$ is not normal, and otherwise is the number of normal $i$-nodes weakly below $A$, counting $A$ itself. Combine this with step 1.1. The unconditioned weakly-below count is not used off normality. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $p=3$ and $\mu=(3,3,2,1,1)$, the normal residue-$2$ nodes are $(3,2)$ and $(5,1)$; the same-residue signature has the two minus signs and no plus sign. The two respective regular removals give multiplicities $2$ and $1$ by step 2.1. At degree one the same argument gives the one-dimensional restriction to $S_0$; degree zero has no removable node. Thus the boundary cases and both displayed cases are included. No Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion is asserted. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The complete count proof is the local first-level supplier, built from the integral root-interval basis and finite essential-subset recurrence. The cited Kleshchev and Brundan papers document the historical source of this formula; they are not external proof premises. The new local contribution here is the conditional class-sum localization and the exact transpose/sign transport. No unconditional count or implication from a zero form quotient to a zero actual module head is used.

items.title: Conormal-node composition multiplicities under residue induction
items.statement:
In the notation of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]], let
$B$ be an addable $i$-node of the $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ such that
$\nu=\mu\cup B$ is again $p$-restricted, and let $F_i$ be the residue-summand
induction functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $B$ is not a conormal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B':\ B'\ \text{conormal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly above }B\}$$
(counting $B$ itself) if $B$ is conormal. The dual Specht-to-induction Hom
criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, an addable residue-$i$ node $B$ such that $\nu=\mu+B$ is $p$-restricted, and the actual residue induction functor $F_i$.

[F1] The actual Schur coefficient foundation and root-interval basis/count supplier holds over every field, for arbitrary dominant polynomial weights and all intervals. Negative coefficient words span, positive coefficient words detect, binary-root weight spaces have dimension $E_a(r,s)=\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, and the finite integer recurrence is $E_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^sE'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s)$, with $E'_a(r,t)=E_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$. Its normal-stack proof includes zero coordinates and killed roots ([[lem-type-a-modular-root-interval-essential-subset-basis-and-count]]).

[F2] The proved local $q=1$ Schur/group corner in steps 14.1–15.1 of [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]] identifies the regular Weyl corner and cell form with the Murphy cell and form, with scalar $1$, and proves equality of their radical corners. Thus $L_N(\lambda)e=D(\lambda)$ for restricted $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise; surviving labels are distinct. Its tensorword convention is explicit, and its proof uses ordinary-group survival rather than the held finite-$e$ classifier. The integral ordinary Specht basis and signed-conjugate identification are [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].

[F3] On the complex ordinary Specht module, the joint Jucys–Murphy spectrum is the tableau-content spectrum ([[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]]). Only its integral central operator-identity consequence is used, not any characteristic-zero composition count.

[F4] The boundary signature is read top to bottom with addable $+$, removable $-$ and cancellation $-+$ ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). The actual primary projections define the direct residue decomposition of induction ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]). Neither primitive-block classification nor an adjunction transfer of composition counts is used.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $d>0$ take $N=d+1$, pad $\mu$ by zeros, set $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$, let $L=L_N(\mu)$ be the actual Schur simple, $V=F^N$, and $M=V\otimes L$. Tensor coefficient operators are the actual polynomial Schur operators of degree $d+1$, obtained by multiplying the two polynomial matrix actions. This works over finite fields without replacing coefficient actions by evaluated group elements. The case $d=0$ is treated below. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Here is the local component identity used below. If a binary root deficit has separated connected components (a zero simple-root coefficient between consecutive components), its negative words split into products supported on those components. All cross-component positive and negative root operators commute, and their Cartan characters on the other component are unchanged: their simple-root supports are nonadjacent. Move the positive words past the other components and evaluate their highest coefficients one component at a time. The positive/negative coefficient matrix is consequently the tensor product of the component matrices. Negative-word spanning and positive detection identify its quotient by the common positive-test kernel with the actual simple weight space. Hence this weight space is the tensor product of the component quotients, including when one is zero. This proves the assertion directly from coefficient words; it does not assume a tensor-product decomposition of the whole simple module. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

3.1 In particular fix one component $\delta$. Choose a negative basis $f_1v,\ldots,f_tv$ of its quotient and positive tests $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ dual to it. They are finite linear combinations of actual coefficient words, with coefficients in $F$; their existence follows from positive detection and ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra. Then $P_\delta=\sum_{h=1}^t f_he_h$ is the identity on every binary weight space having this component and any separated other components. The same tests apply because the other components change none of the Cartan data of $\delta$. If $t=0$, these weight spaces are zero. This is an identity of coefficient operators on those spaces, so it descends to subquotients. [step 2.1, F1, F2, construct]

4.1 Write $\xi_i=\mu+\epsilon_i$. Suppose a simple composition factor with highest weight $\eta$ contributes at $\xi_i$. All weights of $M$ are at most $\mu+\epsilon_1$, and weights of that factor are at most $\eta$. Thus $\xi_i\le\eta\le\mu+\epsilon_1.$ [step 3.1, F1, F2, construct]

5.1 The deficit $\Gamma=\mu+\epsilon_1-\eta$ has simple-root coefficients $0$ or $1$ in positions $1,\ldots,i-1$ and zero elsewhere. On a tensor summand $v_j\otimes L_{\eta-\epsilon_j}$ the deficit in $L$ is $\Gamma-(\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_{j-1}).$ [step 4.1, F1, F2, construct]

6.1 It must be nonnegative. Consequently every possible label $j$ lies before the first missing coefficient in $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ has a component $\delta$ after that first gap, every positive or negative coefficient word supported on $\delta$ fixes the $V$ factor (its nonconstant terms annihilate each of these labels). Its action on this tensor weight is therefore purely its action on $L$. The preceding $P_\delta$ is the identity on the entire weight $M_\eta$, not just on individual tensor summands. [step 5.1, F1, F2, construct]

7.1 Choose a composition series and a lift $x\in M_\eta$ of the nonzero highest vector of the proposed factor in its series quotient. Each $e_hx$ lies in the preceding submodule because it has strictly higher weight, and each $f_h$ preserves that submodule. But $P_\delta x=x$ would then place $x$ in it, a contradiction. If the component quotient is zero there was no such tensor weight to start with. Thus $\Gamma$ has no later component. Its only possible nonzero coefficients form one initial interval, and $\eta=\mu+\epsilon_u\quad\text{for some }u\le i.$ [step 6.1, F1, F2, construct]

8.1 This excludes only highest weights of factors contributing to $\xi_i$. It asserts nothing about distant tensor factors. [step 7.1, F1, F2, construct]

9.1 Since every weight of $L$ is at most $\mu$, $M_{\xi_i}=\bigoplus_{j\le i}v_j\otimes L_{\mu+\epsilon_i-\epsilon_j},\qquad d_i:=\dim M_{\xi_i}=1+\sum_{j<i}E_a(j,i-1).$ [step 8.1, F1, F2, construct]

10.1 Let $b_u$ be the actual composition multiplicity of $L_N(\mu+\epsilon_u)$ in $M$ when that weight is dominant; set $b_u=0$ otherwise. No restrictedness condition is imposed on these auxiliary factors. The support lemma and the one-dimensional highest spaces give $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u<i}b_uE_{a+\omega_u}(u,i-1).$ (equation C). [step 9.1, F1, F2, construct]

11.1 Indeed $\mu+\epsilon_u-\xi_i=\alpha_u+\cdots+\alpha_{i-1}$. On this interval the fundamental coordinates of the dominant weight $\mu+\epsilon_u$ are those of $a$ with its first coordinate $u$ increased by one; the coordinate $u-1$ changed by minus one lies outside the interval. Nondominant rows have multiplicity zero, so their formal summands cause no alteration of (C). [step 10.1, F1, F2, construct]

12.1 For completeness the weight-dimension symmetry needed here is local. Permutation matrices permute the integer weight spaces of $L$. Hence its lowest weight is $w_0\mu$, its space is one dimensional, and every weight lies between $w_0\mu$ and $\mu$. The contragredient dual twisted by $\det^d$ is a polynomial simple of highest weight $\mu^*=(d-\mu_N,\ldots,d-\mu_1).$ [step 11.1, F1, F2, construct]

13.1 One can verify polynomiality without a rational-module classification theorem. The tensorword Schur algebra acts faithfully on $V^{\otimes d}$; its regular module embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of this tensor space by its action on a basis. Thus every simple is a subquotient of copies of this tensor space. Duality and the twist make it a subquotient of $(V^*\otimes\det)^{\otimes d}$; the explicit exterior-complement pairing gives $V^*\otimes\det\cong\bigwedge^{N-1}V$ over every field. It is therefore polynomial. Positive and negative coefficients interchange under duality, so the highest weight just identified determines the same actual Schur simple as in the accepted foundation. These statements are coefficient identities; over a finite field they can equivalently be checked over $F(t)$ and descended as the identical finite matrices. [step 12.1, F1, F2, construct]

14.1 Put $\bar a_t=a_{N-t}$. Duality reverses roots and preserves weight dimensions, yielding $E_a(j,i-1)=E_{\bar a}(N-i+1,N-j).$ [step 13.1, F1, F2, construct]

15.1 This argument applies also to any dominant shifted weight. In particular the first-coordinate shift at $u$ becomes the final-coordinate shift at $N-u$ on the reversed interval. No restriction on its fundamental coordinates is needed. [step 14.1, F1, F2, construct]

16.1 Reverse the indices: $r=N-i+1$, $\bar b_r=b_i$, $\bar d_r=d_i$. On indices $1,\ldots,N$, let the strictly upper triangular matrices be $A[r,v]=\nu'_{\bar a}(r,v-1),\qquad B[r,v]=E'_{\bar a}(r,v-1)\quad(r<v).$ [step 15.1, F1, construct]

17.1 For $r<v$, apply the accepted recurrence to $[r,v-1]$ after increasing coordinate $v-1$. Every earlier interval $[r,u-1]$ with $u<v$ is unaffected, while the tail normal count is shifted at $v-1$. Thus $B[r,v]=A[r,v]+\sum_{r<u<v}B[r,u]A[u,v]$, or $B=A+BA$. Hence $(I+B)(I-A)=I$. Since these are finite integer matrices, the inverse is two-sided and $(I+B)^{-1}=I-A$. Equivalently, the supplier's first-cut recurrence gives $B=A+AB$ and $I+B=I+A+\cdots+A^{N-1}$. [step 16.1, F1, construct]

18.1 Let $H_r=\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)$, with $H_N=0$. Applying the accepted recurrence separately for every endpoint and summing gives $\bar d=\mathbf1+(I+B)H.$ [step 17.1, F1, construct]

19.1 Opposition turns (C) into $\bar d=(I+B)\bar b$. Multiplication by $I-A$ gives, as ordinary integers, $b_i=1+\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\bigl(\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)-\nu'_{\bar a}(r,s)\bigr),\qquad r=N-i+1.$ (equation D). [step 18.1, F1, construct]

20.1 This is finite nilpotent matrix arithmetic. It neither divides in $F$ nor replaces a composition multiplicity by a residue in $F$. [step 19.1, F1, construct]

21.1 Use the accepted normal-stack interpretation; every coordinate and $B,C$ equality tested in this paragraph and the endpoint analysis is modulo $p$, whereas stack heights are ordinary integers. Write $\sigma(r,t)$ for its alive indicator and put $\sigma(r,r-1)=1$. For every dominant coordinate array $\lambda$, $\nu_\lambda(r,s)-\nu'_\lambda(r,s)=\sigma(r,s-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}\right).$ (equation E). [step 20.1, F1, construct]

22.1 If killed before the final step, both counts are zero. Otherwise let its current height be $h\ge1$. The endpoint shift keeps $C(r,s)$ fixed and replaces $B$ and $\lambda_s$ by $B+1$ and $\lambda_s+1$. If $B=-1$ it creates a pop and lowers the count by one; when $\lambda_s=-1$, the unshifted step instead pushes and the shifted zero-coordinate step is neutral, with the same difference. If $B=0$ it removes a pop and increases the count by one; when $\lambda_s=0$, the old step is neutral and the new step pushes, again with that difference. For other $B$ neither change alters the count. If a pop removes the initial root, its new count is zero, still $h-1=0$. At $s=r$ the two counts are $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r\ne0}$ and $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r+1\ne0}$, giving the same formula. These alternatives are exhaustive and valid for $p=2$. [step 21.1, F1, construct]

23.1 Fix an actual addable row $i$ and put $R_j=\mu_j+1-j$, $\rho=R_i\pmod p$. If $i>1$, addability means $a_{i-1}>0$. Since $\mu$ is restricted, $0<a_{i-1}<p$; the reversed root therefore starts alive. For $r=N-i+1$, $s=N-j$, direct substitution gives $B_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_j-R_i-1,\qquad C_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_{j+1}-R_i.$ [step 22.1, F1, F4, construct]

24.1 Thus the two indicators in (E) respectively detect an addable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$ and a removable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$. The normal stack processes the boundary in reverse order, starting with the chosen $+$ in row $i$. At step $j$ its $C=0$ push corresponds to the plus in row $j+1$, and its $B=0$ pop to the minus in row $j$. The top-row plus is a pending final event. This reversal is exactly the stack evaluation of $-+$ cancellation: in a reverse scan, a minus cancels the most recently encountered plus. [step 23.1, F1, F4, construct]

25.1 Here is the precise check at flat row blocks and at the endpoints. Let $D_s=1+\sum_{t=r}^s\sigma(r,t-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=0}\right).$ [step 24.1, F1, F4, construct]

26.1 While the chosen root remains alive, $D_s$ is its current normal-stack height plus the pending indicator $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}$, where $j=N-s$. At the initial step the removable event $B(r,r)=0$ cannot occur since $0<a_{i-1}<p$, and this identity follows immediately. At each subsequent live step the change in height is $\mathbf1_{C(r,s)=0}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}.$ [step 25.1, F1, F4, construct]

27.1 For $a_j\ne0$ these are disjoint push/pop events. For $a_j=0$ the indicators are equal and the step is neutral, as required by the actual stack. Subtracting this height change from the change in $D_s$ gives $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}-\mathbf1_{R_{j+1}=R_i},$ [step 26.1, F1, F4, construct]

28.1 which replaces the previous pending indicator by the next. This proves the invariant by induction, including flat blocks. Equivalently, at each flat boundary $a_j=0$, the virtual removable sign in row $j$ and virtual addable sign in row $j+1$ have the same residue and form an adjacent $-+$ pair in the selected-residue row-boundary word. Deleting these pairs restores exactly the actual boundary word. By signature confluence their insertion or deletion has no effect on the surviving actual nodes. The chosen node is an actual addable, so it is never among the virtual pairs. [step 27.1, F1, F4, construct]

29.1 If the initial root is killed, its preceding height was one, the current event is $B=0$, and $B=-1$ is false. The pending indicator after the step is zero. Thus $D_s=0$, and every later term is zero because the alive indicator remains zero. In the reversed boundary scan, killing the initial plus likewise means that the chosen node is canceled; later pluses above it cannot revive it. At the last step the pending indicator is the actual addable top-row plus. We have therefore evaluated exactly the reverse scan of the prefix ending at the chosen node. A minus below this prefix cannot cancel a plus in it under top-to-bottom $-+$ cancellation; the conormal decisions for this prefix agree with those in the entire signature. [step 28.1, F1, F4, construct]

30.1 Consequently (D) is zero precisely when the chosen plus is canceled. If it survives, (D) is the number of surviving pluses of residue $\rho$ in the prefix, namely the number of conormal nodes weakly above $B$. For $i=1$, (D) is $b_1=1$: the top plus survives and it is the only node weakly above itself. For completeness, a nondominant row $i>1$ has $a_{i-1}=0$; the first endpoint difference is $-1$, killing the virtual initial unit and all later differences, so (D) gives zero as required by (C). These rows were not silently discarded during the integer inversion. [step 29.1, F1, F4, construct]

31.1 Let $\omega=(1^N)$ be the regular degree-$N$ weight. Then $M_\omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N v_j\otimes L_{\omega-\epsilon_j}.$ [step 30.1, F2, construct]

32.1 Let $G=\mathfrak S_N$, $H=\mathfrak S_d$ fixing label $N$, and $W=L_{\omega-\epsilon_N}$. The accepted local $q=1$ corner/form calculation applies to degree $d$ and rank $N$ with regular weight $(1^d,0)$: its surviving semistandard indices are precisely standard tableaux, and evaluating the corner at $1$ gives the same Murphy basis and scalar-$1$ form, regardless of the unused last label. Its radical-corner equality therefore makes $W$ the left group module $D(\mu)$. To fix the action convention, the supplier's right corner element $\rho_h$ permutes tensorword labels by $h^{-1}$; star conversion makes left $g$ act by right $g^{-1}$, hence by label permutation $g$. The same conversion in the degree-$N$ corner gives the output action. Thus the output regular-corner action is ordinary permutation of labels: on tensorwords the corresponding orbit matrix is exactly that label permutation. Since these are identities in the actual tensorword Schur algebra, the same equality holds on $M$; it does not depend on evaluated permutation matrices spanning the Schur algebra. [step 31.1, F2, construct]

33.1 The explicit map $F[G]\otimes_{F[H]}W\longrightarrow M_\omega,\qquad g\otimes w\longmapsto g(v_N\otimes w)$. [step 32.1, F2, construct]

34.1 is well defined and $G$-equivariant. Left cosets of $H$ correspond to the image label $gN$, and their summands map bijectively to the displayed summands of $M_\omega$. It is therefore an isomorphism. This proves $M_\omega\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathfrak S_d}^{\mathfrak S_{d+1}}D(\mu)$, without Frobenius reciprocity or an adjunction multiplicity assertion. [step 33.1, F2, construct]

35.1 Corner projection is exact. Each Schur composition factor $L_N(\eta)$ projects to the distinct restricted group simple $D(\eta)$ if $\eta$ is restricted, and to zero otherwise, by the accepted local form/radical and ordinary-group survival proof. Hence for a restricted $\mu+B=\mu+\epsilon_i$, its total induction multiplicity is exactly $b_i$. Nonrestricted near factors were kept until this exact projection. Distant factors were never excluded; distinct surviving labels ensure that they cannot change this particular count. When $d=0$, the single degree-one tensor/corner gives the unique plus and multiplicity one directly. [step 34.1, F2, construct]

36.1 The generalized Jucys--Murphy induction summands give a direct decomposition of total induction. For the ordinary group elements $L_k=\sum_{j<k}(j,k)$, induction by inserting the letter $n$ into a cycle gives the integral identity $\prod_{k=1}^n(t+L_k)=\sum_{g\in\mathfrak S_n}t^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g.$ [step 35.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

37.1 The factor $t$ makes $n$ a new fixed point; each transposition $(j,n)$ inserts $n$ at the uniquely specified place in the cycle containing $j$. These alternatives are disjoint and exhaust the permutations. Coefficients on the right are class sums, so all coefficients of $Q_n(t)=\prod_{k=1}^n(t-L_k)$ are central over the integers and every field. [step 36.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

38.1 The published [[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]] says that $Q_n(t)$ acts on the complex ordinary Specht module of shape $\lambda$ as $\prod_{A\in\lambda}(t-\operatorname{res}_{\mathbb Z}(A))$. The ordinary integral Specht lattice has the free polytabloid basis provided by the accepted integral bridge. The operator equality has integer matrices on that lattice; its validity after scalar extension to $\mathbb C$ therefore implies its validity over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing and taking its radical quotient proves the same content scalar on ordinary $D^\lambda$ over every field. The accepted signed-conjugate dictionary sends each $L_k$ to $-L_k$ under the sign twist, and transpose negates contents. Hence $Q_n(t)$ acts on restricted $D(\lambda)=D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ by the content polynomial of $\lambda$. This use of the published complex spectrum is an integral operator-identity descent; none of the multiplicity inversion uses characteristic-zero composition counts or semisimplicity. [step 37.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

39.1 Let $\alpha$ be the multiset of residues of $\mu$. The exact central content polynomial on $D(\mu)$ and the central CRT description of the content sums give $e_\alpha^{(d)}D(\mu)=D(\mu)$; this requires no primitive-block assertion. For clarity the functor idempotent $e=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,h}$ implies the following test on $F_hD(\mu)=F\mathfrak S_{d+1}e\otimes_{F\mathfrak S_d}D(\mu)$. On its generating subspace $e\otimes D(\mu)$, the first-$d$ content polynomial has exactly the scalar for $\mu$, and $L_{d+1}-h$ is nilpotent. These operators commute and $(L_{d+1}-h)^m e=0$ for a fixed primary exponent $m$. A coefficient $z$ of $Q_{d+1}(t)-(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$ is central by the integral identity. On $e\otimes w$ it is the corresponding scalar coefficient of $Q_\mu(t)$ times $h-L_{d+1}$: balance the first-$d$ central coefficient across $e$ into $w$. Centrality lets this same calculation iterate, so $z^m(e\otimes w)=0$. Since the whole module is generated by these vectors and $z$ commutes with every group translate, $z^m$ is zero on the whole module. On a simple factor a nilpotent central endomorphism is zero, since every nonzero simple-module endomorphism is invertible. Thus every factor in this summand has content polynomial $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$. [step 38.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

40.1 Distinct residues give distinct polynomials: $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)-(t-k)Q_\mu(t)=(k-h)Q_\mu(t)\ne0$ for $h\ne k$. The content polynomial of $\mu+B$ appends exactly the residue of $B$. Its factors therefore occur only in the corresponding residue summand. The total multiplicity computed above is exactly the multiplicity in $F_iD(\mu)$ required by the target. This argument does not use primitivity or exhaustiveness of any content-block idempotent. [step 39.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

41.1 Transpose preserves boundary types. Literally $(\mu\cup B)'=\mu'\cup B^{\mathsf t},\qquad(\mu\setminus A)'=\mu'\setminus A^{\mathsf t}.$ [step 40.1, F4, construct]

42.1 It sends an addable node to an addable node and a removable node to a removable node; it negates the residue. The appropriate boundary reading order is reversed when transporting the signature convention. It does not exchange addable and removable sets. The proof above needs no claimed equality of induction and restriction multiplicities and no transpose transfer of a restriction count. [step 41.1, F4, construct]

43.1 The finite character inversion, boundary-stack calculation, exact induction corner and residue allocation just proved identify the stated multiplicity with zero off conormality and with the conormal weak-above count on conormality. Both cases hold over every field of characteristic $p$, with nonrestricted auxiliary factors retained until projection and no assertion about other tensor factors. [step 42.1, F1, F2, F4, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The survey documents the formula's origin; its count is not a proof premise. Biadjunction does not equate these composition multiplicities: in characteristic $2$, induction of $D(1)$ to $S_2$ has multiplicity $2$ of $D(1,1)$, whereas restricting that simple has multiplicity $1$ of $D(1)$. The proof instead uses actual tensor weights, finite integer inversion and an explicit coset map.

items.title: The good node gives the simple socle and head of the residue restriction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the
residue-summand functor $E_i$ of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] the
module $E_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to
$D(\nu)$, and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. Thus the Loewy endpoints are simple even though the
formal character of $E_iD(\mu)$ may contain the additional normal-node
factors of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]].
items.strategy: Socle: by ([[cor-socle-of-uncoloured-modular-restriction-is-the-sum-over-good-residues]]) the socle of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)$ is $\bigoplus_{j:\varepsilon_j>0}D(\mu\setminus A_j)$, a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules; the $i$-summand $E_iD(\mu)$ contains precisely the summand $D(\mu\setminus A)=D(\nu)$ (the good $i$-node is unique for its residue). Head: the contragredient dual of $E_iD(\mu)$ is $E_i(D(\mu)^*)\cong E_iD(\mu)$ because the primary idempotents are invariant under the antipode ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]) and $D(\mu)$ is self-dual; for a finite-dimensional self-dual module the head is the dual of the socle, so the head is $D(\nu)$ as well ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Multiplicity: apply the normal-node theorem ([[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]]) with $A$ the good node; the normal $i$-nodes weakly below $A$ are exactly all normal $i$-nodes, whose number is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. The ungraded statement is the one asserted; no graded shift is displayed before the Hecke/KLR bridge. Source: Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.6(ii) with the socle statement of §11.4; the complete proof in the Hecke convention is Brundan 1998 Theorems 5.4 and the §5.5-5.7 transfer, valid at $p=2$.

items.title: The cogood node gives the simple socle and head of the residue induction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$; let $B$ be the cogood
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\cup B$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$F_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to $D(\nu)$,
and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $F_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varphi_i(\mu)$
([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]).
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, a residue $i$ with $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$, its cogood node $B$, and $\nu=\mu\cup B$.

[F1] The integrated Schur endomorphism algebra has normalized semistandard cell maps and actual weight projections, and the right corner is transported by $\rho_h(x)=hx$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Nonzero cellular form quotients are absolutely simple and classify the simples; canonical Schur norm one makes all Schur labels nonzero ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]). All corner and socle-lifting assertions needed below are proved locally.

[F2] The accepted integral root-interval supplier gives the $T,Q$ operators, splitting identity (P), zero criterion (Z), matched norm (M), and triangular hats, including distinct essential hats and the essential-regular characterization of root normality ([[lem-type-a-modular-root-interval-essential-subset-basis-and-count]]). Its global tensor/positive-detection foundation is recalled explicitly below; no characteristic-zero PBW or strong-linkage premise is used.

[F3] The independent Murphy datum and signed-conjugate module/form bridge have form factor one at $q=1$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). The published ordinary group form criterion and classification give distinct absolutely irreducible quotients exactly at regular labels, with nondegenerate invariant quotient forms ([[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]], [[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]). Thus the restricted convention is obtained through the actual sign/inverse dictionary, not a finite-$e$ Hecke classifier.

[F4] The complete locally proved [[thm-conormal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-induction]] gives, over every field of characteristic $p$, zero multiplicity off conormality and otherwise the number of conormal $i$-nodes weakly above the restricted addition $B$. The recovered reviewer independently verified its tensor-weight support, integer opposed recurrence, boundary-stack evaluation, actual induction corner and central-content residue allocation on the guarded companion proposal. Only the final total-multiplicity step uses this interface.

[F5] Normal/good and conormal/cogood mean the surviving signs, first surviving minus and last surviving plus in the top-to-bottom reduced signature ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Primary projectors are commuting polynomials in the Jucys-Murphy elements, inverse fixes them, and $L_{d+1}$ commutes with $FS_d$ ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]). Their needed content/adjunction interfaces are proved locally below. A self-dual finite-dimensional module has head dual to socle ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 We first establish the restriction endpoint locally. Work with left Schur modules through star. In tensor degree $m$, the word of $m_\alpha T_w$ has $j$th letter the row containing $j$ in $t^\alpha w$; at regular type it is $jw^{-1}$, with zero-multiplicity labels omitted. Over $K=F(t)$ the evaluations $g^{\otimes m}$ span the tensor Schur algebra: a functional killing them gives a polynomial zero on invertible matrices; multiplication by $\det$ and the infinite-field polynomial identity force that polynomial to be zero. Schur simples are therefore simple polynomial $\mathrm{GL}_N$ modules. The canonical shape/type diagonal is its permutation-summand projection, whose square gives canonical form value one. Semistandard column strictness bounds entries at most $k$ by the first $k$ rows, so all weights are dominated by the highest weight $\xi$ and the highest space is $Kv$. Integer torus characters, rather than Lie eigenvalues modulo $p$, distinguish these weights. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Gaussian factorization $g=u^-tu^+$ on the big cell shows that negative coefficient operators on $v$ span its simple module: a functional killing them kills $gv$ on that open set and hence everywhere by polynomial identity. Similarly, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\xi-\Gamma$. If every positive highest coefficient vanished, the highest coefficient of $gx$ would vanish on the big cell, because negative operators cannot raise any weight to $\xi$; it would then vanish on the orbit of $x$, which spans the simple and contains $v$. All coefficient operators have integral tensor replacement matrices, and the ranks and Hom kernels of finite matrices preserve extension from $F$ to $K$. These arguments consequently descend to $F$. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\xi_N=0$, $l=N-1$, and let $M$ be the full last-coordinate-one subspace of $L_N(\xi)$. A primitive vector means one killed by every nonconstant coefficient of the upper Levi unipotent group, not merely by its Lie generators. Factor the full upper group as $V U_l^+$, where $V$ has only the last column above the diagonal nontrivial. A positive test of a Levi-primitive vector acts only through $V$, since the right-hand nonconstant Levi coefficients kill it. Raising last coordinate $1$ to highest coordinate $0$ requires a $V$ monomial of degree exactly one. Positive detection therefore gives $E_{rN}x=cv\ne0$ for some $r$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(x)=\xi-\beta_r$, where $\beta_r=\alpha_r+\cdots+\alpha_l$, even when the initial first-level deficit was arbitrary. On that primitive weight space $x\mapsto E_{rN}x$ is injective by the same detection argument, so its dimension is at most one. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Put $a_j=\xi_j-\xi_{j+1}$ and use $B(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^s a_j$ and $C(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^{s-1}a_j$. For nonempty $I$, the canonical $Q(I)$ kills a primitive vector: if $b=\min I$, its ascending-prefix letter $e_{b-1}$ commutes past the remaining ascending letters, whose indices exceed $b$, and becomes a rightmost Levi letter with $b-1<l$. Expand a nonzero primitive vector of weight $\xi-\beta_r$ in the essential $T$ basis and select the largest hat among its nonzero coefficients. The triangular pivot isolates a nonzero term. That hat cannot be nonempty, since its $Q$ test would annihilate the vector. Distinct essential hats therefore leave exactly one essential set with empty hat. Empty is linked precisely to a regular set, and the essential-regular matching theorem says such a set exists precisely when $r$ is normal. This proves necessity of normality. [step 3.1, F2, construct]

5.1 Conversely, for normal $r$ let $R_r=\{s\in(r,l]:B(r,s)=0\}$ and choose its compensation $f$ with $r<f(s)\le s$ and $B(f(s),s)=0$. Put $D=f(R_r)$. The inverse matching makes $D$ regular, so its hat is empty. The matched norm is $\Xi_{r,l}(D)=\prod_{s\in[r,l]\setminus R_r}B(r,s)\ne0$: $B(r,r)=a_r\ne0$, and $R_r$ removes exactly the other zero factors. Thus $T_{r,l}(D)v$ is nonzero, and the maximal-hat assertion gives $h(I,D)=0$ for every nonempty $I$. For $r\le j<l$, every positive test of $e_jT(D)v$ has grade $\beta_r-\alpha_j$. Expanding its root matrices into simple words and appending the rightmost $e_j$ gives full words with nonempty canonical $Q$ index, since $e_j$ acts before $e_{j+1}$. All highest coefficients vanish, so positive detection gives $e_jT(D)v=0$. For $j<r$ the target weight is outside dominance below $\xi$ and is zero. A nonconstant Levi coefficient whose weight is not bounded by $\beta_r$ likewise has zero target. At a weight bounded by $\beta_r$, root-variable exponents are at most one, so the coefficient is a product of positive root matrices, each an iterated simple-root commutator; its rightmost root kills the vector. This proves full group primitivity. The primitive line at $\xi-\beta_r$ is consequently one-dimensional exactly at normal $r$, and we denote any nonzero vector on it by $v_r$. [step 4.1, F2, construct]

6.1 We separate primitive labels integrally, including $p=2$. In tensor degree $b$ for Levi rank $l$, put $H_a=E_{aa}$ and define $\binom{H_a}{2}$ to act on a weight $\zeta$ by the integer $\binom{\zeta_a}{2}$ reduced in $F$. Concretely it is $\sum_{x<y}E_{aa}^{(x)}E_{aa}^{(y)}$, with no division by $2$ in $F$. The tensor action $Z_b$ of the group central transposition sum $z_b=\sum_{x<y}(x,y)$ satisfies the exact integer identity $Z_b=\sum_a\binom{H_a}{2}+\sum_{a<c}(E_{ac}E_{ca}-H_a)$. The equal-position part of $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ is $H_a$; after subtracting it, the terms are exactly the two swaps of unequal labels. The diagonal terms count equal-label pairs. Since $z_b$ commutes with the position group and every Schur endomorphism, this operator belongs to the Schur algebra and is central. [step 5.1, construct]

7.1 On a primitive vector of dominant weight $\zeta$, $E_{ac}$ kills it for $a<c$, so $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ acts by $H_a-H_c$. Therefore $Z_b$ has scalar $\kappa(\zeta)=\sum_a\binom{\zeta_a}{2}-\sum_c(c-1)\zeta_c=\sum_{(c,j)\in[\zeta]}(j-c)$. The binomial here is the actual diagonal weight operator of step 6.1. Centrality makes this scalar constant on the cyclic module generated by the vector. For first-level $\zeta_r=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_l)-\epsilon_r$, it is $\kappa(\zeta_r)=\kappa(\xi)- (\xi_r-r)$, so $\kappa(\zeta_t)-\kappa(\zeta_r)=-C(t,r)$. Thus the cyclic Levi module $\Psi_r$ generated by $v_r$ cannot contain another primitive $v_t$ when $C(t,r)\ne0$. Equality of the scalars alone does not prove simplicity; we treat it explicitly next. [step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Suppose $t<r$ are normal and $C(t,r)=0$. Choose $D$ for the demands of $r$ as in step 5.1. For $w\ge r$, $B(t,w)=B(r,w)$, and $B(t,r)=a_r\ne0$. The demands of $t$ split into $Y=\{y\in(t,r):B(t,y)=0\}$ and $R_r$. Compensation for $Y$, inherited from normality of $t$, has image $E$ below $r$. Since $B(t,r-1)=C(t,r)-1=-1\ne0$, all those targets and $E$ lie at most $r-2$. Combining their matching with $D$ gives compensation for every demand of $t$, so choose $v_t=T_{t,l}(E\cup D)v$ and $v_r=T_{r,l}(D)v$. For each $e\in E$ its matched $y$ gives $B(e,y)=B(t,y)=0$, hence $C(t,e)=0$. If $E\ne\varnothing$ and $e=\max E$, then $C(e,r)=C(t,r)-C(t,e)=0$. [step 7.1, construct]
