9.1 Splitting (P) gives $T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r=v_t-T_{t,l}((E\setminus\{e\})\cup\{r\}\cup D)v-C(e,r)T_{t,l}(E\cup\{r\}\cup D)v$. The last term is zero. The middle term has a (Z) witness with endpoint $r-1$, outside its cuts because $E\le r-2$ and $D>r$. Removing matched source $e$ releases its zero-$B$ target $y_e$; assign $t$ to $y_e$ and retain the matching on $E\setminus\{e\}$. All distinct bounded targets are below $r-1$. Hence that term is zero as well. For $E=\varnothing$, (P) omits the middle term and its last coefficient is $C(t,r)=0$. In both cases $v_t=T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r\in\Psi_r$, without a field denominator. [step 8.1, F2, construct]

10.1 The Gaussian argument on a cyclic module, without assuming simplicity, shows that $\Psi_r$ is spanned by negative Levi coefficients on $v_r$ and has weights at most $\zeta_r$. Any nonzero proper Schur submodule contains a simple Schur submodule and thus a primitive $v_t$ by step 3.1. Dominance gives $t\le r$. For $t=r$, its one-dimensional line is the generating line and would generate all of $\Psi_r$; thus a proper submodule has $t<r$, and the central scalar requires $C(t,r)=0$. Conversely, such an earlier normal $t$ gives a proper nonzero $\Psi_t\subset\Psi_r$ by step 9.1, since its weights are at most $\zeta_t<\zeta_r$. Consequently $\Psi_r$ is simple precisely when $r$ is normal with no earlier normal $t$ satisfying $C(t,r)=0$. All simple Schur submodules of $M$ are exactly these $\Psi_r$, each once: every simple has a primitive highest vector, and each primitive line has dimension one. [step 9.1, F1, construct]

11.1 Now assume $\xi$ restricted. The root criterion is its physical signature criterion: $a_r\ne0$ identifies the removable node in row $r$; scanning $j>r$, a nonzero $a_j$ gives a removable push if $C(r,j)=0$ and an addable pop at row $j+1$ if $B(r,j)=0$. These events have the residue of row $r$; at $a_j=0$ the matching slot supplies and consumes itself and is neutral. For $0<a_j<p$, the two events are disjoint. The compensation-prefix inequalities are exactly survival of the initial push in the signature stack. Also $C(t,r)=(\xi_t-t)-(\xi_r-r)$ compares the residues. Thus the simple cyclic modules in step 10.1 are exactly at the good nodes. Their lower labels are restricted: removing row $r$ decreases $a_r$ by one and increases $a_{r-1}$ by one. The only failure, when $r>1$, would be $a_{r-1}=p-1$. Then $C(r-1,r)=0$, and $r-1$ is also normal, since its later demands are those of $r$, $B(r-1,r)=a_r\ne0$, and the compensation for $r$ is also valid for $r-1$. This contradicts goodness. Hence every Schur socle factor survives the restricted-label corner; no assertion is made about the other composition factors. [step 10.1, F5, construct]

12.1 To transfer without a held generic classifier, for $\xi\vdash m$ choose $N=m+1$ and the regular composition $\omega=(1^{m-1},0,1)$, so $\xi_N=0$ even for columns. Compute the cell corner temporarily in its original right-module convention, then transport through star. Its permutation summand is $M^\omega=FS_m$, and its actual projection $e$ gives $eSe=FS_m$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. Type-$\omega$ tableaux correspond to standard tableaux by increasing relabeling $1,\ldots,m-1,N$ to $1,\ldots,m$. Their normalized map fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ sends $\varphi_{st}$ to $m_{st}$. Higher ideals correspond as equality of corner basis spans. The Weyl weight projection keeps exactly these basis vectors; read its cell action using a fixed outer index of the same type and evaluate at $1$ to get the Murphy action. Thus $W^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)$ with the actual same-shape normalization. [step 11.1, F1, F3, construct]

13.1 In the Schur cell product choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of type $\omega$. Evaluation at $1$ turns $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ into $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so the unique Murphy coefficient gives $B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)=G_\zeta(c_s,c_t)$. The factor is one. Since $e^*=e$, the Weyl splitting $W=We\oplus W(1-e)$ is orthogonal, giving $\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(We)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(W)e$, including zero corner forms. Projection is exact by lifting $ye$ through $xe$ and taking kernels fixed by $e$. Hence $L^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}$. The actual $q=1$ form-unit bridge identifies it with $D^{\zeta'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, nonzero exactly when $\zeta'$ is regular. Transporting these right-cell identities through star gives the corresponding left corners $eW^\zeta$ and $eL^\zeta$ used below. Their nonzero images are exactly the distinct absolutely simple restricted-label modules $D(\zeta)$, with the inverse group convention fixed by the nondegenerate quotient form. [step 12.1, F3, construct]

14.1 Let $\pi_1$ be the sum of actual weight projections with last coordinate one, so $M=\pi_1L_N(\xi)$. The lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$ embeds as $E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$; on each word with one $N$ it preserves that position and applies $E_A$ to the remaining ordered positions. Products agree and the lower identity is $\pi_1$, and transpose/star is respected. The lower regular projection of $\omega'=(1^{m-1},0)$ maps to $e$. On the coset-word convention of step 1.1, $\rho'_h$ acts by label permutation $h^{-1}$ on the used lower labels, fixing $N$, identically to $\rho_h$ for the subgroup fixing the last entry of $S_m$. Thus, in the left convention, $e'M=eL_N(\xi)\downarrow_{S_{m-1}}$. Write $S_L=S(N-1,m-1)$ for this lower Schur algebra; every socle and corner lift of $M$ below is over $S_L$. The inverse/star equivalence passes between right and left modules and commutes with this embedding, restriction and sign; the ordinary simple labels are fixed by their nondegenerate invariant quotient forms. No self-duality of a degenerate Specht module is assumed. [step 13.1, construct]

15.1 Socle preservation requires more than exactness. By step 11.1 every Schur socle simple of $M$ survives $e'$. A nonzero Schur submodule killed by $e'$ would contain a simple submodule inside that socle, whose corner is nonzero, a contradiction. Now a group-simple injection $j:D\to e'M$ corresponds to $S_Le'\otimes_{e'S_Le'}D\to M$, $se'\otimes x\mapsto sj(x)$, $s\in S_L$. Its image $I$ is generated by its corner $e'I=j(D)$. A proper Schur submodule $J$ of $I$ has either $e'J=0$, excluded by the no-killed-submodule property, or $e'J=e'I$, which generates $I$ and forces $J=I$. Thus $I$ is simple. Every group-simple corner submodule lifts to an actual Schur simple submodule, and conversely every surviving Schur simple has simple corner. Exactness on the semisimple sum, distinct labels and the one-dimensional primitive lines yield $\operatorname{soc}_{FS_{m-1}}(e'M)=e'\operatorname{soc}_{S_L} M$, multiplicity-free with exactly the good-deletion labels. The unused coordinate includes columns and $m=1$, whose lower degree-zero corner is $F$. [step 14.1, F1, construct]

16.1 The group central $z_m$ acts on $D(\xi)$ by $\kappa(\xi)$, since its tensor action is step 6.1 and its regular-summand action is $\rho_{z_m}$; right multiplication equals left multiplication for this central element. On the good lower label it acts by $\kappa(\xi-A)$. Therefore $L_m=z_m-z_{m-1}$ has scalar $\operatorname{res}(A)$ on that simple submodule, with the restricted convention $c-r$. Primary projection selects just that residue, and socles respect the actual direct sum. We obtain $\operatorname{soc}E_iD(\xi)=D(\xi-A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\xi)>0$, and zero otherwise. In the latter case $E_iD(\xi)=0$, since a nonzero finite-dimensional module contains a simple submodule. [step 15.1, F5, construct]

17.1 The invariant nondegenerate quotient form makes $D(\xi)$ self-dual. A primary polynomial projector in $L_m$ is self-adjoint, since the inverse involution fixes $L_m$, so its summand has a restricted nondegenerate invariant form. Its head is therefore dual to its simple socle and is the same simple. Thus for every restricted $\eta,\tau$ of consecutive degrees, $\dim_F\operatorname{Hom}(E_iD(\eta),D(\tau))$ is one if $\varepsilon_i(\eta)>0$ and $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\tau$, and zero otherwise. The scalar endomorphism ring is $F$ by absolute simplicity. This all-pairs criterion includes the zero case and all initially possible primitive weights; it does not discard middle composition factors. [step 16.1, F3, F5, construct]

18.1 We justify the needed functor interfaces locally. In $\mathbb ZS_n$ the Jucys identity is $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g$. Induct on $n$: choosing $u$ leaves $n$ fixed, and choosing $(a,n)$ inserts it next to $a$ in a cycle, bijectively covering the non-fixed permutations. Hence each elementary symmetric JM coefficient is central over every field. On a simultaneous primary tuple these operators have generalized eigenvalues equal to its elementary symmetric residue coefficients; nilpotence follows by expanding a polynomial in the commuting nilpotent differences. Distinct residue multisets have distinct coefficient tuples, since their monic products of prime-field linear factors retain multiplicities uniquely even in characteristic $p$. For each elementary symmetric operator, construct its univariate primary projectors by the same polynomial CRT construction as in [F5], then multiply these commuting projectors. This gives the content projector equal to the sum of tuple projectors of that content. This proves content centrality without factorial division, position-dependent symmetric-polynomial claims, or content-block primitivity. The projectors are inverse-fixed. For an input in content $\alpha$, induction projection by right $e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$ is the same as right $P_{d+1,i}$, because $ge_\alpha\otimes x=g\otimes e_\alpha x$. An absolutely simple $D(\mu)$ lies in exactly one of these central contents, since their scalar idempotents are orthogonal and sum to one; denote it by $\alpha$. Thus these interfaces agree with the actual functor definition. [step 17.1, F5, construct]

19.1 Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $E_H:FG\to FH$ truncate group coefficients. For left modules the natural Frobenius map is $\Phi(g\otimes x)(y)=E_H(yg)x$, with coinduction action $(a q)(y)=q(ya)$. It is balanced and $G$-linear by $E_H(hz)=hE_H(z)$ and $E_H(zh)=E_H(z)h$. For a left-coset transversal $T$ of $G/H$, its inverse is $\Psi(q)=\sum_{r\in T}r\otimes q(r^{-1})$. The right cosets $Hr^{-1}$ partition $G$, so evaluation at $y$ has exactly the term $yr\in H$ and returns $q(y)$. On $g\otimes x$ the unique term with $r^{-1}g\in H$ balances back to $g\otimes x$. These verify both identities and naturality with correct cosets and only finite choices. [step 18.1, construct]

20.1 Let $e=e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$, commuting with $FH$ and inverse-fixed. For any such centralizer element, $E_H(eZ)=E_H(Ze)$: the coefficient at $h$ is the group coefficient trace $\tau(h^{-1}eZ)=\tau(h^{-1}Ze)$, by cyclicity and commuting $e$ with $h^{-1}$. Under $\Phi$, the value at one of right projection $R_e$ is consequently $q(e)$. If $f:N\to\operatorname{Coind}X$ is $G$-linear, $f(en)(1)=f(n)(e)$. Evaluation therefore identifies projected maps $N\to F_iX$ with $H$-maps $E_iN\to X$; conversely an $H$-map extends via $q_n(y)=h(yn)$. For $X=e_\alpha X$, every $H$-map already selects the matching content. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_G(N,F_iX)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(E_iN,X)$ exactly, with no duality shift and no asserted equality of composition multiplicities. [step 19.1, construct]

21.1 The labelled signature inverse is local. Adding or removing a corner flips its $i$-sign, and the other boundary statuses that can change have residues $i\pm1$, not $i$ for $p\ge2$. In the stack reduction, flipping the last surviving plus gives the first surviving minus and conversely: before that position the minus stack is empty, and its distinguished minus survives exactly when every suffix prefix has at least as many minus pushes as plus pops, equivalent to no later plus surviving after the flip. Good removal preserves restrictedness by step 11.1. Cogood addition also does: its only possible new forbidden difference is $a_r=p-1$, in which case the addable node in row $r+1$ has the same residue, with no $i$-node between the two pluses. If the earlier plus survives, the later one also survives, contradicting that the earlier is cogood. Hence addition remains restricted and the inverse holds in both directions. In particular $B$ is cogood for $\mu$ exactly when it is good for $\nu=\mu\cup B$. No equality between $\varepsilon_i(\nu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ is used. [step 20.1, F5, construct]

22.1 Apply step 20.1 with $N=D(\eta)$ and $X=D(\mu)$ for every restricted $\eta\vdash d+1$. By step 17.1 the resulting Hom space is one-dimensional precisely when $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\mu$, and zero otherwise. Step 21.1 makes exactly one such label, namely $\nu=\mu\cup B$. The group simple classification covers every simple by these absolutely irreducible labels. The dimensions of all simple-to-module Hom spaces therefore identify the socle of $F_iD(\mu)$ as the single $D(\nu)$, with socle multiplicity one, excluding every other label. [step 21.1, F3, construct]

23.1 Give $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G D(\mu)$ the invariant nondegenerate coset form $\beta(r\otimes x,s\otimes y)=\delta_{rs}\beta_\mu(x,y)$ on a finite left transversal. A group element permutes cosets and acts by $H$ on the fibers, proving invariance. Equivalently its value on general group representatives is $\beta_\mu(x,E_H(g^{-1}h)y)$. The projection $R_e$ is self-adjoint: moving it to the first argument gives $E_H(e^*g^{-1}h)$, which equals $E_H(g^{-1}he^*)$ by the trace calculation of step 20.1, and $e^*=e$. Its image is orthogonal to the complement and inherits a nondegenerate invariant form. Thus $F_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual, and its head is the dual of its simple socle, namely $D(\nu)$ through the nondegenerate invariant quotient form. This proves both endpoints, including characteristic two. [step 22.1, F3, F5, construct]

24.1 For $d=0$, the empty partition has one conormal node $(1,1)$ of residue zero and $\varphi_0=1$. Induction from $S_0$ to $S_1$ is $F$, with $L_1=0$, so $F_0D(\varnothing)=D(1)=F$ has these endpoints; other residue functors are zero. Every use of $F(t)$ above descends to the original field: weight projections and coefficient operators have matrices over $F$, finite Hom ranks preserve extension, and the simple Schur and group labels remain absolutely simple. Therefore the endpoint assertions hold over every original field of characteristic $p$. [step 23.1, F1, F3, construct]

25.1 The total multiplicity is the separate use of [F4]. Apply it to the cogood $B$, which is bottommost conormal. Its conormal nodes weakly above it are exactly all $\varphi_i(\mu)$ conormal nodes, so $[F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]=\varphi_i(\mu)$. Combining this count with the independently constructed endpoints proves the full statement. The implication uses no equality of induction and restriction composition counts and no equality $\varepsilon_i(\nu)=\varphi_i(\mu)$. [step 24.1, F4, F5, construct] ∎

## Remarks

This is the recovered research-only first construction proposal for the exact cogood endpoint case, not a native-ready decision. The saved native50 construction and mathematical steps are reused; recovery has not opened another review or repair round. The endpoint proof is local; the complete target uses the independently reviewed conormal-count companion [F4], which must be integrated first. The actual canonical good-node/uncoloured-socle items and the survey statements are not endpoint proof premises. No general finite-$e$ classifier is used or reopened.

The former unused equality in F3 was false: for $p=2$, $\mu=(1)$, its two addable $1$-nodes are conormal, so $\varphi_1(\mu)=2$; for $\nu=(1,1)$ one has $\varepsilon_1(\nu)=1$. The true labelled good/cogood inverse is proved above. Simple endpoint multiplicity one and total composition multiplicity two in this example are consistent.

The authentic cached Kleshchev 1995 II scan (SHA-256 `6a7a7856d3eb8c8198920c02bdcdd16d8b350f024d39ae96215f072050bc368c`, 51 PDF pages) was recorded by the original native50 constructor as read visually on every printed page 198–212 and 163–166. The recovery constructor read the saved proof, proposal and handoffs; it does not claim to have repeated that visual reading. These include the full Theorems 4.2 and 4.11 proofs/continuations and the actual Theorem 0.5 statement. The scan ends with section 4 and references, not a section 5. The source's strong-linkage citation in 4.11 is replaced here by the integral central tensor operator and explicit compensated containment. No full-article/book reading or new retrieval is claimed. Source reading, preimages, pending interfaces and exact hashes are recorded in the accompanying handoff; all prior K/50 seals and caps remain untouched.

items.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The image $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ is nonzero if and only if $\mu$ is restricted over the original field; the nonzero images are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Every Schur simple $L(\mu)$ is its nonzero cell-form quotient, so the descended symmetric associative form makes $L(\mu)^\circ\cong L(\mu)$ under Schur star. The normalized maps are $\varphi_{ST}(x_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}\in x_\mu H\cap Hx_\nu$ and $m_{TS}=m_{ST}^*$; Schur star is $\varphi_{ST}^*=\varphi_{TS}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The standard coefficient trace satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{uv}q^{\ell(u)}$; its complete generator-block proof is the actual standalone trace construction of [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]. The following proof establishes the restricted-socle conclusion locally over the original field; no quantum-hyperalgebra square-root or unproved classical-specialization premise is used.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $\beta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $\beta_\alpha(aT_i,b)=\beta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $\tau(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q)\beta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_\nu\to M_\mu$, $a=x_\nu h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_\nu m_{TS}=P_\nu m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu\beta_\mu(fa,b)=\tau(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_\nu\beta_\nu(a,f^*b)=\tau(h^*x_\nu m_{TS}k)=P_\nu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k).$$ Cancel the nonzero polynomials only in $A$, then specialize the resulting identity to $F$. The orthogonal sum $\beta=\bigoplus_\alpha\beta_\alpha$ is therefore perfect and satisfies $\beta(sm,m')=\beta(m,s^*m')$ for every actual Schur basis map and hence every $s\in S$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. The last bijection evaluates a map at $e$, with inverse $v\mapsto(se\mapsto sv)$ for $v\in eL$. By [F2], $eL(\mu)$ is nonzero exactly for restricted $\mu$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. The proof does not equate zero form quotients with zero actual module heads. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.2, algebra]


4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

4.2 Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. The length-additive parabolic coset basis makes $H(r)$ free as a LEFT $H(r-1)$-module of rank $r$, so $M_1$ is $r$ copies of $M_0$ as a left lower Schur module. Apply steps 2.2 and 3.2 to $M_0\cong S(n-1,r-1)e_{\rm lower}$: its simple socle labels are exactly the surviving restricted labels. Every simple submodule of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ is a simple submodule of $M_1$, and therefore restricted. At degree zero $M_0=F$, with the unique empty label; at $n=r=1$ this is the convention $S(0,0)=F$. This proves assertion3, without adjoining a square root, using a splitting extension, assuming a quantum-hyperalgebra specialization, or requiring $\lambda_n=0$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]


5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 4.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

The first-level and ordinary-label reconciliation above is the new authored binding repair. The previously accepted source20 cell-form repair and NEW50 ordinary polytabloid construction are unchanged. Actual acceptance requires the repaired current source20/NEW50 supplier carriers after the live writers drain and the same reviewer checks the actual bound interfaces. No further primitive bridge construction is claimed. No identification of cellular and crystal simple labels is used ([[rem-the-crystal-identification-does-not-elementarily-identify-cellular-simple-labels]]).

title: Modular Branching and the Good-Node Crystal — Examples

items.title: A full cogood-addition path from the empty partition to (3,1,1) at p = 3
items.statement:
At $p=3$ the $p$-restricted partition $(3,1,1)$ is reached from the empty
partition by the five cogood additions
$$\varnothing\xrightarrow{\,0\,}(1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(3,1,1),$$
that is, $(1)=\tilde f_0\varnothing$, $(1,1)=\tilde f_2(1)$,
$(1,1,1)=\tilde f_1(1,1)$, $(2,1,1)=\tilde f_1(1,1,1)$,
$(3,1,1)=\tilde f_2(2,1,1)$, where the labels record the residues of the
added nodes
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]]). Reversing the path
gives the good deletions
$$(3,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\,1\,}(1,1)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}(1)\xrightarrow{\,0\,}\varnothing.$$
The relevant reduced signatures are: $(1)$ at $i=0$: $(-)$; $(1,1)$ at
$i=2$: $(-)$; $(1,1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(+,-)$; $(2,1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(-,-)$;
$(3,1,1)$ at $i=2$: $(-)$; and $(1,1)$ at $i=1$: $(+,+)$,
$(2,1,1)$ at $i=2$: $(+)$. This is a case in which the reduced signatures are
not multiplicity-free: the signature $(+,-)$ occurs at $i=1$ for $(1,1,1)$.
items.strategy: Direct computation from the signature definition: list the addable and removable nodes of each partition (for $(1)$: removable $(1,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(1,1)$: removable $(2,1)$ at residue $2$, addables $(1,2),(3,1)$ at residue $1$; for $(1,1,1)$: removable $(3,1)$ at residue $1$, addables $(1,2)$ at residue $1$ and $(4,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(2,1,1)$: removable $(1,2),(3,1)$ at residue $1$, addables $(1,3)$ at residue $2$, $(2,2)$ and $(4,1)$ at residue $0$; for $(3,1,1)$: removable $(1,3)$ at residue $2$, addables $(1,4),(2,2),(4,1)$ at residue $0$), cancel $-+$ pairs top to bottom, and read off the rightmost $+$ (cogood) and the leftmost $-$ (good) of each residue. Every forward step is the addition of a cogood node and every reverse step the deletion of a good node, as predicted by the mutual-inverse property of the crystal operators; the path also verifies the reachability proposition in a case where the reduced signatures are not multiplicity-free. Method: Kleshchev survey §3.4 (printed pp. 18-19).

items.title: Normal and good nodes for the partition (6,4,4,3,2)
items.statement:
Work Brundan's Example 2.8 (complete 34-page author manuscript, p. 5) in his
conventions: $\lambda=(6,4,4,3,2)$ is $\ell$-restricted for $\ell=3$ and
$\ell=4$, residues are $r-c\bmod\ell$ in the source's orientation (the
negative of the $c-r$ convention of this page,
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]),
$R(\lambda)=\{1,3,4,5\}$ is the set of removable rows, and for
$i\in R(\lambda)$ one compares $B_{i,5}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ with
$C_{i,5}(\lambda)\cap R(\lambda)$ in the lattice order $\downarrow$, where
$$B_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in[i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k+1,\lambda_{k+1}+1)\},\qquad C_{i,j}(\lambda)=\{k\in(i..j):\operatorname{res}_\ell(i,\lambda_i)= \operatorname{res}_\ell(k,\lambda_k)\},$$
and $A\downarrow B$ means that there is an injection $\theta:A\to B$ with
$\theta(a)\le a$ for all $a$.

For $\ell=3$ the removable nodes have residues $1,2,1,0$ for
$i=1,3,4,5$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{4\}),\ (\{4\},\varnothing), (\varnothing,\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,4,5\}$ and, since rows $4$ and $1$ share
residue $1$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1,5\}$. For $\ell=4$ the residues are
$3,3,1,3$ and
$$(B\cap R,C\cap R)=(\varnothing,\{3,5\}),\ (\varnothing,\{5\}), (\varnothing,\varnothing),\ (\varnothing,\varnothing);$$
hence row $4$ is normal-refuted by $\{5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$ and
$R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,3,5\}$, and since rows $1,3,5$ share residue $3$,
$R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1\}$. By the branching theorems the restriction of
$D^{\lambda}$ to $H(r-1)$ is therefore decomposable for $\ell=3$ (socle
$D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}\oplus D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$) and indecomposable for $\ell=4$
(socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}$).
items.strategy: A finite verification of Brundan's Example 2.8 (pp. 4-5), carried out in the source's transposed convention and translated back to the $c-r$ dictionary of the page: the removable rows, residues and the index sets $B_{i,j},C_{i,j}$ are recomputed row by row for $\ell=3$ and $\ell=4$, the lattice tests $A\downarrow B$ give $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,4,5\}$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1,5\}$ at $\ell=3$ and $R^{normal}(\lambda)=\{1,3,5\}$, $R^{good}(\lambda)=\{1\}$ at $\ell=4$, and the branching theorems then give decomposability at $\ell=3$ (socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}\oplus D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$) and indecomposability at $\ell=4$ with the corrected simple socle $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}=D^{\lambda(1)}$ (the scaffold's label $D^{(6,4,4,2,2)}$ and its loose (2.9) citation are wrong and are repaired here; Brundan Theorem 2.6 with §2.10 supplies the socle). The example shows that the residue list alone does not determine normality and that good nodes are the minimal normal nodes per residue.

title: Level-One Fock Space and Residue Crystals

items.title: The symmetric-group level-one residue and partition-label convention
items.statement: Fix finite e≥2 and charge0. English nodes(r,c) have residue c−r mod e, with the full independent-root affine datum already fixed. An e-regular partition has every positive-part multiplicity<e; an e-restricted partition has lambda_a−lambda_(a+1)<e for every a. Thus lambda restricted iff lambda-prime regular. The MODULAR/restricted signature lists corners top-to-bottom, cancels −+, takes good removable FIRST surviving− and cogood addable LAST surviving+. Crystal labels of the basic module here are restricted shapes. To make the ambient module comparison exact, define the Q(q)-linear isomorphism J:F_sym→F_QG by J M_lambda=|lambda-prime>. Define E_i^sym=J^-1 E_-i^QG J,F_i^sym=J^-1 F_-i^QG J,K_h^sym=J^-1 K_(tau h)^QG J, and psi_sym=J^-1 psi_QG J; J does not invert q. The standard chart is ⊕ A0 M_lambda. Its full crystal has ALL partitions; its empty component restricted shapes. Weight is Lambda0−Σ_i m_i(lambda)alpha_i; J applies tau:i→−i to weight. The conjugation map exchanges addable/removable node TYPES with themselves and negates residue, and is a map BETWEEN models, not the same-model sign/Mullineux involution. In characteristic p>0 with e=p prime, simple labels satisfy D^mu=D(mu-prime)⊗sgn; for Hecke algebras finite e is the quantum characteristic, not necessarily prime. The source boundary e=0 means no positive e with 1+xi+...+xi^(e−1)=0; colors are Z and every level-one partition is a crystal label. No finite affine datum is claimed there.
items.strategy: Compute c−r→r−c and m_i(lambda)=m_-i(lambda-prime). Adjacent differences count column multiplicities, proving restricted/regular equivalence with <e rather than an exactly-e exclusion. Linear transport defines a genuine full ambient quantum module, crystal lattice and bar, and its operators have the required reflected colors. Kleshchev complete §2.1 defines quantum characteristic; §3.4/Example3.2 gives the top-to-bottom −+ signature and restricted level-one labels. Remark5.5 gives the James simple-label/sign dictionary under its stated symmetric/Hecke regimes. This does not identify lower with upper or a linear J with the semilinear transpose occurring in an adjoint-bar formula. Same-model Mullineux is separately the supplier's universal diagram-reflection involution; restricted version is C M C^-1. All elementary transports are explicit and choice-free; source branching results remain with the actual modular suppliers.

items.title: Residue-node reading orders and the conjugation dictionary
items.statement: For distinct addable/removable corners of one residue i (finite e≥2), smaller row implies strictly larger column and strictly larger content. Hence top-to-bottom=DECREASING content=decreasing column; bottom-to-top=increasing content. A same-residue row or column cannot repeat. Conjugation sends a top-to-bottom i-corner list of lambda to the bottom-to-top (increasing content) −i-corner list of lambda-prime, preserving signs. Thus its modular −+ cancellations, FIRST− good deletion and LAST+ cogood addition agree exactly with the QG INCREASING-content −+ rule on lambda-prime. Equivalently reverse the latter list and use decreasing-content +− cancellation, LAST− deletion and FIRST+ addition. Both versions select the same actual nodes. They apply to all partitions as signatures; the basic graph restriction is imposed separately.
items.strategy: Let rows r<s. Boundary inequalities give c_r≥c_s: check removable/removable, addable/addable, addable/removable directly from weak row lengths; for removable/addable, the upper removable drop and lower addability give the same weak inequality. Equality is possible for mixed types, so the native general 'impossible' assertion was false. If a removable upper corner and an addable lower corner share a column, their rows must be adjacent at that column's boundary, hence their contents differ1; the reverse mixed orientation cannot share a column. Equal-row mixed corners also differ1 in content. Same-residue e≥2 excludes these exceptions. Strict columns and r<s imply strictly DECREASING content. Conjugating exchanges rows/columns and negates content, yielding the stated order reversal. Stack reduction of −+ is uniquely determined: scan with a minus stack, cancel each plus with the last unmatched minus; reversing the word yields +− with first/last extrema reversed. Therefore the surviving-node bijection and selected-node identities are exact, not only an abstract isomorphism. This is the full elementary proof supplementing Fayers §4, whose text records the conventions but omits proofs.

items.title: The QG Fock-crystal arrows are the modular good-node operators
items.statement: Conjugation C sends the restricted/modular crystal on restricted lambda onto the EMPTY COMPONENT of the QG full partition Fock crystal, with colors negated: C tilde-e_i lambda=tilde-e_-i^QG C lambda and C tilde-f_i lambda=tilde-f_-i^QG C lambda, including zero values. Epsilon_i/phi_i are the numbers of surviving−/+, and weight transforms by tau. With the explicitly transported full module F_sym the modular signatures give its Kashiwara operators on ALL partitions, whose restricted subset is its basic component. Good is removable (tilde-e), cogood addable (tilde-f) in BOTH conventions; there is no opposite naming-polarity dictionary. Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers, do not define these arrows.
items.strategy: Apply the supplier order lemma: the modular top-to-bottom word on lambda is exactly the QG increasing-content word on lambda-prime at−i, with identical −+ cancellations and identical FIRST−/LAST+ extrema. Node removal/addition commutes with transpose, so each formula and its zero condition follows. The actual QG fixed-residue cube theorem proves these are normalized Kashiwara operators on the raw A0 partition lattice, without a minimum-Chevalley-exponent argument. The empty-component theorem proves the image of restricted shapes is exactly the regular/basic component; full Fock is larger. Weight and epsilon/phi follow the same bijection. Kleshchev §3.4 and the established modular good-node suppliers supply the restricted reading and inverse property. Native recorded contradictions are resolved at the supplier, not deferred to Step3.

items.title: The restricted-partition component is the basic crystal in the symmetric-group convention
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice exactly through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]], which uses it to split an integrable module with a crystal basis into highest-weight components; the identification of the empty component with the $e$-restricted partitions themselves is choice-free (Kleshchev Theorem 8.2(ii) with Example 3.2(i) and Fayers' restricted model are direct constructions of the crystal on that vertex set). The choice-free alternative is recorded in the strategy.
items.statement: For finite e≥2 the empty component of F_sym is exactly the e-restricted partitions, with modular good deletions/cogood additions and wt(lambda)=Lambda0−Σ m_i alpha_i. It is B(Lambda0), every restricted shape is reached from empty, and epsilon/phi count normal/conormal nodes. The entire F_sym has ALL partitions and is reducible, with the transported full p(k) highest-module decomposition; its other vertices are the nonrestricted shapes. In the symmetric-group regime of algebraically closed characteristic p>0 and xi=1, e=p is PRIME: restricted labels lambda correspond to James simples D^(lambda-prime)=D(lambda)⊗sgn, and if epsilon_i(lambda)>0 then soc E_-i D^(lambda-prime)=D^((tilde-e_i lambda)-prime). The standard E_-i is the residue functor after sign twist. General finite-e Hecke crystal labels remain valid but are not called symmetric-group modules of 'characteristic e'. At quantum characteristic e=0 (colors Z), every level-one partition is in the empty sl_infinity crystal; there are no same-content corner cancellations, and no finite-affine assertion is made.
items.strategy: Apply J/C with color reflection to the proved full QG crystal and its exact regular empty component. Restricted iff conjugate regular proves containment, converse reachability and the unique top. Transfer the full module decomposition through the field isomorphism; this is not an integral splitting claim. The established modular suppliers identify normal/conormal counts and restriction socle. In source Kleshchev §2.1 e is quantum characteristic; §3.4/Example3.2(i),(ii) gives labels and the e0 boundary, Theorem8.2(ii) gives B(Lambda0), and Theorem7.4(i), not Theorem11.6(i), gives the simple socle. Remark5.5 under xi=1 supplies the sign/transposed James labels. Sign twist negates Jucys-Murphy residue, so E_-i(D(lambda)⊗sgn)=E_iD(lambda)⊗sgn and its simple socle gives the displayed label. This consumes the actual modular branching theorem; the stronger normal multiplicities stay with batch22. At e0, distinct corners have distinct integer contents, so no cancellation; any removable corner can be removed and every shape is reached, giving the stated elementary graph boundary. Choice assumptions of the full field decomposition are inherited explicitly, not hidden in the finite signature comparison.

items.title: Level-one global-basis transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice through [[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]] (and hence through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]) for the decomposition of the Fock space into highest-weight components; the definition of the polynomials themselves and the pairing are choice-free. Consumers must carry the same assumption while it is used.
items.statement:
Work in the linear symmetric-group model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: the
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $J M_\mu = |\mu'\rangle$, the transported
action, bar and $A_0$ standard chart $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, and the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$, with
$A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$.

**The basic module and its lower basis.** Let
$M_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1}V(\Lambda_0) = J^{-1}M_{\mathrm{QG}}$ be the
transported highest-weight module of the vacuum; by
[[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]
its crystal is the $e$-restricted component and its labels are the $e$-restricted
partitions. For an $e$-restricted $\lambda$ define
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) := J^{-1}G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda'),$$
where $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\mu)$ is the lower global (canonical) basis element of
the Fock space at the standard vector $|\mu\rangle$
([[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]]).
Then $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) \equiv M_\lambda \bmod q\,(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$
and the family $\{G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)\}$ is the transported lower global
basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$, indexed by the restricted labels. Define the
**level-one transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention** by the
finite weightwise expansion
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) = \sum_\mu d_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q)\, M_\mu ,$$
the sum being over the partitions $\mu$ of the weight of $\lambda$.

**Ambient polarization and ambient upper coordinates.** Define the ambient
polarization by $B(M_\mu,M_\nu) = \delta_{\mu\nu}$ on the standard basis, a
symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each finite weight space. Fix a weight
$w$ and let $V_w$ be the (finite-dimensional) weight space of
$F_{\mathrm{sym}}$; let $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ be the matrix with columns the
coordinate vectors of $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ for the finitely many
$e$-restricted $\lambda$ of weight $w$, and rows the **standard** shapes
$M_\mu$, $\mu$ of weight $w$; let
$$H := D_{\mathrm{rect}}^{\mathsf{t}}\, D_{\mathrm{rect}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda) := \sum_\mu \bigl(D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1}\bigr)_{(\mu,\lambda)}\, M_\mu^* ,$$
where $M_\mu^*$ denotes the ambient orthonormal dual frame of the standard
basis. The $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda)$ are the **ambient upper coordinates**
of the basic module: they are the unique elements of the basic subspace
$(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w\subseteq V_w$ characterized weightwise by $B(G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda), G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda')) = \delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$,
and are viewed in the ambient standard frame; adding a vector of the
$B$-orthogonal complement in $V_w$ gives other ambient representatives with
the same pairings. The coefficients
$e_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q) := (D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1})_{(\mu,\lambda)}$ lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$ but need not be Laurent integral or polynomial. They are
coordinates in the ambient space and not a "standard basis of the basic
module"; the exact integral upper basis is the transported upper global basis of
[[thm-upper-and-lower-global-bases-are-dual-and-crystal-compatible]], whose
restricted graded $A$-dual lattice is free weightwise and perfectly paired with
the basic lower $A$-span, while no lower-$A$ selfduality, no $A$-unit $H$ and no
full algebraic duality in infinite rank is implied. The restriction of $B$ to the basic module equals the normalized transported
contravariant form (proved in step 4.2), so these are the same upper vectors
viewed in the ambient standard frame and in their own integral dual lattice.
Upper bar is the adjoint bar
$\psi^\vee$ with its own dual infinity chart and weighted upper operators, not
the ordinary lower bar.

**The full ambient case.** On the whole Fock space the analogous matrix
$D_{\mathrm{full}}$, with columns the $G(\mu)$ over all partitions and rows the
standard shapes, is unitriangular (diagonal $1$, in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ below the
diagonal), and the dual matrix with respect to $B$ is
$$D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}},$$
which is Laurent integral because the inverse of a unitriangular matrix with
entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$.

**A worked instance.** At $e = 2$ the restricted shape $\lambda = (1,1)$ has
$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = M_{1,1} + q\,M_{2}$, so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has the
single column $(q,1)^{\mathsf{t}}$, $H = 1 + q^2$, and
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{M_{1,1}^* + q\,M_2^*}{1+q^2} = \frac{M_{1,1} + q\,M_2}{1+q^2},$$
an explicit ambient coordinate that is rational but not Laurent integral:
$1 + q^2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$. No specialization of the $d$
to decomposition numbers of Hecke algebras is asserted here without the
separate correct Hecke parameter hypotheses.
items.strategy: Transport the lower Fock basis by the linear transpose-label map J, preserving q; obtain the exact coefficient identity, symmetric dominance direction, same-core and full reflected-weight support. Work weightwise with the rectangular lower-column matrix D and ambient orthonormal form. D(0) has distinct coordinate columns, so H=D^tD satisfies H(0)=I and is field invertible; DH^-1 gives the unique upper vectors inside the basic subspace, with whole-ambient representatives differing by its orthogonal complement. Compute the e=2 rational coordinates and the full ambient transpose-inverse matrix separately. The finite node-count identity Nright+Nleft=N(lambda)-1 proves sigma-adjointness of the orthonormal form; normalized highest-weight form uniqueness identifies its basic restriction with the transported QG form. Thus these upper vectors form the restricted integral dual basis with perfect pairing, while rational standard coordinates imply neither lower-A selfduality nor an A-unit Gram matrix. Transport the exact adjoint upper bar, dual charts and weighted operators; preserve all linear/semilinear and Hecke-parameter boundaries.

items.title: The Fock E- and F-actions on the shape (2,1) at e = 3
items.statement: At e3 the QG standard vector |21> has F0=|22>,F1=q^-1|211>,F2=|31>; E0=0,E1=q^-1|11>,E2=|2>. The transported symmetric standard vector M21 has F0_sym=M22,F1_sym=M211,F2_sym=q^-1 M31; E0_sym=0,E1_sym=M11,E2_sym=q^-1 M2, since J transposes outputs AND reflects colors. The QG normalized crystal residue at21 has f0→22,f1→211,e1→11, and f2=e2=0. In the restricted symmetric model it instead has f0→22,f2→31,e2→2, and f1=e1=0. Raw21 IS a representative of its crystal residue in each model; an ordinary q^-1F coefficient does not refute that fact. Its Chevalley action is not its normalized Kashiwara action.

items.title: The charge-zero level-one crystal through rank four at e = 3
items.statement: At $e=3$, charge $\Lambda_0$, in the symmetric-group convention, the empty component through rank four has exactly the following vertices, one row per rank: rank $0$: $\varnothing$; rank $1$: $(1)$; rank $2$: $(2)$ and $(1,1)$; rank $3$: $(2,1)$ and $(1,1,1)$; rank $4$: $(3,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,1,1)$ and $(1,1,1,1)$. These are exactly the $3$-restricted partitions of each size ($1,1,2,2,4$ of them). The cogood-addition arrows staying within ranks0–4 are: $\varnothing\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(1)$; $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(2)$, $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(1,1)$; $(2)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(2,1)$; $(1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(1,1,1)$; $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(2,2)$, $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(3,1)$; $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(1,1,1,1)$, $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(2,1,1)$; All other additions from ranks0–3 vanish; additions from rank4 leaving the displayed window are omitted, not declared zero. The good-deletion arrows into the listed ranks are: $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}\varnothing$; $(2)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1)$, $(1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(1)$; $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(2)$, $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1,1)$; $(2,2)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}(2,1)$, $(3,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(2,1)$, $(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1,1,1)$, $(1,1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}(1,1,1)$. In particular $(2,1)$ has no arrow of residue $1$ in either direction, and $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(3,1)$ is the arrow whose conjugate is the QG-6 Fock arrow $\tilde f_1$ from $(2,1)$ to $(2,1,1)$.
items.strategy: Finite verification by the reduced $i$-signature, hand-checkable at every vertex. Compute for each listed partition and each $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ the residues $c-r$, list the addable and removable $i$-nodes from top to bottom, cancel $-$ above $+$ pairs and read the topmost surviving $-$ and the bottommost surviving $+$. For example at $(1,1)$ and $i=1$ the two addable nodes $(1,2)$ and $(3,1)$ both survive, giving $\tilde f_1(1,1)=(1,1,1)$; at $(2,1)$ and $i=1$ the removable node $(1,2)$ lies above the addable node $(3,1)$ and the pair cancels, so $\varepsilon_1=\varphi_1=0$ and both arrows vanish; at $(2,1)$ and $i=2$ the addable node $(1,3)$ lies above the removable node $(2,1)$, the word $+-$ does not cancel, and $\tilde f_2(2,1)=(3,1)$, $\tilde e_2(2,1)=(2)$. Residue labels are $c-r$ as fixed in the convention item. The list of $3$-restricted partitions is the direct check of $\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}<3$; the count $1,1,2,2,4$ matches the multiplicity of $V(\Lambda_0)$ (Leclerc, *Fock space representations of U_q(sl_n^)*, sec. 3.14, printed pp. 25-26, where the $n$-regular labels give the basic representation; the restricted reading is the transpose/sign dictionary of the convention item). No module theory is used beyond the vertex list of [[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]. The rank4 outgoing boundary is deliberately omitted; completeness/zero claims concern only ranks0–3. This derived finite signature calculation is not a claimed printed native source example.

items.title: The full Fock space is not automatically the irreducible basic module
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice through [[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]; the exhibited non-containment facts themselves are finite checks.
items.statement: At e3 the entire F_sym is strictly larger than its cyclic basic module. The shape4 is not3-restricted since4−0≥3; its conjugate is1111 (NOT111), which is not3-regular since part1 has multiplicity4≥3. Both raw M4 in F_sym and |1111> in F_QG are nonzero and are OUTSIDE their respective field basic modules, and their ambient lower global lifts are outside too. The full signature rule remains meaningful on these shapes in the full Fock crystal; for example restricted-model e0(4)=3 is an edge of another component, not a route into the empty component. Modular/basic signature statements restricted to restricted labels do not apply to4 as a basic label.
items.strategy: Restricted/regular and transposed size checks are immediate. To prove actual vector exclusion rather than graph-only exclusion, apply the actual top-isotypic crystal-lattice splitting theorem to F_QG at its maximal one-dimensional top Lambda0: F0_QG∩V(Lambda0) is the canonical lower lattice and its residue basis exactly the regular empty component. If raw1111 were in this module, its nonzero nonregular residue would lie in that component's span, contradicting residue-basis splitting. Its ambient lower lift has the same residue and is also excluded. Transport by the genuine field and chart isomorphism J gives M4 and its lift. At4, the sole removable0 node is(1,4), so the full restricted signature yields e0→3; neither shape is in the restricted empty component (3−0≥3), hence this edge is compatible with the full decomposable crystal. This corrects the native assertion that the signature had no ambient crystal meaning, while preserving the modular restricted-vertex hypothesis and the strongest field-vector boundary.

items.title: Arbitrary-level cyclotomic Hecke, Murphy cell and multipartition Schur modules
items.statement:
Let R be a commutative ring, n≥0, ℓ≥1, and z,U_1,...,U_ℓ units of R. Define H_n by commuting invertible X_1,...,X_n, finite generators T_i satisfying (T_i−z)(T_i+1)=0, the type-A braid/distant relations, T_iX_iT_i=zX_(i+1), distant mixed commutation, and ∏_a(X_1−U_a)=0. For n=0 set H_0=R. The grading variable v is not z. An ℓ-multipartition λ of n is an ordered tuple of partitions; dominance compares every cumulative component/row sum. Fill tλ in component,row,column order. Put a_k=Σ_(b<k)|λ^(b)|, uλ=∏_k∏_(j≤a_k)(X_j−U_k), xλ=Σ_(w∈Sλ)T_w, mλ=xλuλ, Mλ=mλH_n. The row subgroup Sλ stabilizes the rows of tλ. The presentation involution * fixes all X_j,T_i and reverses products. For standard s,t of shapeλ put m_st=T_d(s)*mλT_d(t), where tλd(s)=s. Denote by H^{>λ} the span of higher Murphy shapes once their basis/cell law is established by [[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and Sλ the right cell/Specht module with basis m_t and action from that cell law. Its cellular form defines Dλ=Sλ/radSλ; Dλ may vanish.

Types are EXACTLY all ℓ-multipartitions of n, including empty components, not all multicompositions. A semistandard tableau S has labels (row,component) ordered by component then row, weak rows, strict columns, and a label of component a can occur only in physical component b≤a; its type counts each label with the multiplicity of that multipartition row. For a standard s, µ(s) replaces each entry by its row/component in tµ. Set m_(S,t)=Σ_(s:µ(s)=S)m_st and m_(S,T)=Σ_(s,t:µ(s)=S,ν(t)=T)m_st. Define M=⊕_(λ multipartition of n)Mλ and C_n=End_(H_n)(M), with ordinary composition. For S,T of shapeλ and typesµ,ν, the map φ_ST, once justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]], sends mαh to δ_(α,ν)m_(S,T)h. Its right cell module ∆λ has basis v_T for semistandard T of multipartition types, contravariant cell form and quotient Lλ. Let Tλ be the unique tableau of shape/typeλ, and let eλ be the identity projection onto Mλ. Put ω=(∅,...,∅,(1^n)) and e=eω; mω=1, so Mω=H_n. In particular H_n is an actual direct summand of M. Weight projections for Jantzen theory are eν with ν multipartition. Define K_(λ,ν)=#SStdν(λ). All asserted module/form/map laws are discharged by the linked local theorem/lemma suppliers; the definition itself does not claim their proofs or the primitive residue-content classification.

items.title: Laurent binomial valuation at one over any field
items.statement: For nonzero A,B in F and integers u,v, the valuation of A t^u-B t^v is zero if A!=B. If A=B and N=u-v!=0, it is 1 in characteristic zero, and p^{v_p(|N|)} in characteristic p>0. If A=B and N=0 the polynomial is zero and does not have finite valuation.
items.strategy:
**Statement.** For nonzero A,B in F and integers u,v, the valuation of A t^u-B t^v is zero if A!=B. If A=B and N=u-v!=0, it is 1 in characteristic zero, and p^{v_p(|N|)} in characteristic p>0. If A=B and N=0 the polynomial is zero and does not have finite valuation.

**Proof.** Multiplication by B t^v is a unit, so reduce to (A/B)t^N-1. If A/B!=1 its value at t=1 is nonzero. When A=B replace negative N by -N by multiplying by the unit -t^N. If char F=0, t^N-1=(t-1)(1+t+...+t^{N-1}), and the second factor evaluates to N!=0. In characteristic p, write N=p^r m with p not dividing m. Frobenius gives t^N-1=(t^m-1)^{p^r}; the same geometric-series factor for t^m-1 evaluates to the nonzero element m. The valuation is p^r. The zero case is immediate.

In the intended J expression, foot residues are Q_a q_H^{j-i} t^{na+j-i}. This leaf computes their difference exactly when it is nonzero and prevents replacing valuations by an equality-of-residues indicator in positive characteristic.

items.title: Ultra-tight multisets admit integer column potentials
items.statement: Let $r\ge1$ and $L_r=\mathbb Z^r/\mathbb Z(1,\ldots,1)$. For a finite multiset $X$ in $L_r$, call $X$ tight if $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)\le2$ for all occurrences $x,y$ and indices $k,l$. A zero exchange replaces $x,y$ by $x-e_k+e_l,y+e_k-e_l$ when that difference equals2; it is symmetric. Call $X$ ultra-tight if every finite zero-exchange sequence ends in a tight multiset. Then $X$ is ultra-tight iff some $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for every $x\in X,k,l$. This includes the empty multiset and $r=1$.
items.strategy:
For the empty multiset take s=0. For nonempty X the complete finite induction follows.

Work in L_r=Z^r/Z(1,…,1). A finite multiset X is tight if

(x_k−x_l)−(y_k−y_l)≤2 for every x,y∈X and every k,l.

A zero exchange replaces x,y by x−e_k+e_l and y+e_k−e_l when the displayed difference equals 2. This relation is symmetric; call X ultra-tight if every multiset obtainable by finitely many zero exchanges is tight. These notions do not depend on representatives in Z^r.

**Lemma.** X is ultra-tight iff there are integers s₁,…,s_r such that x_k−x_l≤s_k−s_l+1 for every x∈X and every k,l.

The reverse implication has a short direct proof. After replacing x by x−s, every row has maximum minus minimum at most one. A zero exchange must have x_k−x_l=1 and y_k−y_l=−1, so it merely swaps the high and low values in these two coordinates of each row. The row spread remains at most one. The property is preserved by every zero exchange and implies tightness.

Here is a full proof of the forward implication, adapted from the actual proof of Fayers Proposition 2.2 and its induction step Proposition 2.3 (author PDF pp.11–15). We induct on r. The r=1 case is trivial. Projection forgetting the last coordinate takes an ultra-tight multiset to one in L_(r−1): every zero exchange in the projection lifts using the same pair of coordinate indices and the same labeled multiset occurrences. Hence the induction hypothesis supplies potentials for the first r−1 coordinates. It remains to extend them to coordinate r, preserving all previous bounds.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

items.title: DVR cellular Jantzen filtration and exact Gram valuation
items.statement: Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.

**Statement.** Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.

**Proof.** View the form as an O-linear map phi:M -> M*=Hom_O(M,O), x -> b(x,-). Its determinant is nonzero, so it has full rank. A direct Smith reduction needs no characteristic restriction: choose a nonzero matrix entry of least valuation, move it to the upper-left corner, and multiply its row by a unit to make it pi^a. Every entry is divisible by pi^a. Row and column subtraction eliminate its column and row, leaving a smaller matrix over O. Iterate. Since all elimination coefficients belong to O and every operation is invertible over O, this gives independent bases of M and M* in which phi sends u_j to pi^{a_j}v_j, with all a_j>=0. Thus

$$M(s)=\bigoplus_j\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}O u_j,\qquad \dim_F M_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$$

Consequently M_F^s=0 for s>max_j a_j and sum_{s>0}dim M_F^s=sum_j a_j=nu_pi(det G). Reduction mod pi shows directly that M(1)/its reduction consists of exactly the vectors orthogonal to every vector of M_F, proving M_F^1=rad(b_F). Contravariance gives b(ax,y)=b(x,a*y) in pi^s O whenever x in M(s), proving stability.

For the last assertion use the defining cellular multiplication, not merely the word cellularity: in the standard module, for every basis label u and label v the corresponding cell element acts as w -> b_F(v,w)u (with left/right conventions transposed if necessary). If a submodule N contains w outside rad(b_F), choose v with b_F(v,w) !=0. Every basis vector u belongs to N by this rank-one action, so N=M_F. Therefore every proper submodule is contained in rad(b_F). The radical itself is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same argument shows the quotient is simple. It is the unique maximal submodule and equals the module radical. This completes the proof, including characteristic 2: the Smith reduction uses different domain and codomain bases, never diagonalization of a symmetric form.

items.title: Universal nondegenerate affine Hecke ordered monomials form a basis
items.statement: For the affine presentation associated to [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] over the universal Laurent parameter ring R, without imposing the first-variable cyclotomic relation, both families X^aT_w and T_wX^a, a∈Z^n,w∈S_n, are R-bases. Left multiplication by any nonzero Laurent polynomial is injective. Localizing at variable differences embeds this algebra into its rational crossed product; Φ_i=T_i−(z−1)X_(i+1)/(X_(i+1)−X_i) obeys Φ_i f=s_i(f)Φ_i. No cyclotomic basis, BK theorem, trace or primitive-content assertion is used.
items.strategy:
## 1. Affine PBW and the localization used only to prove divisibility

Here is a local PBW proof so that polynomial divisibility does not depend on an unproved affine independence assertion. Bernstein commutation moves every polynomial to the left, and the finite standard-basis relations then give spanning by `X^a T_w`. Set

`c_ij=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)` and `d_ij=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)`.

In the rational crossed product of the polynomial fraction field with S_n, represent `T_i=c_(i,i+1)+d_(i,i+1)s_i`. These operators satisfy Bernstein commutation and the finite Hecke relations. The quadratic relation uses `c_ij+c_ji=z-1` and `d_ij d_ji=z+(z-1)c_ij-c_ij²`. For three distinct variables the single identity

`c_ij c_jk=c_ik(c_ij+c_jk-(z-1))`

proves the braid relation: coefficients of the longest permutation are both `d_ij d_ik d_jk`; coefficients of the two length2 permutations agree by commutativity; the two length1 coefficients reduce to that displayed identity; the identity coefficient reduces to `(c_ij-c_jk)[c_ij c_jk-c_ik(c_ij+c_jk-(z-1))]=0`. Distant generators involve disjoint variable pairs. These equalities are obtained by substituting their displayed rational functions and clearing the three nonzero differences. Thus this is an actual representation of the universal presentation.

For a reduced word w, the coefficient of its permutation in T_w is a nonzero product of d-functions. All other terms are proper Bruhat subwords. Distinct permutations are independent in the crossed product; if desired this is verified as operators by applying a putative dependence to powers of `f=Σ_j j X_j`: the distinct polynomials w(f) form a Vandermonde matrix over the fraction field. A maximal Bruhat term in a putative PBW dependence therefore has nonzero leading coefficient and cannot cancel. This proves independence and hence affine PBW. The same argument gives right PBW by the involution. In particular left multiplication by a nonzero element of P is injective. All this occurs over the universal characteristic-zero domain; its actual polynomial identities then specialize.

Localize P at the differences `X_i-X_j`, i≠j. Define

`Φ_i=T_i-c_(i,i+1)`.

The Bernstein relation gives `Φ_i f=s_i(f)Φ_i` for every polynomial or localized rational f. Expanding a reduced word T_w as a product of Φ_i+c_i shows that `T_w f` is a sum of terms each containing `v(f)` on the left, where v is the permutation of a subword of that reduced word, multiplied by a coefficient whose only denominators are products of variable differences. Every such v is Bruhat-below w: deletion of adjacent cancelling pairs reduces a subword to a reduced subexpression, or equivalently the standard subword characterization gives this inequality. No denominators `U_a-U_b`, quantum factorials, or Gram determinants are inverted.
