items.title: Each padded irreducible family is realised by a finitely generated FI-module
items.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $\lambda$ be a partition with $|\lambda|=m$. There is an FI-module $V(\lambda)$ over $k$ with $$V(\lambda)_n\cong\begin{cases}V_{\lambda[n]},&n\ge m+\lambda_1,\ \varnothing,&n<m+\lambda_1.\end{cases}$$ It is finitely generated in degree $m+\lambda_1$, has $\operatorname{weight}(V(\lambda))=m$ and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V(\lambda))=\lambda_1$.
items.strategy: Put m=|lambda| and d=m+lambda_1. For n>=d, horizontal Pieri in M(lambda)_n gives the multiplicity-one constituent S^{lambda[n]}; take its canonical isotypic subspace and put V(lambda)_n=0 below d. For an injection f:[p]->[n] with p>=d, f_* is S_p-equivariant and its image is fixed by permutations of the complementary n-p points, since these permutations compose with f to f itself. Hence the image is a quotient of Ind_{S_p x S_{n-p}}^{S_n}(S^{lambda[p]} x 1). Any target shape nu in both this induced representation and M(lambda)_n satisfies nu_i>=lambda[p]_i for i>=2 and nu_{i+1}<=lambda_i by the two horizontal-strip interlacing conditions. Since lambda[p]_i=lambda_{i-1} for i>=2, these force nu_{i+1}=lambda_i for all i, i.e. nu=lambda[n]. Thus f_* preserves the selected subspaces; no map from the zero rank m space is used. Free-FI injection maps are injective on the direct sums indexed by image subsets, so a nonzero V(lambda)_d maps nontrivially at every n>=d; the S_n-span is the irreducible V(lambda)_n. Hence the family is generated in degree d and has weight m. Its injectivity degree is zero by containment in M(lambda). The evaluation map M(S^{lambda[d]}) -> V(lambda) is onto, and the exact free-module bound gives surjectivity degree at most lambda_1, because the first part of lambda[d] is lambda_1. At a=m, Phi_m(V(lambda))_{lambda_1} is nonzero while the previous graded piece is zero (when lambda_1>0), so the bound is sharp. For the empty partition, d=0 and the constant family has stability degree zero. All representations and interlacing arguments are finite-dimensional over the rational model, then extended to k; no field embeds into C.

items.title: Dimensions of finitely generated FI-modules are eventually polynomial
items.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be a finitely generated FI-module over $k$ with finite-dimensional values, weight $d$ and stability degree $s$, with character polynomial $P_V$ as above. Then $$\dim_kV_n=P_V(n,0,0,\dots)$$ for every $n\ge s+d$; in particular $\dim_kV_n$ is given by a polynomial in $n$ of degree at most $d$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
items.strategy: Evaluate the character polynomial identity at the identity permutation: $\chi_{V_n}(\mathrm{id})=P_V(X_1(\mathrm{id}),X_2(\mathrm{id}),\dots)=P_V(n,0,0,\dots)$, because the identity has $n$ fixed points and no cycles of length $\ge2$, and $\dim_kV_n=\chi_{V_n}(\mathrm{id})$ for a finite-dimensional module.

title: Character Polynomials, FI-Modules, and Representation Stability — Examples

items.title: The permutation FI-module has character polynomial $X_1$
items.statement: For every finite set $S$ let $V_S$ be the free $k$-module on $S$, and on an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ let $V(f)$ be the linear extension of $f$. This is the FI-module $M(1)$ ([[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]) with $V_n\cong k^n$ the permutation representation of $S_n$; it is generated by $V_{\{1\}}$. Its character is the character polynomial $X_1$ of weighted degree $1$ ([[def-character-polynomial-in-cycle-counts]]): for every $n$ and every $\sigma\in S_n$, $\chi_{V_n}(\sigma)=X_1(\sigma)$, the number of fixed points.
items.strategy: The transition maps are functorial by construction, so $V$ is an FI-module, and $M(1)$ has the stated basis of injections $1\to S$; the image of the generating element is all of $M(1)$ because every injection $1\to S$ is the image of the single injection $1\to\{1\}$ for some bijection of $S$. The matrix of $\sigma$ in that basis is a permutation matrix, so its trace is the number of $1\times1$ blocks, i.e. the number of fixed points, which is $X_1(\sigma)$; this holds for every $n$, matching the character-polynomial identity on the whole range.

items.title: The exterior square of the permutation FI-module has character polynomial $\binom{X_1}{2}-X_2$
items.statement: Let $V=M(1)$ be the permutation FI-module of the previous example and define $W_S:=\Lambda^2V_S$ with $W(f)=\Lambda^2V(f)$; this is an FI-module, and $W_n\cong\Lambda^2(k^n)$ as an $S_n$-module. Its character is the character polynomial $\binom{X_1}{2}-X_2$ of weighted degree $2$: for every $n$ and every $\sigma\in S_n$, $\chi_{W_n}(\sigma)=\binom{X_1(\sigma)}{2}-X_2(\sigma)$, where $X_1(\sigma)$ is the number of fixed points and $X_2(\sigma)$ the number of $2$-cycles.
items.strategy: Functoriality of $\Lambda^2$ makes $W$ an FI-module with the same transition-map compatibility. Fix $\sigma\in S_n$ and use the basis $x_i\wedge x_j$, $i<j$: the coefficient of $x_i\wedge x_j$ in $\sigma\cdot(x_i\wedge x_j)$ is nonzero exactly when $\sigma$ preserves the unordered pair $\{i,j\}$, and it equals $+1$ when both elements are fixed and $-1$ when they are exchanged by the $2$-cycle $(i\,j)$; a permutation that preserves a two-element set acts on it either as the identity or as its transposition, so there are no other diagonal entries. Hence the trace is $\binom{X_1(\sigma)}{2}-X_2(\sigma)$, which is a character polynomial of weighted degree $2$ ([[def-character-polynomial-in-cycle-counts]]), using that the character of $\Lambda^2$ is determined by the character of $V$ ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]).

items.title: The padded family $V((2,1))$ begins at rank five, with weight three and stability degree two
items.statement: Let $\lambda=(2,1)$, so $|\lambda|=3$ and $\lambda_1=2$. The first-row padding $\lambda[n]=(n-3,2,1)$ ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]) is a partition exactly for $n\ge5=3+2$: for $n=3$ the sequence $(0,2,1)$ is not weakly decreasing and $\lambda[3]$ is not a partition, for $n=4$ one gets $(1,2,1)$, still not a partition, and for $n\ge5$ it is. Accordingly the FI-module $V((2,1))$ of [[prop-fi-module-realizing-one-padded-irreducible-family]] has $$V((2,1))_n\cong\begin{cases}V_{(n-3,2,1)},&n\ge5,\ \varnothing,&n<5,\end{cases}$$ is generated in degree $5$, and has $\operatorname{weight}(V((2,1)))=3$ and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V((2,1)))=2$.
items.strategy: Check the padding threshold from the definition: $\lambda[n]$ is a partition iff $n-|\lambda|\ge\lambda_1$, i.e. $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1=5$; for $n=3,4$ the first part is smaller than the second, and for $n\ge5$ the sequence is weakly decreasing. Then apply the realization proposition, which gives generation in degree $5$, weight $|\lambda|=3$ and stability degree $\lambda_1=2$; the two divergences from the padding threshold $n=|\lambda|=3$ are exactly the point of the example.

items.title: A pointwise one-dimensional FI-module that is not finitely generated
items.statement: Over a field $k$, define $V_S:=k\,e_S$ for every finite set $S$ (so $V$ is pointwise one-dimensional), let $V(f)\colon V_S\to V_{S'}$ send $e_S\mapsto e_{S'}$ when $f\colon S\to S'$ is a bijection, and $e_S\mapsto0$ when $f$ is not a bijection. Then $V$ is an FI-module with $\dim_kV_S=1$ for every $S$, but $V$ is not finitely generated: no finite set of elements generates it.
items.strategy: Functoriality: composites of bijections are bijections and give the identity on $k e_S$, and if $f\circ g$ is a bijection then both $f$ and $g$ are bijections; so if either of $f,g$ fails to be a bijection, the composite $V(f)V(g)$ and $V(f\circ g)$ are both $0$. Non-finite-generation: given finitely many generating elements, choose $M$ at least as large as the sizes of the finite sets on which they live; every generator lies in some $V_S$ with $|S|\le M$, and every injection from such an $S$ into a set $T$ with $|T|>M$ is a non-bijection, so its image is $0$; hence the generated sub-FI-module is contained in $\bigoplus_{|T|\le M}V_T$ and misses $e_T$ for $|T|=M+1$. The pointwise spaces are one-dimensional, so pointwise finite generation (even finite-dimensionality) does not imply finite generation.

title: Murnaghan Stability via FI-Modules

items.title: Specializations of symmetric functions and the series $\sigma$
items.statement: Work in the algebra of symmetric functions over Q in an alphabet X, in which the power sums p_1,p_2,... are algebraically independent generators. A specialization is an algebra homomorphism f |-> f[A] to a commutative Q-algebra; it is determined by the sequence (p_k[A])_{k>=1}, and conversely every sequence of values gives one. For specializations A,B define p_k[A+B]:=p_k[A]+p_k[B], p_k[-A]:=-p_k[A] and p_k[AB]:=p_k[A]p_k[B]. For a coefficient multiplicity c write c dot A with p_k[c dot A]:=c p_k[A]. Distinguish this from a one-letter alphabet t, for which p_k[t]:=t^k and therefore p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A]; all occurrences of tX, t^{-1} and sigma[t] below use this one-letter convention. The symbol 1 is the one-letter alphabet with p_k[1]=1, and -1 is its plethystic negative, with p_k[-1]=-1 (not the ordinary one-letter alphabet whose letter is minus one). Write f[A+B], f[-A], f[AB] and f[c dot A] for the corresponding specializations. Define X^perp to be the specialization with f[X^perp]:=f^perp for all f, where f^perp denotes the adjoint of multiplication by f with respect to the Hall inner product. Define the series sigma[X]:=sum_{n>=0} h_n[X]. Sigma is interpreted in the graded completion, or with a formal degree variable; every use of Hall pairing with a polynomial means its finite degree truncation. No convergence of a scalar infinite sum is asserted.
items.strategy: Existence and uniqueness of a specialization with prescribed p_k-values is the universal property of the polynomial ring Q[p_1,p_2,...]: the p_k are algebraically independent, so a homomorphism is specified by arbitrary images of the p_k and such a homomorphism exists. The operations on specializations are defined on the p_k and extended multiplicatively, again by the universal property. The adjoint f^perp of multiplication by f exists and is unique because the Hall form is nondegenerate and each graded piece of the symmetric function ring is finite dimensional (the Schur functions are an orthonormal basis). No choice is used. The adjoints of commuting multiplication operators commute: (fg)^perp=g^perp f^perp=f^perp g^perp. Thus the commuting algebra they generate is the target for the specialization X^perp; a noncommutative ambient endomorphism algebra is not being used as the coefficient algebra.
items.axiom_use: None: algebraic independence of the power sums over Q and finite-dimensional nondegenerate bilinear algebra.

items.title: Threefold Schur coefficients $c^\delta_{a,b,c}$
items.statement: For partitions delta,a,b,c with |delta|=|a|+|b|+|c| define the threefold Schur coefficient c^delta_{a,b,c}:=[s_delta] s_a s_b s_c, the coefficient of s_delta in the ordinary product of the three Schur functions. These are nonnegative integers, they are symmetric in a,b,c, and they satisfy the iterated Littlewood-Richardson identity c^delta_{a,b,c}=sum_phi c^phi_{a,b} c^delta_{phi,c}=sum_psi c^psi_{a,c}c^delta_{psi,b}, the sums over partitions phi (respectively psi) of |a|+|b| (respectively |a|+|c|). Equivalently c^delta_{a,b,c}=<s_a s_b s_c | s_delta>.
items.strategy: Nonnegativity follows from the iterated LR expansion below, and symmetry in a,b,c follows from commutativity of the product. The iterated identity is the associativity of the Schur product: s_as_bs_c = (s_as_b)s_c = sum_phi c^phi_{a,b}s_phi s_c = sum_{phi,delta}c^phi_{a,b}c^delta_{phi,c}s_delta, compared with the definition. The inner-product form is orthonormality of the Schur basis.
items.axiom_use: None.

items.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion $s_\mu$, the operators $U_n$ and $V$, and $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$
items.statement: Let alpha=(alpha_1,...,alpha_k) be a partition and n>=0; the padded sequence is alpha[n]:=(n-|alpha|,alpha_1,...,alpha_k). For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers mu=(mu_1,...,mu_m) define s_mu by the Jacobi-Trudi determinant det(h_{mu_j+i-j})_{1<=i,j<=m} with h_k=0 for k<0, as in the source; every such determinant is either 0 or +-1 times a Schur function. Define Z-linear endomorphisms of the ring of symmetric functions by U_n(s_lambda):=s_{lambda[n]} and V(s_lambda):=s_{lambda+(1)} on the Schur basis, extended linearly. Finally, for partitions alpha,beta define stab(alpha,beta) to be the least n_0>=0 such that s_{alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{beta[n_0+k]}=V^k(s_{alpha[n_0]}*s_{beta[n_0]}) as elements of the symmetric function ring for all k>0, where * is the internal product; stab(alpha,beta) is not shown to exist by this definition alone (its existence and value are the sharp global threshold theorem).
items.strategy: U_n and V are well-defined by linear extension from the Schur basis, which is a Z-basis. The Jacobi-Trudi completion is well-defined by the published Jacobi-Trudi identities with the convention h_k=0 for k<0, and the sign statement is the standard column-permutation computation. The definition of stab(alpha,beta) only records the source's convention; no existence statement is claimed here. For the straightening assertion, take q_i=mu_i+m-i. If two q_i coincide, the corresponding Jacobi-Trudi rows (or columns in the transposed convention) coincide and the determinant is zero. Otherwise sort q decreasing; the sorting sign multiplies the determinant, and the new index sequence q_sorted_i-(m-i) is weakly decreasing. If its last part is negative, its final row has only negative h-indices and is zero; otherwise it is a partition after discarding zeros. This proves the claimed zero-or-signed-Schur rule, including invalid initial padding.
items.axiom_use: None: the Jacobi-Trudi completion and the linear extensions are Z-linear algebra on the free abelian group on partitions.

items.title: Schur functions on sums and products of alphabets
items.statement: For all partitions lambda,mu,nu and all specializations A,B: (a) s_lambda[A+B] = sum_{mu,nu} c^lambda_{mu,nu} s_mu[A] s_nu[B], the sum over pairs with |mu|+|nu|=|lambda|; (b) s_lambda[AB] = sum_{mu,nu} g^lambda_{mu,nu} s_mu[A] s_nu[B], the sum over pairs with |mu|=|nu|=|lambda|, where g^lambda_{mu,nu} is the ordinary Kronecker coefficient. Both sums are finite.
items.strategy: (a) Use the published Schur Cauchy kernel: sigma[(A+B)Z]=sigma[AZ]sigma[BZ]. The left is sum_lambda s_lambda[A+B]s_lambda[Z]; expand the right as sum_{mu,nu}s_mu[A]s_nu[B]s_mu[Z]s_nu[Z], then use the proved LR Schur-product expansion in Z. Comparing the s_lambda[Z] coefficient gives exactly (a). (b) Use the same Cauchy theorem on sigma[ABZ]=sum_rho p_rho[A]p_rho[B]p_rho[Z]/z_rho. For fixed ordinary Schur functions f[A]=s_mu[A],g[B]=s_nu[B], their Hall pairing with this kernel is f*g in Z: in power coordinates f=sum a_rho p_rho and g=sum b_rho p_rho, the pairing is sum a_rho b_rho z_rho p_rho[Z], exactly the actual local internal-product normalization. The Schur expansion f*g=sum_lambda g^lambda_{mu,nu}s_lambda[Z] therefore gives the s_mu[A]s_nu[B]s_lambda[Z] coefficients of the kernel. Its Schur Cauchy expansion sum_lambda s_lambda[AB]s_lambda[Z] gives the other side of (b), so comparing coefficients proves (b). Every fixed Z-degree involves only finitely many partitions; these polynomial identities can then be evaluated at arbitrary specializations A,B. No multiplicativity/bilinearity of s_lambda in the alphabet variables or unproved Schur-functor decomposition is assumed.
items.axiom_use: None.

items.title: The series $\sigma$: product formula, Cauchy identity, adjunction and reproducing kernel
items.statement: Let sigma[X]=sum_{n>=0}h_n[X]. (1) sigma[X]=prod_{x in X}(1-x)^{-1} and sigma[-X]=prod_{x in X}(1-x); in particular sigma[t]=(1-t)^{-1} and sigma[-t]=1-t for a scalar t. (2) sigma[A+B]=sigma[A]sigma[B] and, for the one-letter alphabet t, sigma[tA]=sum_{n>=0}t^n h_n[A]. (3) Cauchy identity: sigma[XY]=sum_lambda s_lambda[X]s_lambda[Y]. (4) For every specialization A the operator sigma[AX^perp] is the adjoint of multiplication by sigma[AX]: sigma[AX^perp]f[X]=f[X+A] for all f. (5) Reproducing kernel: <sigma[AX] | f[X]>_X = f[A] for all f.
items.strategy: (1) is the elementary product formula for the generating function of complete homogeneous functions, together with p_k[-A]=-p_k[A]; (2) is immediate from (1) and the multiplicativity p_k[AB]=p_k[A]p_k[B]. (3) is the exact Schur expansion of the locally proved thm-cauchy-kernel-has-power-complete-and-schur-expansions; its power expansion also supplies the kernel normalization used by the compatibility lemma. For (4) and (5): by Cauchy, sigma[AX]=sum_rho s_rho[A]s_rho[X], so multiplication by sigma[AX] is the operator sum_rho s_rho[A](multiplication by s_rho); for f=s_lambda and any g, <sigma[AX^perp]s_lambda,g>=<s_lambda,sigma[AX]g>=sum_rho s_rho[A]<s_lambda,s_rho g>=sum_rho s_rho[A] c^lambda_{rho,mu}=[s_mu]s_lambda[X+A] using the coproduct identity (a) of the previous lemma and orthonormality of the Schur basis. Taking g=s_mu shows (4); (5) is its equivalent dual form (evaluate on f=s_lambda and expand). The one-letter scaling uses p_k[t]=t^k, whereas coefficient multiplicity c dot A uses p_k[c dot A]=c p_k[A]; these operations are not conflated. The adjoint formula for arbitrary polynomial f involves only finitely many degree-lowering terms. Formal series and kernels are paired degree by degree; specializing a naked divergent scalar sigma[1] is never required.
items.axiom_use: None.

I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press 1995; Chapter I sections 2, 4 and 5 (complete functions, Hall inner product, adjoint operators)

items.title: Vertex-operator generating series for the padded Schur functions
items.statement: Let alpha be a partition and t a formal variable. With the Jacobi-Trudi convention of the first definition item for the integer sequences alpha[n]=(n-|alpha|,alpha_1,alpha_2,...), one has the identity of formal Laurent series with coefficients in the symmetric function ring: sum_{n in Z} s_{alpha[n]}[X] t^n = sigma[tX] . s_alpha[tX - 1] = t^{|alpha|} . sigma[tX] . s_alpha[X - t^{-1}], where s_alpha[tX-1] is evaluated through the specialization p_k |-> t^k p_k[X] - 1 and s_alpha[X-t^{-1}] through p_k |-> p_k[X]-t^{-k}. Equivalently, sum_{n in Z} s_{alpha[n]}[X]t^n = sigma[tX] sum_{mu: alpha/mu a vertical strip} (-1)^{|alpha|-|mu|} t^{|mu|} s_mu[X]. (This is the growth paper's identity (6) p. 7, displayed there as t^{|alpha|}Gamma(t|X)s_alpha[X] = sigma[tX]s_alpha[tX-1].)
items.strategy: Apply the Schur coproduct to the negative one-letter alphabet: s_alpha[tX-1]=sum_{i=0}^{ell(alpha)}(-1)^i t^{|alpha|-i} s_{alpha/(1^i)}[X], because s_nu[-1]=(-1)^{|nu|} for a column nu=(1^i) and is zero otherwise. The skew functions are the Hall adjoints e_i^perp s_alpha by def-skew-schur-function-by-hall-adjointness, and their determinants are supplied by thm-skew-jacobi-trudi-and-tableau-expansion. On the right, the coefficient of t^n in sigma[tX]s_alpha[tX-1] is sum_i(-1)^i h_{n-|alpha|+i}s_{alpha/(1^i)}. In the ordinary (non-transposed) Jacobi-Trudi matrix for (n-|alpha|,alpha), expand along the first row: its i+1-st entry is h_{n-|alpha|+i}, and deleting that column leaves exactly the skew Jacobi-Trudi matrix for alpha/(1^i), with sign (-1)^i. Equivalently expand the first column in the transposed convention printed in the Definition. Thus the coefficient equals s_{alpha[n]} for every integer n. Negative total degree gives zero: every nonzero determinant monomial would have that negative degree, impossible with h_k=0 for k<0. Homogeneity with the one-letter alphabet t gives s_alpha[tX-1]=t^{|alpha|}s_alpha[X-t^{-1}], so both generating formulas hold. All coefficient sums are finite; no scalar-divergent sigma[1] is evaluated.
items.axiom_use: None.

items.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion is compatible with the internal product
items.statement: For partitions alpha,beta with a=|alpha|, b=|beta|, define R_{alpha,beta}[Z]=<s_alpha[A]s_beta[B] | sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]>_{A,B}. This is a finite symmetric-function polynomial of Z-degree at most a+b. For every n>=0, (U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)=U_n R_{alpha,beta}, where U_n uses Jacobi-Trudi completion, including when the padded sequences are not partitions. Equivalently sum_{n>=0}(U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)t^n=sigma[tX]R_{alpha,beta}[tX-1], with t a one-letter formal alphabet. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression R=sum_{delta,epsilon,tau} ((s_delta s_tau)^perp s_alpha) ((s_epsilon s_tau)^perp s_beta) (s_delta*s_epsilon), all factors evaluated in Z.
items.strategy: First establish the internal-product kernel from the actual published normalization p_rho*p_tau=delta_{rho,tau} z_rho p_rho and <p_rho,p_tau>=delta_{rho,tau} z_rho: for homogeneous f,g of the same degree, <f[A]g[B] | sigma[XAB]>_{A,B}=f*g in X, by the power expansion sigma[XAB]=sum_rho p_rho[X]p_rho[A]p_rho[B]/z_rho; unequal degrees pair to zero. Write f=s_alpha, g=s_beta. The padded vertex series has A-degree-n component U_n f in sigma[A]f[A-1] and B-degree-n component U_n g in sigma[B]g[B-1]. Therefore F(t):=sum_n(U_n f)*(U_n g)t^n=<sigma[A]f[A-1] sigma[B]g[B-1] | sigma[tXAB]>_{A,B}. Move multiplication by sigma[A] and sigma[B] to the kernel by Hall adjunction: translate A and B each by the one-letter 1, obtaining <f[A-1]g[B-1] | sigma[tX(A+1)(B+1)]>. Moving the two negative translations on f,g to the kernel multiplies it by sigma[-A]sigma[-B]. Factor out sigma[tX], and multiplicativity of sigma gives F(t)=sigma[tX]<f[A]g[B] | sigma[tXAB+tXA+tXB-A-B]>. On setting Z=tX-1 in ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB, the negative AB term from ZAB cancels the positive AB, leaving exactly tXAB+tXA+tXB-A-B. Hence F(t)=sigma[tX]R[tX-1]. Finiteness of R: in the factorization sigma[ZAB]sigma[ZA]sigma[ZB]sigma[AB], terms with degrees i,j,k,l satisfy i+j+l=a and i+k+l=b; Z-degree i+j+k=a+b-i-2l<=a+b. Only finitely many indices and partitions contribute. The vertex formula applied linearly to this finite R identifies the coefficient of t^n as U_nR. Every manipulation is degree-by-degree: for fixed t^n the first kernel has A/B-degree n, and the shifted kernel has A/B-degree at most n; polynomial f,g or the fixed-degree components bound the remaining pairings. No scalar sum sigma[1] or analytic convergence is evaluated, and no unproved Littlewood identity or current-rank injectivity is assumed. To identify the classical Littlewood expression, expand sigma[AB]=sum_tau s_tau[A]s_tau[B], sigma[ZA]=sum_theta s_theta[Z]s_theta[A] and sigma[ZB]=sum_pi s_pi[Z]s_pi[B], and use the proved triple internal-product kernel on sigma[ZAB]. The Hall coefficients in A and B are <s_alpha,s_delta s_tau s_theta> and <s_beta,s_epsilon s_tau s_pi>. Reproducing in Z identifies their sums over theta and pi with (s_delta s_tau)^perp s_alpha and (s_epsilon s_tau)^perp s_beta, while the remaining Z-factor is s_delta*s_epsilon. This gives exactly the finite Littlewood sum printed in BOR (9), with its compatibility now proved rather than cited.
items.axiom_use: None: rational finite-degree power-sum/Hall algebra and formal coefficient extraction; no infinite choice.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Lemma 2.1 and Littlewood's identity (9), pp. 7-8 (the element R_{alpha,beta}, the operator U_n, and the Littlewood sum)
Emmanuel Briand, Amarpreeet Rattan and Mercedes Rosas, On the growth of the Kronecker coefficients, arXiv:1607.02887v1 (2016); section 2.4, identity (6), p. 7 (vertex operator series)

items.title: Murnaghan stability for Kronecker coefficients
items.statement: Fix partitions alpha, beta, gamma. Put m(gamma):=max{|alpha|+alpha_1, |beta|+beta_1, |gamma|+gamma_1} and, for n >= m(gamma), let g_n(alpha,beta,gamma):=g^{gamma[n]}_{alpha[n],beta[n]} be the multiplicity of the Specht module V_{gamma[n]} in V_{alpha[n]} (x) V_{beta[n]}; set g_n(alpha,beta,gamma):=0 for n<m(gamma). Then the sequence n |-> g_n(alpha,beta,gamma) is eventually constant. More precisely there is a finite set S(alpha,beta) of partitions and nonnegative integers bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} for gamma in S(alpha,beta), with bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}:=0 for gamma not in S(alpha,beta), such that g_n(alpha,beta,gamma)=bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} for all sufficiently large n and every partition gamma. No explicit bound on the stable rank is asserted here (the sharp global bound is a separate claim).
items.strategy: FI-module route of Church-Ellenberg-Farb. By CEF Proposition 3.4.1 the assignments V(alpha)_n:=V_{alpha[n]} for n>=|alpha|+alpha_1 and V(alpha)_n:=0 below define a finitely generated FI-module. By CEF Proposition 2.3.6 the tensor product V(alpha)(x)V(beta) is finitely generated and its value in rank n is V_{alpha[n]} (x) V_{beta[n]}. CEF Theorem 1.13 states that a finitely generated FI-module over a field of characteristic 0 is uniformly representation stable: there is a finite set of partitions nu and fixed multiplicities c_nu such that the rank-n value is the direct sum of c_nu copies of V(nu)_n for all n in a stable range. Restricting to the single irreducible family nu=gamma and reading off multiplicities gives the eventual constancy of n |-> g_n(alpha,beta,gamma); the finiteness of the support is the finiteness of the constituent list. All inputs are the in-run suppliers named in deps; the argument is choice-free. The corrected batch27 rational-model weight Definition, finite-orbit restriction proof and padded-family supplier retain the exact finite-dimensional complex Specht interfaces used here. Tensor rank n is the product of the two distinct families alpha and beta. The finite constituent support and uniform fixed multiplicities come from the finite-generation/stability equivalence, without using the later all-rank identity or sharp threshold.
items.axiom_use: None: the proof is finite-dimensional representation theory over a characteristic-zero field plus the choice-free FI-module finite-generation machinery of the cited suppliers.

references.title: Thomas Church, Jordan S. Ellenberg and Benson Farb, FI-modules and stability for representations of symmetric groups, arXiv:1204.4533v4 (2014); Proposition 3.4.1 pp. 23-24, Proposition 2.3.6 pp. 12-13, Theorem 1.13 pp. 6-7
Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Murnaghan's theorem, p. 4

items.title: The reduced (stable) Kronecker coefficient $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$
items.statement: For partitions alpha, beta, gamma define the reduced (stable) Kronecker coefficient bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} to be the eventual value of the padded sequence n |-> g_n(alpha,beta,gamma) furnished by the Murnaghan stability theorem; equivalently bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} := lim_{n to infinity} g^{gamma[n]}_{alpha[n],beta[n]}, where the sequence is defined for n>=max{|alpha|+alpha_1,|beta|+beta_1,|gamma|+gamma_1} and set to 0 below. Well-definedness is exactly the Murnaghan stability theorem. Two immediate conventions: bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}=bar-g^gamma_{beta,alpha} (commutativity of the tensor product), and for fixed alpha,beta only finitely many gamma have bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} nonzero. Values used later and verified in the source's introduction for alpha=beta=(2): bar-g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2 and bar-g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1.
items.strategy: Well-definedness is the preceding theorem: the eventual constant of an eventually constant sequence of nonnegative integers is a unique nonnegative integer, no choice is involved. The symmetry in alpha,beta is the commutativity of the tensor product of representations. The two displayed values are read from the source's introduction's product table and are not used as logical inputs.
items.axiom_use: None.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Introduction pp. 2 and 5 (definition of the reduced Kronecker coefficients) and the displayed product table p. 2

items.title: Brion's formula for the reduced Kronecker coefficients
items.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta,gamma: bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} = < s_alpha[X] s_beta[Y] | sigma[XY] s_gamma[XY+X+Y] >_{X,Y}, the inner product being the extension of the Hall inner product to symmetric functions in two alphabets X,Y. Equivalently, introducing a third alphabet Z, sum_{alpha,beta,gamma} bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} s_alpha[X]s_beta[Y]s_gamma[Z] = sigma[XYZ+XY+XZ+YZ], the symmetric Cauchy-type identity of the source.
items.strategy: Define R_{alpha,beta}[Z]=<s_alpha[A]s_beta[B] | sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]>_{A,B}, the finite polynomial of the padding/internal-product compatibility lemma. That lemma proves the complete all-n identity (U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)=U_n R without using reduced coefficients. Expand R=sum_gamma r_gamma s_gamma with finite support of degree at most |alpha|+|beta|. Choose n sufficiently large that alpha[n], beta[n] and every gamma[n] in both this finite support and the FI-stable finite support are partitions. Distinct gamma have distinct tails, hence distinct padded Schur labels. Comparing the compatibility identity with the FI-stable expansion identifies r_gamma with bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}; this uses injectivity only at sufficiently large n, not at every admissible n. To compute r_gamma, factor the kernel as sigma[AB] sigma[Z(AB+A+B)] and apply Cauchy in Z: the coefficient of s_gamma[Z] is sigma[AB]s_gamma[AB+A+B]. Pairing with s_alpha[A]s_beta[B] gives exactly the claimed Brion formula. Reproducing in the three alphabets yields the symmetric sigma[XYZ+XY+XZ+YZ] identity. No Littlewood identity, geometric result or unproved vertex compatibility is imported.
items.axiom_use: None: the proof uses the lambda-ring calculus, Cauchy's identity and formal power series in one variable over a characteristic-zero algebra.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Amarpreeet Rattan and Mercedes Rosas, On the growth of the Kronecker coefficients, arXiv:1607.02887v1 (2016); Proposition 3.2 and identity (10), pp. 9-10 (Brion's formula and the symmetric Cauchy-type identity)
Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Murnaghan's theorem p. 4 and Lemma 2.1 pp. 7-8

items.title: The nonnegative expansion of a reduced Kronecker coefficient
items.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta,gamma one has the finite nonnegative expansion bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} = sum_{mu,lambda,eta,rho,theta,pi} c^gamma_{mu,theta,pi} c^alpha_{rho,lambda,theta} c^beta_{rho,eta,pi} g^mu_{lambda,eta}, the sum over all six-tuples of partitions (only finitely many summands are nonzero), where the c's are threefold Schur coefficients and the g's are ordinary Kronecker coefficients. Consequences: (i) bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}>0 if and only if there exist partitions mu,lambda,eta,rho,theta,pi with c^gamma_{mu,theta,pi}, c^alpha_{rho,lambda,theta}, c^beta_{rho,eta,pi} and g^mu_{lambda,eta} all positive; (ii) for every nonzero summand the degree equations |alpha|=|rho|+|lambda|+|theta|, |beta|=|rho|+|eta|+|pi|, |gamma|=|mu|+|theta|+|pi| and |mu|=|lambda|=|eta| hold; (iii) for fixed alpha,beta the index set is finite because rho,lambda,theta are contained in alpha, rho,eta,pi in beta, and |mu|=|lambda|. All summands are nonnegative integers, so no cancellation occurs.
items.strategy: Expand Brion's formula in the two alphabets X,Y: sigma[XY] = sum_rho s_rho[X]s_rho[Y] by Cauchy, and s_gamma[XY+X+Y] = sum_{mu,nu} c^gamma_{mu,nu} s_mu[XY] s_nu[X+Y] by the coproduct identity, then s_mu[XY] = sum_{lambda,eta} g^mu_{lambda,eta} s_lambda[X]s_eta[Y] and s_nu[X+Y] = sum_{theta,pi} c^nu_{theta,pi}s_theta[X]s_pi[Y] by the coproduct and plethysm identities. The right-hand side becomes sum c^gamma_{mu,nu} c^nu_{theta,pi} g^mu_{lambda,eta} s_rho s_lambda s_theta[X] s_rho s_eta s_pi[Y]; the coefficient of s_alpha[X]s_beta[Y] is sum over rho,lambda,theta of c^alpha_{rho,lambda,theta} (respectively rho,eta,pi) times the rest. Using the iterated identity sum_nu c^gamma_{mu,nu}c^nu_{theta,pi}=c^gamma_{mu,theta,pi} gives the displayed formula. Consequences (i),(ii) are the positivity and degree bookkeeping of the individual summands (the supports of threefold coefficients and of g are governed by containment and total degree). This proves the source's Lemma 2.1 in the derived index pattern; the source's displayed equality (8) prints a third-factor index set that is a typographical variant of the same K_4 index pattern (the version proved here is the one used by the source's proof and by their if-and-only-if statement).
items.axiom_use: None: the expansion is an elementary computation in the lambda-ring with Cauchy's identity and the coproduct/plethysm identities; all coefficients are nonnegative integers.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Lemma 2.1 and equation (8), pp. 7-8 (nonnegative expansion of the reduced coefficients)
I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press 1995; Chapter I sections 3 and 5 (Littlewood-Richardson coefficients)

items.title: The Murnaghan expansion at every admissible rank
items.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta and every n >= max{|alpha|+alpha_1, |beta|+beta_1}: s_{alpha[n]} * s_{beta[n]} = sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} s_{gamma[n]}, an identity in the symmetric function ring, where s_{gamma[n]} is the Jacobi-Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence gamma[n] (zero or +-1 times a Schur function). For an ordinary partition delta of n, the coefficient is g^{delta}_{alpha[n],beta[n]}=sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}<s_{gamma[n]},s_delta>, where each Hall factor is zero or a sign from Jacobi-Trudi straightening. At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce; individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range displayed is precisely the set of n for which alpha[n] and beta[n] are partitions.
items.strategy: The local padding/internal-product compatibility lemma proves (U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)=U_n R_{alpha,beta} coefficient by coefficient for every n>=0, with R finite. Brion identifies R=sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}s_gamma by comparison only at sufficiently large n where every finite-support gamma[n] is an ordinary partition and labels are distinct. Apply the same linear U_n at the present n, without requiring injectivity: its definition gives U_n R=sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}s_{gamma[n]}. In the admissible range the left inputs are ordinary Schur functions, so this is the promised full all-rank identity. Pair with each ordinary s_delta for the exact signed coefficient formula. For example alpha=beta=gamma=(2), n=4 gives ordinary coefficient 1 although the reduced coefficient is 2; straightening s_(1,3)=-s_(2,2) supplies the missing cancellation in the complete expansion. No coefficientwise stability is asserted before the actual stable range.
items.axiom_use: None: finite Hall coefficient extraction, proved vertex/Hall compatibility and linear Jacobi-Trudi completion suffice.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Murnaghan Theorem (2) p. 4, Example 1 p. 4 and Lemma 2.1 pp. 7-8
Emmanuel Briand, Amarpreeet Rattan and Mercedes Rosas, On the growth of the Kronecker coefficients, arXiv:1607.02887v1 (2016); section 2.3 pp. 5-6

items.title: Murnaghan–Littlewood: top-degree reduced coefficients are Littlewood–Richardson coefficients
items.statement: Let alpha,beta,gamma be partitions with |gamma|=|alpha|+|beta|. Then bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}=c^gamma_{alpha,beta}, the Littlewood-Richardson coefficient. In particular bar-g^{alpha+beta}_{alpha,beta}=c^{alpha+beta}_{alpha,beta}=1.
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative expansion of the preceding lemma. For every nonzero summand the degree equations give |alpha|+|beta|-|gamma| = (|rho|+|lambda|+|theta|)+(|rho|+|eta|+|pi|)-(|mu|+|theta|+|pi|) = 2|rho|+|lambda|+|eta|-|mu| = 2|rho|+|mu|, using |lambda|=|eta|=|mu|. If |gamma|=|alpha|+|beta| then 2|rho|+|mu|=0, so rho=mu=empty; then |lambda|=|eta|=0, so lambda=eta=empty; hence c^alpha_{rho,lambda,theta}=c^alpha_{empty,empty,theta}=delta_{alpha,theta} and c^beta_{empty,empty,pi}=delta_{beta,pi}, and the six-fold sum collapses to the single summand g^empty_{empty,empty} c^gamma_{alpha,beta} = c^gamma_{alpha,beta}. For gamma=alpha+beta the LR coefficient equals 1: the Pieri/LR rule gives the unique Littlewood-Richardson tableau of shape (alpha+beta)/alpha whose row i is filled with i's. The row-i filling is lattice because beta is weakly decreasing. Any LR tableau has only 1s in its first skew row, which has beta_1 boxes and exhausts that content; inductively each successive row exhausts the next content, so the filling is unique. Empty rows/partitions use zero content and the unique empty tableau.
items.axiom_use: None.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Murnaghan–Littlewood Theorem, p. 4
I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press 1995; Chapter I §5 (Littlewood-Richardson rule)

items.title: The support of the reduced Kronecker coefficients satisfies the size triangle inequalities
items.statement: If bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}>0 then |alpha| <= |beta|+|gamma|, |beta| <= |alpha|+|gamma| and |gamma| <= |alpha|+|beta| (Murnaghan's inequalities). Hence the support Supp(alpha,beta) of the nonzero reduced coefficients with fixed alpha,beta lies in the triangle region of the weight lattice.
items.strategy: Take a nonzero summand of the nonnegative expansion and use its degree equations |alpha|=|rho|+|lambda|+|theta|, |beta|=|rho|+|eta|+|pi|, |gamma|=|mu|+|theta|+|pi| with |lambda|=|eta|=|mu|. Subtracting pairwise: |alpha|+|beta|-|gamma| = 2|rho|+|mu| >= 0; |alpha|+|gamma|-|beta| = |lambda|+2|theta|+|mu|-|eta| = 2|theta|+|mu| >= 0; |beta|+|gamma|-|alpha| = 2|pi|+|mu| >= 0. Each difference is a sum of nonnegative integers, giving the three inequalities for that summand, hence for their positive sum.
items.axiom_use: None.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Murnaghan's inequalities, p. 4

items.title: The exact global stabilization threshold for a fixed Kronecker product
items.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta, with missing parts zero: stab(alpha,beta)=N:=|alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1. At every n>=N all support labels gamma[n] are ordinary partitions, and the full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}s_{gamma[n]}; the family is V-stable from N onward. If both alpha and beta are nonempty, N-1 is admissible and the product at N is not V of the product at N-1: the coefficient of s_{(alpha+beta)[N]} is 1, its first two parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of V. If exactly one input is empty, N is already the least ordinary input rank; the same image obstruction at N excludes any earlier stabilization index in the Jacobi-Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty, N=0, s_(n)*s_(n)=s_(n) (including s_(0)=1) and V^n(1)=s_(n), so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.
items.strategy: Source route: Briand-Orellana-Rosas Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, pp. 8-9. (i) Support maximum: every nonzero summand of the nonnegative expansion satisfies |gamma|+gamma_1 <= |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1 - the chain is |gamma|+gamma_1 <= |mu|+mu_1+|theta|+theta_1+|pi|+pi_1 <= 2|mu|+|theta|+theta_1+|pi|+pi_1 = |lambda|+|theta|+theta_1+|eta|+|pi|+pi_1 <= |alpha|+alpha_1+|beta|+beta_1, using the threefold containment theta subset alpha, pi subset beta, the row bound gamma_1 <= mu_1+theta_1+pi_1 from the LR rule, mu_1 <= |mu|, |mu|=|lambda|=|eta| and |lambda|+|theta| <= |alpha|, |eta|+|pi| <= |beta|; combined with the top-degree lemma, which shows that gamma=alpha+beta attains the value |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1, this identifies max{|gamma|+gamma_1 : bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}>0} = |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1. (ii) Put N equal to the support maximum established in (i). For n>=N all gamma[n] in the finite positive support are partitions, so the proved all-rank identity is now an ordinary nonnegative Schur expansion; U_{n+k}s_gamma=V^k(U_n s_gamma) there. Thus the whole product is V-stable from N. When N>0, gamma*=alpha+beta is nonempty, its reduced coefficient is 1 by the top-degree lemma and the unique LR tableau, and gamma*[N] has equal positive first two parts. Distinct support tails give distinct Schur labels, so this coefficient does not cancel. Every V(s_mu)=s_{mu+(1)} has first part strictly larger than the second, hence the product at N is not in the image of V. Any putative stabilization index n_0<N would make the product at N equal V^{N-n_0} of its rank-n_0 Jacobi-Trudi-completed product, a contradiction. For both inputs nonempty, N-1 is an ordinary admissible rank; for exactly one empty, N is the minimum ordinary input rank, and no ordinary product below that domain is invoked. If N=0 both inputs are empty: the degreewise internal-product unit h_n=s_(n) gives h_n*h_n=h_n and V^n(1)=h_n, proving threshold zero directly. The two-factor LR first-row inequality used in (i) is explicit: every entry of a nonempty first skew row is 1, since the LR reading word begins at its rightmost (largest) entry and must be lattice; hence the added first-row boxes number at most the 1-content beta_1. Thus lambda_1<=alpha_1+beta_1 for positive c^lambda_{alpha,beta}. Iterating the positive intermediate LR coefficients gives the threefold row inequality. At gamma*=alpha+beta the row-i filling by i is lattice because beta is weakly decreasing; the first row exhausts all beta_1 ones, then the next row exhausts all beta_2 twos, and induction proves uniqueness and coefficient 1.
items.axiom_use: None: the proved finite all-rank expansion, LR row bounds/unique top tableau and the Schur-basis image of V suffice; empty cases are explicit.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 1.2, pp. 4, 8-9
Emmanuel Briand, Amarpreeet Rattan and Mercedes Rosas, On the growth of the Kronecker coefficients, arXiv:1607.02887v1 (2016); Lemma 3.1 and the proof of Proposition 3.2, pp. 9-10

title: Murnaghan Stability via FI-Modules — Examples

items.title: Murnaghan stability for $\alpha=\beta=(2)$, ranks 4 to 9
items.statement: For alpha=beta=(2) the source's introduction displays s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}=s_4+s_{1,1,1,1}+s_{2,2}; s_{3,2}*s_{3,2}=s_5+s_{2,1,1,1}+s_{3,2}+s_{4,1}+s_{3,1,1}+s_{2,2,1}; s_{4,2}*s_{4,2}=s_6+s_{3,1,1,1}+2s_{4,2}+s_{5,1}+s_{4,1,1}+2s_{3,2,1}+s_{2,2,2}; s_{5,2}*s_{5,2}=s_7+s_{4,1,1,1}+2s_{5,2}+s_{6,1}+s_{5,1,1}+2s_{4,2,1}+s_{3,2,2}+s_{4,3}+s_{3,3,1}; s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}=s_8+s_{5,1,1,1}+2s_{6,2}+s_{7,1}+s_{6,1,1}+2s_{5,2,1}+s_{4,2,2}+s_{5,3}+s_{4,3,1}+s_{4,4}; s_{7,2}*s_{7,2}=s_9+s_{6,1,1,1}+2s_{7,2}+s_{8,1}+s_{7,1,1}+2s_{6,2,1}+s_{5,2,2}+s_{6,3}+s_{5,3,1}+s_{5,4}; and the stable row s_{bullet,2}*s_{bullet,2}=s_bullet+s_{bullet,1,1,1}+2s_{bullet,2}+s_{bullet,1}+s_{bullet,1,1}+2s_{bullet,2,1}+s_{bullet,2,2}+s_{bullet,3}+s_{bullet,3,1}+s_{bullet,4}. Consequently the reduced coefficients for the pair ((2),(2)) are bar-g^gamma_{(2),(2)} = 1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1,1 for gamma = empty, (1,1,1), (2), (1), (1,1), (2,1), (2,2), (3), (3,1), (4) respectively, and bar-g^gamma=0 for all other gamma; in particular bar-g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2 and bar-g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1. The displayed data also verify directly, for this pair, that the whole product is V-stable at rank 8 and not at rank 7: applying V (adding a box to the first row of every Schur function) to the rank-8 expansion s_{6,2}*s_{6,2} reproduces the rank-9 expansion s_{7,2}*s_{7,2} term by term, whereas applying V to the rank-7 expansion s_{5,2}*s_{5,2} misses the single term s_{4,4} of s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}, the other nine terms matching term by term (the rank-7 product does contain s_{4,3} and s_{3,3,1}, whose V-images s_{5,3} and s_{4,3,1} are present at rank 8). The proved threshold theorem establishes V-stability for every rank from 8 onward, with exact least global index 8=|(2)|+|(2)|+2+2; the displayed finite data independently verify the six listed products and the failure of the preceding step.
items.strategy: For every n=4,...,9 compute the actual characters and every Schur coefficient, not merely dimensions. Youngs rule gives M^(n-2,2)=S^(n)+S^(n-1,1)+S^(n-2,2), while the point-permutation module is S^(n)+S^(n-1,1). Hence chi^(n-2,2)=binom(X_1,2)+X_2-X_1, by counting fixed two-element subsets and fixed points. For every partition delta of n, expand s_delta by Jacobi-Trudi and each h_k in power sums; the Frobenius dictionary gives chi^delta(rho)=z_rho[p_rho]s_delta. The tensor multiplicity is sum_{rho partition n}(chi^(n-2,2)(rho))^2 chi^delta(rho)/z_rho, a finite rational sum. Evaluating these finitely many sums gives exactly each displayed product (and zero for unlisted delta). Evaluating these character identities at the identity permutation provides a supplementary dimension check, not the proof of the products. At rank 8 the coefficient of s_(4,4) is 1 and cannot be in the V-image; the other nine shifted rank-7 terms agree with rank 8. General V-stability from 8 and its exact minimality follow from the now-proved threshold theorem, and comparing rank 8 with rank 9 checks the first stable step. The stable reduced list follows from that theorem and the rank-8 decomposition.
items.axiom_use: None.

references.title: Emmanuel Briand, Rosa Orellana and Mercedes Rosas, The stability of the Kronecker product of Schur functions, arXiv:0907.4652v2 (2009); Introduction p. 2 (the displayed product table for alpha=beta=(2) at ranks 4 to 9 and the stable row)
I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press 1995; Chapter I §7 (Frobenius characteristic and character values)

items.title: A global product threshold is not a per-coefficient sharpness claim
items.statement: For alpha=beta=(2) the individual coefficient bar-g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2 is already attained at rank 6: the rank-6 product s_{4,2}*s_{4,2} contains 2s_{4,2}, i.e. g^{(4,2)}_{(4,2),(4,2)}=2, which is the stable value bar-g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2 read off from the stable row. Thus this single coefficient stops growing strictly before the whole product stabilizes: the rank-7 and rank-8 products still contain 2s_{5,2} and 2s_{6,2} respectively, matching the stable value, while the whole product is not even V-stable at rank 7 (applying V to s_{5,2}*s_{5,2} misses the term s_{4,4} occurring in s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}) and only becomes V-stable at rank 8. Therefore the exact global product threshold (the least rank from which the whole product is V-stable) is not a per-coefficient sharpness statement: single coefficients may stabilize earlier, and no claim that a coefficient first becomes stable at the global threshold is valid.
items.strategy: Verification from the source's displayed products: read the coefficient of s_{4,2} in s_{4,2}*s_{4,2} (equal to 2), the coefficients of s_{5,2} and s_{6,2} in the ranks 7 and 8 products (2 in both cases), and the stable coefficient 2s_{bullet,2} in the stable row; compare the ranks 6,7,8 products under the operator V (V of the rank-7 product equals the rank-8 product minus the single term s_{4,4}). This shows the stabilization rank of the single coefficient (2) is at most 6, strictly below the global V-stability rank 8. The counterexample does not use the general threshold theorem; it is a finite boundary witness warning against quantifying the global threshold as a sharp per-coefficient bound. To justify constancy for every later rank, use the proved threshold through the example: all ranks n>=8 have the stable coefficient 2, and the explicit ranks 6 and7 already have that value. The rank 5 value is1 by the verified product table. Thus this coefficient has stabilization rank 6, strictly below the whole-product threshold 8; it is not inferred solely from matching adjacent products.
items.axiom_use: None.

title: Relative Smooth Triangulation And Bundle Fitting

items.title: Relative smooth triangulations, strong approximation and bundle fitting
items.statement: A finite geometric simplicial complex $K$ is considered with its Euclidean realization and induced metric; subcomplex, closure, star and link terminology follows [[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]. For $b\in|K|$ the **tangent star** is the union of the tangent cones at $b$ of all simplices containing $b$, that is, the rays locally contained in the closed star. A map $f:|K|\to M$ is **piecewise smooth** when every restriction $f|\sigma$ to a closed simplex extends smoothly to a neighbourhood in its affine hull and the extensions agree on common faces; in a target coordinate chart the differential $df_b$ is then the well-defined continuous piecewise linear map on the tangent star that equals $D(f|\sigma)(b)$ on the cone of each simplex $\sigma$ containing $b$. A **smooth immersion of a complex** requires $df_b$ injective on the entire tangent star at every point, not merely on each simplex tangent space; a **smooth embedding** requires in addition that $f$ be a homeomorphism onto its image, and a **finite smooth triangulation** of $M$ is such an embedding onto $M$. A corner-adapted triangulation must be face compatible: every local corner face is the image of a subcomplex, and the differential fan maps the source tangent star homeomorphically onto the appropriate tangent orthant, or its specified face sector. After an ambient Euclidean realization of the target, or in a fixed finite family of compact target chart patches, $g:K'\to M$ on a finite subdivision $K'$ of $K$ is a **strong $C^1$ $\delta$-approximation** to $f$ if $\sup_b|g(b)-f(b)|<\delta$ and $|dg_b(v)-df_b(v)|<\delta|v|$ for all $b$ and all tangent-star vectors $v$. A relative approximation **fixed on $L$** means $g|_{|L|}=f|_{|L|}$, subdivision of $L$ permitted unless explicitly prohibited. **Shape control** means a positive lower bound on $r(\sigma)/\operatorname{diam}\sigma$ for every positive-dimensional simplex, where $r(\sigma)$ is the distance from the barycentre to the relative boundary; it is not asserted for arbitrary iterated barycentric subdivisions. Two embeddings $f_i:K_i\to M$ **fit in a subcomplex** if the inverse images of $f_1(|K_1|)\cap f_2(|K_2|)$ are subcomplexes $L_i$ and $f_2^{-1}f_1:L_1\to L_2$ is a simplexwise affine isomorphism; the fit is **full** if every simplex all of whose vertices belong to $L_i$ belongs to $L_i$. Gluing along that isomorphism defines the union realization and union map. For a smooth bundle $\pi:E\to B$ and a supplied base triangulation $h:D\to B$, a **projection-preserving diagram** consists of $F:K\to E$ and a map $r:K\to D$ that is affine on each simplex into a simplex of the original $D$ and satisfies $\pi F=hr$; the affine/PL requirement does not require domain vertices to map to vertices of the original fixed base complex. Fitting preserves the projection when all modified maps satisfy the same equality with the original $h$ and the original affine $r$ restricted to their subdivisions; a fixed relative bundle piece must already carry such a diagram. No generic smooth map is called a bundle merely because it is proper. For relative extension on a compact manifold with corners, supplied boundary data are admissible only when they are compatible on all corner-face intersections and satisfy the tangent-orthant condition above; the extension keeps their pointwise parametrization, with compatible subdivisions permitted, and no extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.
items.strategy: This is a definition; the mathematical content is the contract itself, and no existence assertion is made here. Consistency facts that the later proofs use and that are fixed by the wording: agreement on common faces makes $df_b$ independent of the chosen containing simplex and continuous on the tangent star; gluing along a simplexwise affine isomorphism on a full subcomplex produces a well-defined finite complex and a well-defined union map; a projection-preserving diagram is determined by the pair $(F,r)$ together with its restrictions to subdivisions, so a modification supported away from a piece leaves the original diagram there exactly on the nose. The tangent-star formulation is deliberate: simplexwise injectivity of the differential is insufficient for an immersion, while injectivity on the whole tangent star is the condition stable under strong approximation (see the stability lemma below). No choice is used, and no mesh or shape bound is imposed on subdivisions unless a statement says so. The conventions for ``linear'' maps of complexes and for fitting in a (full) subcomplex are those of the cited sources, with domain vertices not required to map to vertices of a fixed base complex.
items.axiom_use: None: a definitional contract, using only the Euclidean realization and the induced metric.

items.title: Whole-star smooth embeddings are stable under strong piecewise $C^1$ approximation
items.statement: Let $K$ be finite and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ a whole-star smooth immersion in the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]]. There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong piecewise $C^1$ $\delta$-approximation $g:K'\to\mathbb R^q$, on any finite subdivision $K'$, is a whole-star immersion. If $f$ is also an embedding, $\delta$ may be chosen so that $g$ is an embedding. The subdivision need not have a mesh or shape bound.
items.strategy:
Whole-star injectivity includes the affine tangent space of every simplex containing a point, so each simplex differential has full rank; on the unit sphere of each such tangent space $|D(f|\sigma)(b)v|$ has a positive minimum over the closed simplex, and the finite minimum over positive-dimensional simplices gives $\mu>0$ ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). Derivative norms changing by less than $\mu/2$ preserve ranks, and $|W-V|<\delta$ with $|V|\ge\mu$ forces the angle between $V$ and $W$ to be small, since $|W/|W|-V/|V||\le 2\delta/(\mu-\delta)$; thus strong derivative approximation gives arbitrarily small uniform angle approximation, independently of the subdivision.

For a proper common face $\tau=\sigma_1\cap\sigma_2$, project $p=(1-t)x+ty\in\sigma_1\setminus\tau$ (with $x\in\tau$, $y$ in the opposite face, $t\in(0,1]$) to $x_p=p+t(c-y)$, where $c$ is the barycentre of $\tau$; set $x_p=c$ for $t=1$. This projection is continuous, fixes $\tau$ and gives $p-x_p=t(y-c)$. Applied to the images under the linear embedding $df_b$ of the two simplices, the angle between $p-x_p$ and $z-x_p$ for $z\in\sigma_2$, $z\ne x_p$, is bounded below by the angle from $\sigma_1$ to $\sigma_2$: translate the ray $x_pz$ to start at $c$, extend it to the boundary of the truncated cone $\sigma_2-c$, and note that the endpoint ranges over a compact set on which its angle with $y-c$ has a positive minimum (equal ray directions would put a ray in both simplices outside their common face). Continuous dependence on $b$ makes the minimum over $b\in\tau$ positive; the finite minimum $\alpha>0$ over ordered pairs of simplices is therefore positive (take $\alpha=\pi/2$ when there are no such pairs).

Fix $b\in|K|$. Continuity of the finitely many simplex derivatives makes $f$ an angle approximation to the frozen piecewise linear map $df_b$ with tolerance $\alpha/8$ near $b$, and a sufficiently small $\delta$ makes $g$ an angle approximation to $f$, hence to that frozen map, with tolerance $\alpha/4$ on a common neighbourhood $U_b$. Shrink to a neighbourhood $V_b$ such that for $p,q\in V_b$ the two-segment path $pxq$ (midpoint when $p,q$ lie in one original simplex, the projection above otherwise) stays in $U_b$. Integrate each subdivided segment with [[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]: the endpoint difference lies in the closed cone of vectors making angle at most $\alpha/4$ with its frozen image direction, whereas the two frozen rays from $x$ make angle at least $\alpha$ (or $\pi$ in the midpoint case), so the perturbed endpoint differences keep the sign of their frozen projections under the projection onto the line perpendicular to the bisector of the two frozen directions (the frozen image line in the antiparallel midpoint case), which separates the two open segments strictly. Hence $g(p)\ne g(q)$ for distinct $p,q\in V_b$, for every subdivision.

The same two-segment argument applied to the piecewise linear map $dg_b$, whose derivatives on each refined cone differ from $df_b$ by at most $\delta$, shows that $dg_b$ is injective on the tangent star: distinct cone vectors can be scaled simultaneously into the region where the projected paths are defined, and the positive rank bounds cover two vectors in one cone. Finitely many $V_b$ cover $|K|$, so all tolerances and the resulting $\delta$ can be chosen simultaneously, proving stability of immersion. If $f$ is an embedding, keep the cover and let $\eta>0$ be the minimum of $|f(p)-f(q)|$ over the compact set of pairs lying in no common $V_b$ (omit the constraint when that set is empty); with $\delta<\eta/3$ we get $|g(p)-g(q)|\ge\eta-2\delta>0$ on that set, while the $V_b$ separate all other distinct pairs. Then $g$ is continuous and injective on a compact space, hence a homeomorphism onto its image in the Hausdorff target, and together with the immersion statement it is an embedding. No mesh or shape bound on $K'$ is used.
items.axiom_use: None: finite minima over compact sets and segment integration.

items.title: Shape-controlled secants and relative piecewise smooth extension
items.statement:
Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]]. There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise $C^1$ to $f$.

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original simplices is preserved.

There is also a local extension statement: given a finite subcomplex $A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the subdivision of $A$. If the correction $g-f$ has zero component under an affine linear target map $p$ on $A$, then the extended correction has zero $p$ component everywhere. This last extension does not assert a shape bound on its coned simplices.
items.strategy:
Thickness construction. Realize the abstract complex as a union of faces of one standard simplex $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^N$ with vertices $0,e_1,\dots,e_N$; the original geometric realization differs by linear isomorphisms on finitely many simplices with uniformly bounded operator norms and inverse norms. In $\mathbb R^N$ cut the unit lattice cubes by the hyperplanes $\sum_i x_i=j$ and all their faces; the resulting locally finite convex cell complex has only finitely many cell shapes up to translation, so triangulating each cell compatibly ([[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]]) with a translation-invariant choice of interior point (for example the average of the vertices) gives finitely many simplex shapes, with maximal diameter $D$ and positive minimum thickness $\theta_0$ in positive dimensions. The simplex $m\Delta$, defined by $x_i\ge0$, $\sum_i x_i\le m$, and each of its faces are unions of these cells, so scaling by $1/m$ gives subdivisions of $\Delta$, and hence of $K$, with mesh at most $D/m$ and thickness at least $\theta_0$; restrictions to all faces agree because one global cell complex is used. Transport back to the original realization; the finitely many original simplices multiply diameter and inradius by factors bounded above and below, leaving one positive $\theta$. This is the lattice construction of Munkres 9.4; iterated barycentric subdivision does not have this property (9.4(a)).

Secant estimate. Let $s$ be a refined simplex inside an original simplex $\sigma$, with barycentre $b$, diameter $h$ and radius $r\ge\theta h$; put $T_b(x)=f(b)+Df(b)(x-b)$. On the compact $\sigma$ the derivative has a modulus of continuity $\omega_\sigma(h)\to0$, so segment integration ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]) gives $|f(x)-T_b(x)|\le h\omega_\sigma(h)$ for $x\in s$. The affine difference $S_m-T_b$ interpolates the vertex errors, so its sup norm is at most $h\omega_\sigma(h)$; for an affine map $A$ on $s$ with $\sup_s|A|\le E$, a unit vector $v$ in the affine span satisfies $|DA(v)|=|A(b+rv)-A(b)|/r\le2E/r$, whence $\|DS_m-Df(b)\|\le2\omega_\sigma(h)/\theta$ and, by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) and derivative continuity, $\|DS_m-Df(x)\|\le(2/\theta+1)\omega_\sigma(h)$. Taking the maximum of the finitely many moduli over original simplices proves strong $C^1$ convergence, including vectors in every refined tangent cone.

Relative version. Subdivide barycentrically once if necessary so that $L$ is full ([[def-barycentric-subdivision-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]]: the vertices are face chains, and a chain all of whose barycentric vertices lie in $L$ lies in $L$). Then the sum $d$ of the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside $L$ is a global continuous piecewise affine nonnegative function with zero set exactly $|L|$, whose minimum on the compact complement of $U$ is positive. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\chi(d)$ that is $0$ near $d=0$ and $1$ on that complement; its piecewise derivative is bounded by a fixed constant. Set $g_m=f+\chi(d)(S_m-f)$: this fixes $f$ near $L$, is a secant map outside $U$, and its derivative error is bounded by that of $S_m$ plus the fixed cutoff-derivative constant times the value error, which tends to zero. Affine target planes are preserved, since both vertex interpolation and affine combinations of points in a plane stay in that plane.

Local extension. Extend a subdivision of $A$ combinatorially in increasing dimension: keep every original simplex outside its closed star, and for each affected simplex whose boundary has already been subdivided, cone that boundary subdivision from the original barycentre. These cones are simplices and agree on faces by the ray description of a simplex. For an original simplex $\sigma$ with barycentre $c$, write each $x\ne c$ uniquely as $x=c+t(y-c)$ with $0<t\le1$ and $y\in\partial\sigma$, choose a smooth scalar taper $a$ that is $0$ for $t\le1/3$ and $1$ for $t\ge2/3$, and define $G(x)=f(x)+a(t)e(y)$, $G(c)=f(c)$, where $e=g-f$; on each coned simplex this extends smoothly across $c$ (it equals $f$ near $c$) and takes the given boundary values. On $t\ge1/3$, $t$ is affine in $x$ divided by the fixed barycentre-to-face height and $y=c+(x-c)/t$, so $|Dt|$ and $\|Dy\|$ are bounded by constants depending only on the original simplex, not on the subdivision of $A$; therefore the value and derivative norms of the correction are bounded by $C_\sigma\|e\|_{C^1}$. Applying the construction to the finitely many affected simplices in increasing dimension, the product of these finite bounds converts any requested final error into a sufficient bound on the initial error, uniformly over all subdivisions of $A$. If $p$ is affine linear with $p(e)=0$ then $p(a(t)e(y))=0$, so a zero $p$ component is preserved; and $G=f$ outside the closed star of $A$ by construction. No shape bound is claimed for the coned simplices.

items.title: Corner-adapted strong approximations preserve orthant sides
items.statement:
Let $F:K\to[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$ be a finite whole-star smooth embedding, and write $\rho_iF$ for its first $c$ coordinate functions. Assume for each original simplex $\sigma$ and each $i$ that $Z_{i,\sigma}=\{x\in\sigma:\rho_iF(x)=0\}$ is a union of faces and that, at every $b\in Z_{i,\sigma}$, the linear form $d(\rho_iF)_b$ on the tangent cone of $\sigma$ is nonnegative with zero set precisely the tangent cone of $Z_{i,\sigma}$. These are the adapted face/tangent conditions, not merely simplex rank conditions.

There is $\delta>0$ such that every strong $\delta$-approximation $G$ preserving each of these coordinate planes on the specified zero subcomplexes maps all of $K$ into the same closed orthant and has exactly the same coordinate zero sets. It is an embedding for this choice of $\delta$. Thus plane-preserving fitting and extension can be used in corner charts when the initial pieces satisfy these adapted face conditions.
items.strategy:
Fix $i$ and an original simplex $\sigma$. On the zero set $Z_{i,\sigma}$ the form $d(\rho_iF)_b$ is nonnegative on the tangent cone of $\sigma$ and vanishes exactly on the tangent cone of $Z_{i,\sigma}$; the zero set of a nonnegative linear functional on a convex cone is a face of the cone, so locally at a point of a face of $Z_{i,\sigma}$ the zero cone is a single face and the form is strictly positive on every other generating direction. The finitely many normalized generating directions give a positive minimum there, and the finitely many zero faces give finitely many neighbourhoods with a uniform positive lower bound; away from these neighbourhoods the continuous positive ratio $\rho_iF/\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,Z_{i,\sigma})$ has a positive minimum by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]].

Consequently there is $a>0$ with $\rho_iF(x)\ge a\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{i,\sigma})$ on $\sigma$ whenever the zero set is nonempty. Near a zero face, project barycentric coordinates to that face by deleting the coordinates outside it and renormalizing those inside; on a neighbourhood where the sum of the retained coordinates is at least $1/2$ the segment to the projection has length at most a fixed constant times the distance to the face, and its outward displacement is a nonnegative combination of the nonzero generating directions whose supporting-form value is bounded below by the previous paragraph; integrating along the segment, after shrinking so the derivative varies by less than half that bound, gives the displayed lower bound. Finitely many faces give one constant $a$.

Let $G$ be a strong $\delta$-approximation that preserves the coordinate planes on the specified zero subcomplexes. For $x\in\sigma$ choose a closest point $z\in Z_{i,\sigma}$ (compactness); since $\rho_iG(z)=\rho_iF(z)=0$, segment integration of the piecewise smooth difference gives $|\rho_iG(x)-\rho_iF(x)|\le\delta|x-z|=\delta\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{i,\sigma})$ ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] applied and added over the finitely many refined pieces). With $\delta<a/2$ it follows that $\rho_iG(x)\ge(a/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{i,\sigma})$, so $\rho_iG$ is positive off the zero set and the zero sets of all coordinates are exactly the prescribed ones. If $Z_{i,\sigma}$ is empty, $\rho_iF$ has a positive compact minimum and a value error less than half of it keeps $\rho_iG$ positive everywhere on $\sigma$. Taking the minimum of these finitely many positive bounds and imposing the embedding bound of [[lem-piecewise-smooth-embeddings-are-stable-under-fine-c-one-approximation]] gives one $\delta$ with all the asserted properties. The adapted face/tangent hypotheses are essential: by Munkres 9.8(e), affine-plane preservation alone does not preserve a half-space, so the distance-uniform lower bound is exactly the missing side control.
items.axiom_use: None: compactness minima, a supporting-functional face argument and segment integration.

items.title: Finite smooth fitting with exact bundle projection and protected regions
items.statement:
Let $F:K\to M$ and $G:L\to M$ be whole-star smooth embeddings of finite complexes into a smooth manifold without boundary. Given any positive strong $C^1$ tolerance, there are approximations on finite subdivisions fitting in a full subcomplex whose union is a whole-star smooth embedding.

The same conclusion holds for bundle diagrams $\pi F=hr_K$, $\pi G=hr_L$ over a fixed whole-star smooth base embedding $h:D\to B$, when all relevant images are in a smooth bundle with product trivializations. The final approximations satisfy these same diagrams with $h$ and $r_K,r_L$ unchanged as point maps, so the bundle projection is preserved exactly. The union map has the induced affine map to $D$.

The construction may be supported in a prescribed open neighbourhood $V$ of the new piece being fitted, including only the old pieces whose images meet that neighbourhood. In particular it fixes a closed protected region $R$ pointwise whenever all newly processed pieces and their required closed stars have images in $V$, with $\overline V\cap R=\varnothing$, and the maps already fit on the pieces outside this support. This is the fixed-collar relative interface: it does not assert arbitrary pointwise fixed-side fitting without the neighbourhood/separation hypotheses. Additional local affine plane constraints are preserved if the chosen charts make them coordinate planes and the already supplied diagrams respect them. For corner targets the same construction applies when all pieces satisfy the adapted face/tangent hypotheses of [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] in these charts; that lemma proves every altered piece remains in its original orthant.
items.strategy:
Elementary compactness and chart margins. A finite geometric realization is compact: use [[prop-a-finite-simplicial-complex-has-compact-hausdorff-realization]] on the abstract vertex/face complex and its continuous simplexwise affine realization into the given Euclidean space (on finitely many closed simplex pieces, inverse images of closed sets are finite unions of their closed traces). Continuous images of compact sets are compact, because an open cover pulls back to a cover with a finite subcover; a closed subset of a compact set is compact, by adjoining its open complement to a cover. In a local Euclidean chart a compact set is closed: for an outside point separate it from each compact-set point by disjoint balls, cover the compact set by finitely many such balls, and intersect the corresponding outside-point neighbourhoods. For a nonempty compact set A disjoint from a nonempty closed set C, a positive gap follows directly from compactness: the admissible pairs (a,r) with B(a,3r) disjoint from C give a cover of A by B(a,r), choose a finite subcover B(a_j,r_j), and then for x in A and y in C the triangle inequality gives d(x,y)>2r_j for a covering j. The finite minimum of r_j is positive. Empty complements impose no gap constraint. All operations take place on compact source realizations or compact coordinate patches; no unspecified global target metric is needed. For a compact metric source and an open chart cover, [[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]] gives a positive margin; its direct finite-ball proof chooses a finite cover by B(a_j,r_j) with B(a_j,3r_j) lying in chart-cover members. If a set S has diameter less than min r_j, one point in B(a_j,r_j) forces S into B(a_j,2r_j), hence the same member. No infinite choice is used. A closed star of a vertex has diameter at most twice the mesh; a fixed k successive simplex-adjacency neighbourhood has diameter at most 2(k+1) times the mesh, by a path through at most k+1 incident simplices. Hence sufficiently fine subdivision puts all finitely many required support stars inside their assigned source chart preimages and preserves the protected-region separation. This proves the separation/margin facts used below, rather than leaving them as unnamed metric primitives.

Euclidean fitting step. Two finite linear embedded complexes in $\mathbb R^q$ can be placed in one finite convex cell complex even when their underlying sets differ: cut a bounding box by all affine hyperplanes defining the affine hulls and barycentric facet inequalities of the finitely many simplices of both complexes. Each resulting cell is determined by choosing one weak side of each hyperplane; intersection activates further equalities and is a common face; each original simplex is a union of cells because its equalities and weak inequalities are among the cuts; and relative cell interiors are either contained in the simplex or disjoint from it; closed cells outside the simplex can still meet its boundary along common faces. Triangulate this complex compatibly ([[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]]) and restrict to the two original polyhedra; their intersection is now a subcomplex, and one barycentric subdivision makes it full (if a face chain has all barycentric vertices in the intersection, its largest face lies there, hence the whole simplex does). Pulling these subdivisions back through the linear embeddings gives fitting in a full subcomplex by arbitrary-overlap refinement; no same-polyhedron common-refinement theorem is used beyond its scope.

Local fitting of an attached piece. Work in $\mathbb R^q$ with a finite complex $P=Q\cup A$ and a piecewise smooth map $T$ such that $T|_Q$ and $T|_A$ are embeddings, $A$ being the new piece. Let $P_0$ contain the closed stars of all simplices meeting $T^{-1}(T(A))$ and let $P_1$ be its closed star; then $T^{-1}(T(A))$ lies in the relative interior of $|P_0|$, so the compact image of the complement of that interior has positive distance from $T(A)$. If this complement is empty omit the distance constraint; otherwise choose the approximation tolerance below a quarter of that positive distance and small enough for [[lem-piecewise-smooth-embeddings-are-stable-under-fine-c-one-approximation]] on the two separate embeddings, and use [[lem-relative-shape-controlled-secants-approximate-smooth-simplex-maps]] to make $T$ secant on $P_1$ and to extend the change over its star while leaving $T$ outside. Every new intersection of the two images lies in $P_0$ by the distance bound and the triangle inequality, and both maps remain embeddings; on $P_1$ they are linear on a finite subdivision, where the Euclidean step fits them. Pull the subdivisions back and extend them over the whole complexes by coning subdivided faces from original simplex barycentres without changing the altered map. The union is a whole-star embedding: at a point of the intersection a neighbourhood is an actual geometric linear complex whose differential is the translated affine realization, hence injective on the whole tangent star; elsewhere one is locally inside a single embedded piece; the glued map is continuous and bijective from a compact space, hence a homeomorphism.

Bundle projection. In a product chart $M=B\times N$ write $T(x)=(h(r(x)),v(x))$. If $h$ is affine on every base simplex reached by the affected domain simplices, a secant of $T$ still has first coordinate $hr$ (both $r$ and $h$ are affine there and the secant matches vertex values), and every boundary correction has zero first coordinate, so the tapered extension preserves $\pi T=hr$ exactly; injectivity of $h$ forces equal $r$-values on identified points, so $r$ descends to the glued union and is affine on its simplices. In general, subdivide and choose a secant approximation $h'$ of $h$ on a finite base subcomplex covering the affected projections and their stars, extend it with the shape-controlled lemmas, and temporarily replace $T$ by $T_1=(h'r,v)$: equality of two $T_1$-values gives equal $r$, then equal $v$, hence equal $T$-values, and at the differential level injectivity of $h'$ and of the whole-star $dT$ gives injectivity on the tangent star, so $T_1$ is again an embedding. Apply the affine-base fitting to obtain $T_2=(h'r,v')$, then shift back to $T_3=(hr,v')$: the same argument shows each embedding and the embedding of their fitted union survive, and two points intersect under $T_3$ exactly when they intersect under $T_2$, because $h$ and $h'$ are injective and the fibre coordinate is unchanged. The first-coordinate changes cancel, leaving the original diagram; choosing the temporary secant and fitting errors successively small gives the prescribed final strong error by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) on finitely many compact charts.

Finite induction and supports. In a general smooth target, subdivide the new complex so that each closed simplex and the old pieces in its intersection neighbourhood lie in one coordinate chart; in the bundle case choose product charts and base charts with the same property. Order the finitely many new simplices with faces first. Start with the old embedding and suppose the already processed new simplices fit it in a full subcomplex and their union is an embedding; attach the next simplex along its already processed boundary, giving $P=Q\cup A$, and apply the local step, or the projection-preserving steps in product charts. The changed map on the processed new subcomplex extends over the unprocessed simplices with arbitrarily small prescribed error, and in product charts its correction has zero base component, so the diagram is preserved. Choose the error at each of the finitely many stages small enough to retain the previous embeddings and fit margins, with total error below the requested tolerance. Unlike a locally finite argument, no unevidenced limiting map or infinite subdivision arises. Every local change and its extension is supported on the closed stars used in that construction, so if those supports have images in $V$ disjoint from the protected region $R$, the parametrizations and diagrams on $R$ are untouched and previously fitted pieces keep their identifications. Affine-plane constraints are preserved because secants and correction translations stay in the planes; for corner targets, after each plane-preserving local change the image still lies in the chart orthant by [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]], before the chart inverse is applied.
