items.title: Finite smooth triangulation of compact corners, relative to admissible boundary data
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$ and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation. Every local corner face, and any specified finite union of such closed faces, is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation $f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same relative conclusion applies to a fixed triangulated closed neighbourhood piece whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.
items.strategy:
Metric and collar margins. The needed compact-source and separation constructions are the explicit finite-cover arguments in [[lem-relative-smooth-triangulations-can-be-fitted-while-preserving-a-bundle-projection]], not an additional unproved metric lemma. Here M is compact by hypothesis, and every closed coordinate box and each closed collar subpiece is compact. The smaller protected collar through epsilon/4 is closed and disjoint from all new core pieces chosen outside the open collar through epsilon/3; after pulling the chart cover and protected complement back to each finite source piece, the finite-ball construction gives positive support margins. Coordinate core margins themselves are the minimum of finitely many positive distances to the artificial box faces, or are explicitly epsilon/12 between the retained collar levels; no positive distance is assigned to an empty complement. Finitely many extended ODE charts give finitely many positive flow times, whose minimum is positive. All target separation calculations are restricted to compact coordinate patches, and the already supplied fitting support hypotheses remain explicit.

Box pieces. If $M$ is empty take the empty complex; if $M$ has dimension zero, compactness makes it a finite discrete set. Otherwise choose finitely many corner charts and closed coordinate boxes $Q_i=[0,R_i]^{c_i}\times[-R_i,R_i]^{n-c_i}$ contained in them whose smaller relative interiors cover $M$; at a point of smaller depth shrink the chart so that all remaining corner coordinates are strictly positive and treated as ordinary. Each box has a finite cell triangulation ([[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]]), and its inverse chart map is a whole-star embedding, being the restriction of an invertible smooth coordinate map to an actual geometric complex; the preimages of the local corner planes are subcomplexes. In any other corner chart on an overlap the transition and its inverse map the corresponding tangent orthant and its faces isomorphically to the target orthant and faces (their derivatives preserve these tangent cones by taking directional limits), so the adapted face/tangent hypotheses of [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] hold for the box pieces in every chart used to fit them.

Collar. If the boundary is empty, the nonrelative construction also gives the relative result. For nonempty boundary, build a piecewise smooth collar directly. Around each boundary point choose a small corner chart and a smooth vector field whose active corner-coordinate components are strictly positive; restrict ordinary Euclidean smooth bump functions to these orthants, extend by zero, normalize their finite sum and form the weighted sum $V$, which is strictly inward along every active local face, because the inward tangent cone is preserved by chart transitions and its strict interior is convex. Extend $V$ over $M$ by the same finite bump construction; in each corner chart its coefficients extend smoothly to a neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^n$, so [[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]] solves the local ODE and uniqueness makes the solutions agree while in $M$; compactness gives a common positive time for starts on $\partial M$, and [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]] gives smooth dependence on the initial point. The forward flow lies in the interior for small positive times because every active boundary coordinate has positive derivative. The map $\partial M\times[0,\epsilon]\to M$, $(y,t)\mapsto\Phi(y,t)$, is injective for small $\epsilon$: if two values agree, reverse the common interior orbit by uniqueness; different times would make an earlier boundary start occur at positive time on an orbit starting elsewhere, impossible once that orbit has entered the interior; equal times give equal starts. On the compact product it is a homeomorphism onto its image, which contains a neighbourhood of $\partial M$, since following $-V$ decreases a first active face coordinate at a uniformly positive rate until it reaches zero, within a time bounded by a constant times the distance to the boundary; finitely many boundary charts give a uniform neighbourhood and time. Composing with the supplied admissible boundary triangulation $f$ gives a corner collar: on each boundary simplex the product $L\times[0,\epsilon]$ is smooth, and at a corner the differential $(w,t)\mapsto df(w)+tV$ is injective on the full tangent star and fills the orthant, each orthant vector having the unique expression $v=w+tV$ with $t=\min_j v_j/V_j$ over the active corner coordinates.

Fitting and coverage. Fit the box pieces and the collar to one another using the supported construction of [[lem-relative-smooth-triangulations-can-be-fitted-while-preserving-a-bundle-projection]]; the additional verification in a corner chart is that the specified corner planes are affine, so the fitting keeps simplices in their planes, and [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] keeps every altered piece in its orthant with unchanged face zero sets; the support margins keep the images inside the relatively open charts. On overlaps the local face germs are permuted by the chart transition, so preserving them in the active chart preserves the same geometric faces in every chart. To see that the union covers $M$ rather than merely lying close to it: each initial box has a compact smaller core, and in its coordinates a sufficiently small perturbation of its map is $x\mapsto x+e(x)$ with $\|e\|_\infty$ less than the margin of that core from the artificial box faces and $e_j(x)=0$ on $x_j=0$ for a true corner face. For a target $y$ in the smaller core the self-map $x\mapsto\operatorname{clip}_{Q_i}(y-e(x))$ of the box (or of a ball under a radial parametrization) has a fixed point by [[thm-brouwer-fixed-point-theorem]]; clipping at an artificial face cannot occur at a fixed point because the error is smaller than the core margin; at a true corner face $x_j=0$ the constraint $e_j(x)=0$ makes clipped equality imply $y_j=0$ and the original equation $x_j+e_j(x)=y_j$ still holds; for unclipped coordinates it holds by definition. So the perturbed box still contains its entire core, and choosing the total fitting error below all finitely many margins makes the union image equal to $M$. The local differential fans are homeomorphisms onto the tangent orthants: for a target ray $y+tv$, preimages $x_t$ under the finite union homeomorphism converge to the preimage $b$ of $y$ and lie in one closed simplex containing $b$ on a subsequence; full rank gives $|x_t-b|\le Ct$, and a subsequential limit of $(x_t-b)/t$ is a tangent-cone vector mapping to $v$, while injectivity of the fan (the immersion statement) gives continuity of the resulting finite piecewise linear inverse. Thus the union is a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation and all intersections are full after the prescribed barycentric refinement.

Relative case. Given the admissible boundary triangulation $f$, triangulate the finite product cells $\sigma\times[0,2\epsilon/3]$, $\sigma\in L$, keeping the given bottom-face subdivisions and coning the untriangulated higher cells; composing with the collar flow gives a whole-star embedding agreeing with $f$ on its bottom. Protect the smaller collar through time $\epsilon/4$. The compact complement of the open collar through time $\epsilon/3$ lies in the smooth interior of $M$ and is covered by finitely many ordinary closed chart boxes whose smaller cores cover it; choose them and all fitting stars disjoint from the protected collar. Fit these boxes and the outer collar pieces with the supported construction; all modifications occur away from the protected region in a boundaryless interior target, so the original $f$ remains pointwise fixed, while the coverage argument of the previous paragraph applies to the interior cores and to the compact intermediate collar annulus. A fixed triangulated closed neighbourhood piece with a smaller protected subcomplex is handled by the same supported fitting and core-coverage argument. The construction uses only finitely many chart pieces and finite subdivisions, keeps the face zero sets, and never inverts a corner chart outside its domain; no extension of arbitrary incompatible boundary data is asserted.
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is declared as an ambient hypothesis and carried in deps for the frozen manifest graph, but no essential use is identified: the finitely many charts, bumps and ODE data involve only finite choices, and the cited Picard-Lindelof and smooth-dependence suppliers are choice-free.

items.title: Finite smooth bundle triangulation over a fixed base, relative to a supplied collar diagram
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\pi:E\to B$ be a smooth bundle with compact total space, compact smooth base and compact smooth fibre, permitting corners. A bundle here comes with finite smooth local product trivializations, whose transition maps preserve all local source/target corner faces; a boundary face in a product chart is either a base face or a fibre face. Let $h:D\to B$ be a supplied finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.

Then there is a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation $F:K\to E$ and a piecewise affine map $r:K\to D$ with $\pi F=hr$. Thus the actual bundle projection is PL over the fixed base parametrization. Refining base pieces for local construction does not change $h$ or the original complex $D$ in the final diagram: $r$ on a domain simplex is affine into a simplex of the original $D$.

The construction is relative to any supplied finite diagram $C:J\to E$, $\pi C=hr_J$, embedding onto a closed neighbourhood of a protected subpolyhedron $R$ contained in its relative interior, provided the fitting supports of the remaining pieces can be chosen disjoint from $R$. In particular this applies when $C$ is an already triangulated collar neighbourhood of the entire boundary and $R$ is a smaller collar: the original boundary and all its corner-face intersections are kept pointwise, with compatible subdivisions allowed. All union intersections are full subcomplexes.

This relative contract requires the collar diagram, not just an arbitrary triangulation of the boundary without any projection-preserving neighbourhood extension. Nor does proper smoothness of $\pi$ alone replace the supplied bundle trivializations.
items.strategy:
Compact base and star margins. The metric source |D| is compact because h is a homeomorphism onto the compact B: an open cover of |D| transports by h to a cover of B and has a finite subcover. Pull back the finite product-chart base cover to |D| and use [[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]. Explicitly choose finitely many balls B(a_j,r_j) covering |D| with B(a_j,3r_j) contained in a chosen chart preimage; a subset of diameter less than min r_j lies in one such chart preimage by the triangle inequality. A closed vertex star has diameter at most 2 times the mesh; k successive required support stars have diameter at most 2(k+1) times the mesh. Thus choose the mesh with 2(k+1)mesh below this margin, using the actual finite k needed by fitting/extension. All D_i and their support stars then have compact images inside their assigned product-chart domains. Relative protected-piece separation uses the finite-ball compact-versus-closed argument already proved in [[lem-relative-smooth-triangulations-can-be-fitted-while-preserving-a-bundle-projection]] on compact source pieces; the closed smaller collar and the closed fitting pieces are disjoint by the stated buffer hypothesis, so it gives a positive gap. Empty source pieces or complements require no bound. These are local metric constructions, not an invocation of an unnamed global metric or of properness as bundle structure.

Fibre and base pieces. If $E$ is empty take the empty total complex and map. Otherwise triangulate the compact fibre $N$ by [[thm-compact-smooth-manifolds-with-corners-admit-relative-finite-triangulations]], say $g:L\to N$. Subdivide $D$ finely enough that the closed stars of the relevant simplices have images under $h$ in the base domains of the finitely many bundle product charts: continuity of $h$ and the finite product-chart cover give a positive Lebesgue margin on the compact realization, and the mesh can be made as small as needed. Choose finitely many closed base subcomplex pieces $D_i$ with interiors covering $D$ and $h(D_i)$ compactly contained in a product-chart base domain, the subdivision inclusion being affine on each simplex into an original simplex of $D$. For each $i$ the product map $F_i(x,y)=\phi_i(h(x),g(y))$ on $D_i\times L$ is a whole-star smooth embedding (the product of embeddings through a face-compatible product chart); triangulate its finite product cells compatibly ([[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]]), so that projection onto $D_i$ is affine on each product simplex and $\pi F_i=h\operatorname{pr}_1$. The face/tangent conditions transfer from those of $h$ and $g$ and the face-compatible product chart, so these are admissible bundle diagrams.

Fitting. Apply [[lem-relative-smooth-triangulations-can-be-fitted-while-preserving-a-bundle-projection]] to fit the finitely many diagrams in turn, choosing the accumulated strong error as small as needed on every compact chart. The fitting construction never changes $h$ or the original point map $r_i=\operatorname{pr}_1$ of a piece, and on an identified overlap injectivity of $h$ forces the same base point, so the maps $r_i$ descend to one map $r$ on the glued finite complex; after the subdivisions each is still affine into a simplex of the original $D$, so $r$ is a valid final affine-base map. The union map is a whole-star embedding, all intersections are full, and [[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]] retains every corner face.

Coverage fibre by fibre. Fix $x\in D_i$ and $b=h(x)$. Since the original $r_i$ is unchanged, the perturbed embedding $F_i'$ maps the entire slice $\{x\}\times|L|$ into the same fibre $E_b$, with original fibre map $g$. Cover $N$ by finitely many closed local corner boxes by their smaller cores and parametrize the input slice over one such box by $g^{-1}$ (continuous because $g$ is a homeomorphism); there the perturbed fibre map is a continuous small perturbation $u\mapsto u+e(u)$ of the identity, uniformly in $x$, with $e_j=0$ on every true fibre-boundary face because the fitting preserved those zero sets ([[lem-corner-adapted-strong-approximations-remain-in-the-same-orthant]]). For a target point $v$ in the smaller core the self-map $u\mapsto\operatorname{clip}(v-e(u))$ of the box has a fixed point by [[thm-brouwer-fixed-point-theorem]]; if the error is below the core margin no artificial box face can clip at a fixed point, and at a true face $u_j=0$ the constraint $e_j=0$ makes clipped equality imply $v_j=0$, so the original equation still holds and $v$ lies in the perturbed slice. Hence each perturbed slice hits every core and therefore all of $N$; since the $D_i$ cover the base, the union embedding is onto $E$ and is the required triangulation.

Relative case. Start with the supplied diagram $C:J\to E$, $\pi C=hr_J$, embedding onto a closed neighbourhood of the protected subpolyhedron $R$ in its relative interior. Cover the compact complement of a still smaller open neighbourhood contained in $C(J)$ by finitely many local product pieces of the form $D_i\times Q_i$, with $Q_i$ a closed fibre coordinate box; the separation hypothesis and compactness let us choose their images and all necessary fitting stars disjoint from $R$. The domain base pieces come from sufficiently fine subdivisions of $D$, and the product simplices retain affine projection into the original $D$. Fit these pieces to $C$ and to one another by the supported construction, which leaves $C$ pointwise unchanged on $R$ and keeps the exact original projection on every piece; the smaller cores still cover the complement by the box fixed-point argument, the compact intermediate overlap in the old neighbourhood piece is retained under a sufficiently small approximation, and the protected region itself is untouched. In the collar application the entire boundary lies in $R$, so the prescribed boundary parametrization and all its corner-face intersections remain fixed, with compatible subdivisions. All constructions are finite; no Ehresmann theorem, generic algebraic-map triangulation or unproved smooth fitting primitive is substituted for the actual product charts and the local fitting proof.
items.axiom_use: The Axiom of Choice is assumed in the Statement and declared in deps; the finite product-chart construction uses only finite choices, and the cited ODE, Brouwer and fitting suppliers are choice-free, so no essential AC use is identified beyond the ambient declaration retained by the frozen manifest graph.

title: Relative Smooth Triangulation And Bundle Fitting Examples

items.title: Projection-preserving product triangulation of a trivial smooth bundle
items.statement: Let $h:D\to B$ and $g:L\to N$ be supplied finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulations. The trivial bundle $\pi:B\times N\to B$ has a finite smooth triangulation $F:K\to B\times N$ satisfying $\pi F=hr$ for a piecewise affine map $r:K\to D$, with $h$ unchanged. Product corner faces are subpolyhedra.
items.strategy: The cells $\sigma\times\tau$ with $\sigma$ a simplex of $D$ and $\tau$ a simplex of $L$ form a finite convex cell complex: the intersection of two is the product of their respective common faces, hence a common face. Apply [[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]] to obtain a finite compatible triangulation $K$ of $|D|\times|L|$. Define $F(x,y)=(h(x),g(y))$ and $r(x,y)=x$: every simplex of $K$ lies in a product cell, so $F$ is smooth there with matching face values, $r$ is affine into a simplex of the original $D$, and $\pi F=hr$ holds pointwise with $h$ unchanged. The product map is a homeomorphism because both factors are, and its tangent-star differential $(u,v)\mapsto(dh(u),dg(v))$ is injective: equality of two images gives $dh(u)=dh(u')$ and $dg(v)=dg(v')$, and the whole-star hypotheses give $u=u'$, $v=v'$, even after the product-cell subdivision. The corner-face fans and their zero sets are products of those of the factors, so the triangulation is corner adapted, and every product face is a union of the triangulated cells. The construction is elementary and does not invoke the general bundle theorem.
items.axiom_use: None: an explicit finite product-cell triangulation.

title: Sequences and Limits

items.title: Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences
Convergence depends only on the tail
A sequence has at most one limit
Every convergent sequence is bounded
Every convergent sequence is Cauchy
A null sequence times a bounded sequence is null
Algebra of limits: sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients
Limits preserve non-strict inequalities
The squeeze theorem
The absolute value is compatible with limits
Divergence to $+\infty$ and to $-\infty$
For positive terms, null and divergence to $+\infty$ are reciprocal
A strictly increasing index map satisfies $n_k \ge k$
Subsequences inherit the limit
FALSE: every bounded sequence converges

Conventions for sequences: indexing, eventually, $\lim$, and rational $\varepsilon$

title: Sequences and Limits: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The sequence $1/(k+1)$ converges to $0$
items.statement: The sequence of reals $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$, with $k+1 = \sigma(k)$ the successor of $k$ read in $\mathbb{R}$ through the canonical-natural embedding ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]], [[def-sequence]]). Every term is defined and positive. This is the real-sequence counterpart of the rational null sequence $1/n$ of the construction page, and it is the reference null sequence of this page: the later examples and counterexamples compute with it. The argument spends only density of $\mathbb{Q}$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the Archimedean property of $\mathbb{Q}$ ([[lem-rat-archimedean]]) and reciprocal reversal ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]); no completeness beyond the Archimedean property and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Given a real $\varepsilon > 0$, density of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ supplies a rational $q$ with $0 < q < \varepsilon$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the Archimedean property of $\mathbb{Q}$ supplies a natural $N \ge 1$ with $N^{-1} < q$ ([[lem-rat-archimedean]]). For every $k \ge N$ one has $k+1 \ge N+1$ ([[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]]) and $N+1 > N \ge 1$, so $0 < (k+1)^{-1} \le (N+1)^{-1} < N^{-1} < q < \varepsilon$ by the strict increase of the canonical naturals ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]) and reciprocal reversal ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]). Hence $|x_k - 0| = (k+1)^{-1} < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge N$.

items.title: A rational expression in $k$: $(2(k+1)+3)/(5(k+1)+1) \to 2/5$
items.statement: The sequence $x_k := \dfrac{2(k+1)+3}{5(k+1)+1}$ converges to $2/5$ ([[def-real-limit]]). The point is method: an explicit rational expression of $k$ is evaluated from the algebra of limits ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]) once a single null sequence is known, without an $\varepsilon$-estimate fitted to the expression. Dividing numerator and denominator by the positive factor $k+1$ turns the expression into a quotient of two affine expressions in the null sequence $(k+1)^{-1}$ of [[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]].
items.strategy: By field arithmetic $x_k = \big(2 + 3(k+1)^{-1}\big)\big/\big(5 + (k+1)^{-1}\big)$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). The sequence $(k+1)^{-1}$ converges to $0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]), so by the scalar-multiple and sum clauses of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] the numerator converges to $2 + 3 \cdot 0 = 2$ and the denominator to $5 + 0 = 5$. The denominator sequence is nonzero at every index — $5 + (k+1)^{-1} > 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[lem-of-add-order]]) — and its limit $5$ is nonzero ([[cor-of-one-positive]]), so the quotient clause of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] gives $x_k \to 2/5$.

items.title: The alternating sequence $(-1)^k/(k+1)$ converges to $0$
items.statement: Let $(s_k)$ be the sequence with $s_0 = 1$ and $s_{\sigma(k)} = -s_k$ — the sequence usually written $(-1)^k$, introduced and proved non-convergent as a bounded sequence in [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]. The sequence $y_k := s_k (k+1)^{-1}$ converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]): a null sequence may oscillate in sign at every term. The proof is the null-times-bounded lemma ([[lem-null-times-bounded]]) applied to the null sequence of [[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]] and the bounded sequence $(s_k)$, so no estimate depending on the sign pattern is needed.
items.strategy: (1) $|s_k| = 1$ for every $k$: the set $\{1,-1\}$ is closed under negation, $|-1| = 1$ and $|uv| = |u||v|$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]], [[def-real-order]]), so induction from the recursion $s_0 = 1$, $s_{\sigma(k)} = -s_k$ ([[thm-recursion]], [[thm-induction-principle]]) gives $|s_k| = 1$. Hence $(s_k)$ is bounded with bound $M = 1$ ([[def-sequence]]). (2) $(k+1)^{-1} \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]), so [[lem-null-times-bounded]] gives $s_k (k+1)^{-1} \to 0$.

items.title: The square roots $\sqrt{k}$ diverge to $+\infty$
items.statement: Let $\sqrt{k}$ denote the unique nonnegative square root of the canonical natural $k \in \mathbb{R}$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]). Then $(\sqrt{k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ diverges to $+\infty$ ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]): it is unbounded, hence not convergent ([[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]]). The proof is the Archimedean comparison $k > M^2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{k} > M$; it uses only that $\mathbb{R}$ is Archimedean ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and that squaring is monotone on the nonnegatives ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).
items.strategy: Let $M \in \mathbb{R}$ be given. If $M < 0$, then $\sqrt{k} \ge 0 > M$ for every $k$, so $K = 0$ witnesses the condition. If $M \ge 0$, apply [[thm-of-archimedean]] to the real $M^2$ to obtain a natural $n$ with $n > M^2$; for $k \ge n$ the canonical naturals are increasing, so $k \ge n > M^2$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). Since $M \ge 0$, $\sqrt{k} \ge 0$ and $(\sqrt{k})^2 = k$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]), the equivalence $M < \sqrt{k} \iff M^2 < (\sqrt{k})^2$ of [[lem-of-square-monotone]] gives $M < \sqrt{k}$. Hence $\sqrt{k} > M$ for all $k \ge n$.

items.title: The successive differences $\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}$ converge to $0$
items.statement: The sequence $z_k := \sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}$ converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]). Since $(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k})(\sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}) = 1$, the differences are the reciprocals of the sequence $w_k := \sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}$, which diverges to $+\infty$ because $w_k \ge \sqrt{k}$ and $(\sqrt{k})$ does ([[ex-square-roots-diverge-to-infinity]]); the converse direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] then gives $z_k \to 0$. Thus a difference of two sequences that both diverge can converge, so the algebra of limits has no difference rule for divergent sequences.
items.strategy: For every $k$, the field identity $(a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2$ ([[def-field]]) together with $(\sqrt{k+1})^2 = k+1$ and $(\sqrt{k})^2 = k$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $z_k w_k = (k+1) - k = 1$. The factor $w_k = \sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}$ is positive ([[lem-of-add-order]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]) and therefore invertible, so $z_k = w_k^{-1}$ ([[def-field]]). The sequence $(w_k)$ is positive with $w_k \ge \sqrt{k}$, and $(\sqrt{k})$ diverges to $+\infty$ ([[ex-square-roots-diverge-to-infinity]]); hence $w_k \to +\infty$ directly from the definition ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]), and the converse direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] gives $z_k \to 0$. Equivalently in $\varepsilon$ terms: given real $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $K$ with $\sqrt{k} > 1/\varepsilon$ for $k \ge K$, then $0 < z_k \le (\sqrt{k})^{-1} < \varepsilon$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

items.title: Changing the first hundred terms leaves convergence to $0$ and boundedness intact
items.statement: Let $u_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ and let $(x_k)$ be $u$ modified in its first hundred terms: $x_k := k+1$ for $k < 100$ and $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ for $k \ge 100$. Then $x_k \to 0$ and $(x_k)$ is bounded, indeed $|x_k| \le 100$ for every $k$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]). The initial block is arbitrary prescribed data: convergence depends only on the tail ([[lem-limit-of-tail]]), while the bound is read off the finite block and the tail separately. This is the worked form of the tail theorem.
items.strategy: Convergence: $(x_k)$ agrees with $(u_k)$ from index $100$ on, and $u_k \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]); the 'agree from some index on' clause of [[lem-limit-of-tail]] gives $x_k \to 0$. Boundedness: if $k < 100$ then $k+1 \le 100$ by the immediate-successor form of discreteness ([[lem-nat-discrete]]), and the canonical naturals are increasing, so $|x_k| = x_k = k+1 \le 100$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]); if $k \ge 100$ then $0 < (k+1)^{-1} \le 1 \le 100$ ([[prop-of-reciprocal-order]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]). Hence $|x_k| \le 100$ for every $k$.

items.title: Two squeeze computations: $1/((k+1)\sqrt{k+1}) \to 0$ and $(k+(-1)^k)/(k+1) \to 1$
items.statement: (i) The sequence $a_k := \big((k+1)\sqrt{k+1}\big)^{-1}$ converges to $0$, squeezed between the constant sequence $0$ and $(k+1)^{-1}$. (ii) With $(s_k)$ the alternating sequence of [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]], the sequence $b_k := (k + s_k)/(k+1)$ converges to $1$, squeezed between $1 - 2(k+1)^{-1}$ and the constant $1$. Both use [[thm-squeeze]]; in (ii) the middle sequence is not presented as a sum of two sequences whose limits are known in advance, which is what the squeeze theorem is for.
items.strategy: (i) $\sqrt{k+1} \ge 1$ because $1 \le k+1$ and squaring is monotone on the nonnegatives ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]); hence $0 \le a_k \le (k+1)^{-1}$ for every $k$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]). The constant sequence $0$ converges to $0$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]) and $(k+1)^{-1} \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]), so [[thm-squeeze]] gives $a_k \to 0$. (ii) By induction from $s_0 = 1$, $s_{\sigma(k)} = -s_k$, one has $s_k \in \{1,-1\}$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]); if $s_k = 1$ then $b_k = (k+1)(k+1)^{-1} = 1$, and if $s_k = -1$ then $b_k = (k-1)(k+1)^{-1} = 1 - 2(k+1)^{-1}$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]). So $1 - 2(k+1)^{-1} \le b_k \le 1$ for every $k$. The lower bound converges to $1$: the sequence $2(k+1)^{-1}$ is a scalar multiple of a null sequence, so it converges to $0$ ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]]), and $1 - 2(k+1)^{-1} \to 1 - 0 = 1$; the constant $1$ converges to $1$. [[thm-squeeze]] gives $b_k \to 1$.

items.title: Even and odd subsequences of $1/(k+1)$ converge to $0$
items.statement: Let $(x_k)$ be the null sequence of [[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]], and let $n, m : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the strictly increasing index maps constructed in [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]] (the even and the odd index map). Then the subsequences $x_{n_j}$ and $x_{m_j}$ both converge to $0$ ([[lem-subsequence-inherits-limit]]): removing infinitely many indices from this already convergent sequence, even all odd ones, preserves its inherited limit. A convergent subsequence of a divergent sequence can exist, so no converse is asserted, and by [[lem-index-map-grows]] the index maps satisfy $n_j \ge j$ and $m_j \ge j$, so the subsequences are genuine thinnings of the sequence.
items.strategy: $(x_k)$ converges to $0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]). The maps $n$ and $m$ are strictly increasing, as proved in [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]; [[lem-subsequence-inherits-limit]] then gives $x_{n_j} \to 0$ and $x_{m_j} \to 0$. The growth bound $n_j \ge j$ and $m_j \ge j$ is [[lem-index-map-grows]]. No further estimate is needed: the limit of a subsequence is inherited, not recomputed.

items.title: The absolute value of the limit, and the limit of the absolute value
items.statement: Let $x_k := (k+1)^{-1} - 1$. Then $x_k \to -1$, and $|x_k| \to 1 = |-1|$ ([[lem-limit-abs]], [[def-real-limit]]). Since $|x_k| = 1 - (k+1)^{-1}$ converges to $1$ while $x_k$ converges to $-1 \ne 1$, this separates the two halves of [[lem-limit-abs]]: the absolute value of the limit is recovered from the absolute values, but the limit itself is not, and the reversal of the implication fails for a nonzero limit exactly as it does for the boundedness direction discussed in the remarks of that item.
items.strategy: $(k+1)^{-1} \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and the constant sequence $-1$ converges to $-1$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]), so the sum clause of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] gives $x_k \to -1$. The first claim follows from [[lem-limit-abs]]: $|x_k| \to |-1| = 1$ ([[def-abs-value]]). For the separation, $0 < (k+1)^{-1} \le 1$ ([[prop-of-reciprocal-order]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]), so $x_k \le 0$ and $|x_k| = 1 - (k+1)^{-1}$ for every $k$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-real-order]]). If the implication of [[lem-limit-abs]] could be reversed for this limit, $|x_k| \to 1$ would give $x_k \to 1$, contradicting $x_k \to -1$ by uniqueness of limits ([[lem-limit-unique]]) since $1 \ne -1$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]], [[def-real-order]]).

items.title: The sum of two divergent sequences can converge: $k + (-k)$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** if the sum $(x_k + y_k)$ of two sequences of reals converges, then $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ both converge. The witnesses are $x_k := k$ and $y_k := -k$, where $k$ denotes the canonical natural of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]): $(x_k)$ diverges to $+\infty$ and $(y_k)$ to $-\infty$, while the sum is the constant sequence $0$, which converges to $0$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]). This is the caution noted immediately after the algebra of limits: the clauses of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] may not be read backwards.
items.strategy: $k \to +\infty$: given $M \in \mathbb{R}$, [[thm-of-archimedean]] gives a natural $N$ with $M < N$; the canonical naturals are increasing, so $k \ge N$ implies $k \ge N > M$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). Then $y_k = -k \to -\infty$ by [[def-divergence-to-infinity]] and the rules for negation: $y_k < -M$ for $k \ge N$ whenever $M \in \mathbb{R}$, applied with the arbitrary real $-M$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]], [[def-ordered-field]]). A sequence diverging to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is unbounded and hence not convergent ([[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]], [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]). Finally $x_k + y_k = k + (-k) = 0$ for every $k$ ([[def-field]]), and the constant sequence $0$ converges to $0$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]); so the refuted claim fails.

items.title: A null sequence times an unbounded sequence need not be null: $(k+1)^{-1}\cdot(k+1) = 1$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** if $(x_k)$ converges to $0$, then $x_k y_k$ converges to $0$ for every sequence $(y_k)$. The witnesses are $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ and $y_k := k+1$: $(x_k)$ is null ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and $(y_k)$ diverges to $+\infty$, but $x_k y_k = 1$ for every $k$, so the product converges to $1 \ne 0$. The boundedness hypothesis of [[lem-null-times-bounded]] therefore cannot be dropped, and it is the only hypothesis that the null-times-bounded lemma uses beyond convergence of the null factor.
items.strategy: $(x_k)$ converges to $0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and $(y_k) = (k+1)$ diverges to $+\infty$: given $M \in \mathbb{R}$, [[thm-of-archimedean]] gives a natural $N$ with $M < N$, and then $k+1 > M$ for all $k \ge N$ by the strict increase of the canonical naturals ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]). Each factor $k+1$ is positive, hence invertible, and $(k+1)^{-1}(k+1) = 1$ for every $k$ ([[def-field]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]); the constant sequence $1$ converges to $1$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]) and $1 \ne 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]]). So the product does not converge to $0$, and [[lem-null-times-bounded]]'s boundedness hypothesis is essential. Directly from [[def-real-limit]], the product cannot tend to $0$: at the rational test value $\varepsilon=1/2$, its distance $|1-0|=1$ never becomes smaller than $1/2$. Thus this rejection does not silently assume an undeclared uniqueness theorem.

items.title: The quotient rule needs a nonzero limit in the denominator: $1\big/(k+1)^{-1} = k+1$
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** if $x_k \to x$ and $y_k \to y$ and $x_k \ne 0$ for every $k$, then $y_k/x_k$ converges. The witnesses are $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ and $y_k := 1$: both converge — to $0$ and to $1$ — and every $x_k$ is nonzero, but $y_k/x_k = k+1$ diverges to $+\infty$. The quotient clause of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] requires the limit of the denominator to be nonzero, and the example is the extremal failure of exactly that hypothesis. It also instantiates the reciprocal bridge of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]].
items.strategy: $x_k > 0$ for every $k$ and $x_k \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]), so the 'only if' direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] gives $1/x_k \to +\infty$. Since $y_k$ is the constant sequence $1$ and $y_k/x_k = 1 \cdot (k+1) = k+1 = 1/x_k$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]), the quotient diverges to $+\infty$. A sequence diverging to $+\infty$ is unbounded and hence not convergent ([[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]], [[def-sequence]]), so the refuted claim fails. By contrast [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] concludes $y_k/x_k \to y/x$ only under its hypothesis $x \ne 0$, and here $x = 0$.

references.title: John K. Hunter, An Introduction to Real Analysis (complete author-hosted lecture notes, 307 pp.)
references.locator: §3.4, the paragraph after Theorem 3.26 (printed pp. 46-47): the algebra of limits and its cautions; the quotient hypothesis is the one isolated here

items.title: The squeeze theorem needs the two bounds to share their limit
items.statement: **Refuted claim:** if $a_k \le x_k \le b_k$ eventually and $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$ both converge, then $(x_k)$ converges. The witnesses are the constant sequences $a_k := -1$, $b_k := 1$ and the alternating sequence $x_k := s_k$ of [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]; the inequalities hold at every index, the two bounds converge to $-1$ and $1$ respectively, and $(s_k)$ does not converge. So [[thm-squeeze]] genuinely needs the two limit values to coincide, not merely the two bounds to exist.
items.strategy: $a_k = -1$ is the constant sequence with value $-1$ ([[def-sequence]]) and likewise $b_k = 1$; constant sequences converge to their values ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]). For the inequalities, $|s_k| = 1$ for every $k$ by induction from $s_0 = 1$ and $s_{\sigma(k)} = -s_k$ ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]]), so $s_k \in \{1,-1\}$ and $-1 \le s_k \le 1$ ([[def-real-order]], [[cor-of-one-positive]], [[lem-of-add-order]]). Non-convergence of $(s_k)$ is the content of [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]. Since $-1 \ne 1$ ([[def-real-order]]), [[thm-squeeze]] gives no conclusion here, and indeed the conclusion is false.

items.title: Geometric sequences: the complete classification for every real ratio
items.statement: For every real $r$, let $a_k=r^k$ for natural $k\ge0$, using the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], so $a_0=1$ even when $r=0$, and $a_{k+1}=a_k r$. This notation is valid for negative real ratios and is not rational exponentiation of a negative base. The complete classification is: if $|r|<1$, then $r^k\to0$; if $r=1$, the sequence is constantly $1$ and converges to $1$; if $r=-1$, its even and odd subsequences are constantly $1$ and $-1$, so it is bounded but divergent; if $r>1$, then $r^k\to+\infty$; if $r<-1$, then $|r^k|\to+\infty$, while the even subsequence diverges to $+\infty$ and the odd subsequence to $-\infty$, and the whole sequence neither converges nor diverges to either signed infinity. Consequently $(r^k)$ converges exactly when $-1<r\le1$. Here signed-infinity assertions mean [[def-divergence-to-infinity]], not a finite limit value. Quantitative checks: if $0<|r|<1$ and $h=|r|^{-1}-1>0$, then $|r^k|\le(1+kh)^{-1}$ for every natural $k$, and for $k\ge1$ one has $|r^k|<(kh)^{-1}$; if $|r|>1$ and $d=|r|-1>0$, then $|r^k|\ge1+kd$. The weak Bernoulli estimates have equality for $k=0,1$ and are strict for $k\ge2$. Thus $(1/2)^k$ and $(-1/2)^k$ are both null, $2^k$ diverges positively, and $(-2)^k$ grows in absolute value while alternating sign.
items.strategy:
Every field occurrence of a natural index means its canonical real image, transported in order by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]. Induct from the integer-power recursion and the multiplicative absolute-value law in [[lem-of-abs-value]] to prove $|r^k|=|r|^k$, including the base $|r^0|=|1|=1$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]]). Do not use the later geometric-sequence lemma or monotone convergence.

For $r=0$, $r^0=1$ and $r^k=0$ for every $k\ge1$, by the power recursion and zero multiplication in [[def-field]], so the rational-epsilon definition of [[def-real-limit]] gives convergence to $0$ with threshold $1$. For $0<b:=|r|<1$, inverse-order reversal in [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $b^{-1}>1$; put $h=b^{-1}-1>0$. The nonzero integer power laws give $b^k(b^{-1})^k=1$, and all powers of the positive bases are positive by [[lem-power-monotone]]. The actual [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]] gives $(b^{-1})^k=(1+h)^k\ge1+kh>0$. Reverse reciprocals to obtain $|r^k|=b^k\le(1+kh)^{-1}$ for every $k$. Its equality clause gives equality in this weak estimate exactly at $k=0,1$, because $h>0$. For $k\ge1$, $1+kh>kh>0$, so $(1+kh)^{-1}<(kh)^{-1}$. Given any positive rational $\varepsilon$ (identified with its real image as in [[def-sequence]]), the real Archimedean property [[thm-of-archimedean]] gives a natural $N\ge1$ with $N>1/(h\varepsilon)$. For every $k\ge N$, order transport and inverse reversal give $|r^k|<(kh)^{-1}\le(Nh)^{-1}<\varepsilon$. This proves nullity directly on the negative and positive small-ratio ranges alike. Each threshold is a single existential choice for the given epsilon; no simultaneous choice function or choice principle is needed.

For $r=1$, induction gives $r^k=1$, and constant sequences converge to their value by [[def-real-limit]]. For $r=-1$, the power recursion is the recursion $s_0=1$, $s_{k+1}=-s_k$ of the actual published [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]; induction identifies the sequences. Use its already constructed natural even and odd index maps $e_0=0$, $o_0=1$, $e_{j+1}=e_j+2$, $o_{j+1}=o_j+2$, which the published item proves strictly increasing. Two-step power recursion gives $a_{e_j}=1$ and $a_{o_j}=-1$ by induction. The constant subsequences have different finite limits, so [[lem-subsequence-inherits-limit]] with [[lem-limit-unique]] rules out convergence. Their indices grow at least like $j$ by [[lem-index-map-grows]], hence beyond every prescribed threshold both signs recur; at test bound $0$, neither the positive- nor negative-infinity eventual condition holds. Also $|a_k|=1$, so the sequence is bounded.

For $b:=|r|>1$, put $d=b-1>0$. Bernoulli gives $|r^k|=b^k=(1+d)^k\ge1+kd$ for every natural $k$, with equality exactly for $k=0,1$ and strictness for $k\ge2$. Given any real $M$, choose a natural $N\ge1$ with $N>1+|M/d|$; then $k\ge N$ gives $b^k\ge1+kd>M$. Thus $|r^k|\to+\infty$ by definition, so the full sequence is unbounded and cannot have a finite limit by [[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]]. If $r>1$, $b=r$ and this already proves $r^k\to+\infty$. If $r<-1$, $r=-b$. The same natural even/odd maps and integer-power product laws give $r^{e_j}=b^{e_j}$ and $r^{o_j}=-b^{o_j}$: verify $(-1)^{e_j}=1$, $(-1)^{o_j}=-1$ by the two-step recurrence, then use $(-b)^k=(-1)^k b^k$. The index growth $e_j,o_j\ge j$ makes the preceding lower bound apply eventually along each map, proving the even subsequence tends to $+\infty$. For the odd subsequence, given real $M$, apply that lower bound at the real threshold $-M$ to get $-b^{o_j}<M$ eventually, proving divergence to $-\infty$. Since both index maps are cofinal and both signs occur past every whole-sequence threshold, the full sequence fails both signed-infinity tests at bound $0$. These five cases exhaust every real ratio by order trichotomy and the definition of absolute value. The displayed numerical ratios are substitutions into the proved classification, with all integer-power conventions unchanged.

title: Analytic Constructible Sheaf Foundations

items.title: Analytic topology and finite smooth algebraic stratifications of complex varieties
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps, i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on $Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by polynomial quotient functions and are therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies. Hence the topologies transported from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$ ([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is continuous for the analytic topologies, and the analytic topology refines the Zariski topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and $x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring $\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies $\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$ ([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ - the **strata** - such that each $S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure (locally the polynomial-quotient function sheaf on the locally closed algebraic set), is a smooth algebraic subvariety of $X$, and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure $\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is the **frontier condition**: the frontier $\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata. An open subset of an affine model is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety for the induced structure sheaf.
items.strategy: Every clause is a definition together with its well-definedness check; no existence theorem for stratifications is asserted. (i) Analytic topology: on the intersection of two affine models the transition isomorphism and its inverse are regular, so locally they are polynomial quotient functions, which are Euclidean-continuous; a topology transported along such a homeomorphism is equal to the restriction of the transported topology on the overlap, and the glued topology on $X$ is therefore forced and unique. Continuity of regular maps and the comparison with the Zariski topology (whose open sets are complements of Euclidean-closed polynomial zero sets) are checked in the same local coordinates. (ii) Smoothness is the intrinsic regular-local-ring condition of [[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]] on the algebraic stalk. An isomorphism of classical varieties induces an isomorphism of its local ring, maximal ideal and cotangent space, so the condition is chart-independent. This definition asserts no existence of smooth strata and no analytic-chart comparison theorem. (iii) A locally closed subvariety has its own reduced polynomial-quotient function sheaf; the inverse-image of the ambient structure sheaf is not substituted for that quotient structure. (iii) Strata: a locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is open in its closure, so intersecting the finite affine cover of $X$ with $S$ and using that principal open subsets $D(h)$ of an affine model are affine models exhibits $S$ as a classical variety with the induced structure sheaf. (iv) The frontier condition is a condition on the given finite partition only. No choice principle is used: nothing is selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.
items.axiom_use: None: the definition is choice-free and makes no selection; the cited published suppliers are stated without choice.

items.title: Locally constant sheaves of finite rank
items.statement:
Let $S$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $S$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]). Then $\mathcal F$ is **locally constant of finite rank** if every point $x\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq S$ for which there are an integer $n\ge0$ and an isomorphism of sheaves on $U$
$$\mathcal F|_U\;\cong\;k_U^{\,n},$$
where $k_U$ is the constant sheaf on $U$ with value $k$ and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$ to the open subspace $U$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]], [[def-morphism-of-presheaves]], [[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). A sheaf with this property is also called a **finite-rank local system of $k$-vector spaces** on $S$. This is a property of the sheaf on the space; no identification of such sheaves with functors on the fundamental groupoid is part of the definition.
items.strategy: The definition is read literally: near each point there is an isomorphism onto a finite free constant sheaf. The constant sheaf $k_U^n$ is the $n$-fold direct sum of $k_U$, whose sections are the locally constant $k$-valued functions ([[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]); restricting a sheaf to an open subspace is the construction of [[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]; an isomorphism of sheaves is a morphism of presheaves ([[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]) with a two-sided inverse. The integer $n$ is quantified locally, so no global rank is asserted, and the final sentence only records that a functorial groupoid presentation is a different, uncompared object.
items.axiom_use: None.

items.title: Algebraically constructible complexes of analytic field sheaves
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as a topological space with its analytic topology ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large; and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$ ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent sheaves. We use the shift convention of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.
items.strategy: Every clause is definitional. The analytic topology and the stratification convention come from [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]], local constancy from [[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]], and the derived category with its shift convention from [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]; abelianness of $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ is the published abelian-category theorem for modules over the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ ([[def-module-on-ringed-space]]). Cohomological boundedness and constructibility are conditions on the cohomology sheaves of a bounded complex; shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves a bounded range, so the class is shift-stable by construction. Constructibility quantifies existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted. No choice principle is used.
items.axiom_use: None.

items.title: Analytic field sheaves have injective derived models
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$ ([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific injective resolution ([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below injective complexes model the bounded derived category: $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded derived category are computed by these replacements ([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let $\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier condition of $X$ ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$ ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.
items.strategy: (1) The ringed-space identification makes the published enough-injectives lemma applicable to $(X,k_X)$; its proof supplies local smallness, the Grothendieck axioms and a functorial embedding of every $k$-sheaf into an injective one, and iterating the embedding on the canonical cokernel produces one specific injective resolution with no further selection. (2) These resolutions are bounded-below injective replacements in the sense of the published model theorem, and AC supplies the dependent choice that theorem requires ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]); the equivalence identifies Hom groups in $D^b$ with homotopy classes of maps into the injective models. (3) Closure. Shifts preserve bounded cohomological constructibility. For a mapping cone of $f:A\to B$ constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$, restriction to a stratum $S$ is exact and commutes with finite direct sums and shifts, so $C(f)|_S$ is the mapping cone of $f|_S$. Locally trivializing the finite-rank local systems $H^j(A)|_S$ and $H^j(B)|_S$, the differentials become matrices of locally constant functions; on a small connected neighbourhood such a matrix is constant, so kernels, images and cokernels of the maps induced by $f$ are finite free constant sheaves ([[def-kernel-cokernel-image-sheaves]]). The long exact cohomology sequence of the cone then exhibits each $H^j(C(f))|_S$ as an extension of such local systems. Such an extension is locally split: around a fixed point trivialize the quotient and kernel, lift the finitely many quotient basis germs along the stalkwise epimorphism, represent those lifts by sections on a common neighbourhood, and shrink until their images equal the constant quotient basis sections. Those lifts define a sheaf section of the epimorphism and hence a direct-sum trivialization of the extension. Thus it is locally constant of finite rank; the cone is cohomologically bounded as well. Since the ambient cone triangles make $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ triangulated ([[thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure]]) and a full subcategory closed under shifts and cones is triangulated ([[def-triangulated-subcategory]]), this proves that $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory; the last sentence repeats the same argument when the two complexes are given with a common stratification. Only steps (1)-(2) use AC, exactly as stated.
items.axiom_use: AC is used exactly through the functorial injective-embedding theorem for the Grothendieck category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ (which produces the functorial injective resolutions) and through AC $\Rightarrow$ DC for the bounded-below injective model equivalence. The constructibility closure argument is choice-free. No other choice principle is used.

items.title: Finite poset diagrams have bounded finite bar models
items.statement: Let $P$ be a finite nonempty poset, regarded as a category with one arrow $p\to q$ exactly when $p\le q$, and let $h$ be the largest number of strict inequalities in a chain of $P$. Let $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ be the abelian category of covariant diagrams of $k$-vector spaces on $P$, i.e. the functor category of $k$-vector spaces indexed by $P$, with its cochain complexes as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. If $M$ is a bounded complex of diagrams in $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ whose vector spaces are finite-dimensional and vanish outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, then the derived inverse limit $\mathbf R\lim M:=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ ([[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]) has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$. If $A,B$ are such complexes, concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ respectively, then their derived Hom has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. These models commute with every field extension. For the empty poset, the diagram sections and the derived Hom model are zero by convention.
items.strategy: Representables are projective: for $p\in P$ let $Q_p$ be the diagram with $Q_p(q)=k$ for $p\le q$ and $Q_p(q)=0$ otherwise, with identity structure maps where both values are nonzero. Then $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p,N)=N(p)$ by evaluation at $p$, so $Q_p$ is projective, and $Q_p\otimes_k V$ is projective for finite-dimensional $V$ by decomposing $V$ along a finite basis into copies of $Q_p$. For a diagram $N$ put $\mathcal B_n(N)=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}\otimes_k N(p_0)$ with the standard face maps: delete $p_0$ and apply the structure map $N(p_0)\to N(p_1)$, delete an inner vertex with the coefficient unchanged, or delete $p_n$ using the natural map $Q_{p_n}\to Q_{p_{n-1}}$, with alternating signs. The face identities hold because diagram transport is functorial, so $\partial^2=0$, and $\mathcal B_n=0$ for $n>h$. Augment $\mathcal B(N)\to N$ by the structure maps $Q_p\otimes N(p)\to N$. Evaluated at $q$, the augmented complex is the simplicial $k$-vector space of chains $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ with coefficient in $N(p_0)$; the explicit contraction that appends $q$ with sign $(-1)^{n+1}$ when $p_n<q$ and is the augmentation section in degree $0$ is an objectwise contracting homotopy, so the augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism, and $\mathcal B(N)$ is a projective resolution of $N$ when the values of $N$ are finite-dimensional. Applying this to each internal degree of a bounded finite-dimensional diagram complex and using total degree (internal degree) minus (bar degree) gives a complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams quasi-isomorphic to $A$ and concentrated in $[a-h,b]$, with total differential $d_A+(-1)^{u}\partial$ squaring to zero. The inverse limit is $\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,-)$, so resolving the constant diagram $\underline k$ by its bar complex gives in bar degree $n$ the finite product $\prod_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}M(p_n)$, concentrated in total degrees $[a,b+h]$ with finite-dimensional terms; by the projective model this computes $\mathbf R\lim$. Replacing $A$ by its bar model and applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,B)$ gives terms $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A(p_0),B(p_n))$, a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$, and the projective model identifies its cohomology with the derived Hom. Every term is a finite sum or product of spaces of linear maps between finite-dimensional vector spaces, so extension of scalars commutes with the terms, with the differentials and hence with cohomology; the empty poset contributes zero by the stated convention.
items.axiom_use: None: all constructions are finite direct sums, finite products and Hom spaces of finite-dimensional vector spaces.

items.title: Locally contractible metric spaces have singular constant sheaf cohomology
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective resolutions supplied by [[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.
items.strategy:
Write $C^n(U;k)$ for the $k$-vector space of functions on the singular $n$-simplices in the open set $U$; this is a presheaf whose sheafification $\mathcal C^n$ is the sheaf of singular $n$-cochains, and sheafification preserves stalks ([[thm-sheafification-preserves-stalks]]).

(1) Flasque $k$-sheaves are acyclic for derived sections. An injective $k$-sheaf $\mathcal I$ is flasque: for open $U\subseteq V$ the extension-by-zero map $j_{U!}k_U\to j_{V!}k_V$ is a monomorphism ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]]) and the extension-by-zero adjunction identifies $\operatorname{Hom}(j_{U!}k_U,\mathcal I)$ with $\mathcal I(U)$ ([[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]]), so injectivity makes the restriction $\mathcal I(V)\to\mathcal I(U)$ surjective. Embed a flasque $F$ into an injective $\mathcal I$ ([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]); the quotient $Q$ is flasque and every section of $Q$ over an open lifts along $\mathcal I\to Q$ ([[lem-flasque-kernel-lifts-quotient-sections]], [[def-flasque-sheaf]]). The long exact sequence then gives $H^1(U,F)=0$ and $H^{n+1}(U,F)\cong H^n(U,Q)$, so induction on $n$ gives acyclicity of $F$ in all positive degrees. Only underlying section groups are used; no claim that a $k$-injective is an injective abelian sheaf is made.

(2) Every section of $\mathcal C^n$ over an open $U$ is represented by cochains $c_i$ on a cover $\{U_i\}$ of $U$. Since $X$ is metric, hence paracompact, choose a locally finite open cover $\{W_i\}$ refining the $U_i$ with $\overline{W_i}\subseteq U_{j(i)}$ ([[thm-stone-metric-spaces-are-paracompact]]); write $c_i$ for $c_{j(i)}$. For a singular simplex whose image lies in some $W_i$, assign the value $c_i$ of one such chosen index, and assign $0$ if the image lies in no $W_i$. To see that the resulting cochain represents the given section of $\mathcal C^n$, fix $x$: local finiteness makes the set $J_x=\{i:x\in\overline{W_i}\}$ finite, and the finitely many cochains $c_i$, $i\in J_x$, represent the same germ of $\mathcal C^n$ at $x$, so by the stalk comparison they agree as presheaf cochains on one common neighbourhood of $x$; taking the intersection of these finitely many neighbourhoods and shrinking into a single $W_{i_0}$ containing $x$ makes the value assigned to every simplex contained in the resulting neighbourhood independent of the chosen index and equal to that of $c_{i_0}$. Hence the map $C^n(V;k)\to\mathcal C^n(V)$ is onto for every open $V$, and a section over $U$ extends to one over any larger $V$ by the same construction; in particular every $\mathcal C^n$ is flasque.

(3) The augmented complex $k_X\to\mathcal C^0\to\mathcal C^1\to\cdots$ has stalk at $x$ the filtered colimit of the singular cochain complexes $C^*(V;k)$ over the open neighbourhoods $V$ of $x$ ([[thm-sheafification-preserves-stalks]]). By hypothesis a cofinal family of these neighbourhoods is contractible, and a contraction gives a chain homotopy between the identity and a point map ([[thm-singular-chain-homotopy-formula]]), so their singular cohomology is $k$ in degree $0$ and $0$ in positive degrees. Filtered colimits of $k$-vector spaces are exact, so the stalk complex is exact in positive degrees with kernel $k$ in degree $0$; hence the augmented complex is a flasque resolution of $k_X$ and its sections compute the derived cohomology of $k_X$ by (1), where the derived groups are formed with the $k$-linear injective resolutions of [[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]] ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]).

(4) The map $C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$ of (2) is surjective, and its kernel $N^*$ consists of the cochains that vanish on all simplices of some open cover; it is the directed union, over open covers $\mathcal U$, of the subcomplexes $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ of cochains vanishing on the $\mathcal U$-small singular chains. For one cover, the inclusion of small chains into all chains is a homology isomorphism ([[thm-cover-small-singular-chains-compute-singular-homology]]), so the quotient chain complex is acyclic; over a field an acyclic chain complex splits degreewise into its boundaries and a complementary subspace, and dualizing such a splitting shows that $\operatorname{Hom}(-/\text{small},k)$ is acyclic, i.e. $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ is acyclic. A cocycle in the union lies in one $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ and is a coboundary there, so $N^*$ is acyclic; the long exact sequence of the short exact sequence of complexes $0\to N^*\to C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)\to0$ therefore identifies $H^*_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$ with $H^*\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$, and (3) identifies the latter with $H^*(X,k_X)$.

(5) All maps are built from restriction and sheafification, so the comparison is natural and restricts to any open subspace, which is again metric and inherits the contractible-open basis; for a nonempty contractible space the chain homotopy formula gives the cohomology of a point. In a finite polyhedral realization, a point of a simplex $\sigma$ has arbitrarily small contractible open neighbourhoods obtained by requiring its $\sigma$-coordinates to stay close to their positive values and the sum of its other coordinates to be sufficiently small, and an open star or a nonempty intersection of an open star with a closed simplex contracts linearly to the barycentre of the supporting simplex; so the comparison and the acyclicity conclusion apply to those neighbourhoods. This deduction uses no derived face-diagram equivalence.
items.axiom_use: AC is used in four places only: the locally finite refinement of open covers ([[thm-stone-metric-spaces-are-paracompact]]), the functorial injective resolutions of $k$-sheaves ([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]), the flasque section-lifting lemma ([[lem-flasque-kernel-lifts-quotient-sections]]), and the degreewise splitting of acyclic complexes of possibly infinite-dimensional vector spaces over a field. No other choice principle is used.

title: Analytic Constructible Sheaf Foundations Examples

items.title: Point operations and the open closed constructible line
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and let $k$ be a field. (1) The constructible category of a point is the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces, $D_c^b(\operatorname{pt};k)\simeq D^b(k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}})$ ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). For the identity map of the point, all four pullback/pushforward operations $f^*,f_*,f_!,f^!$ are the identity functors of that category, the tensor product and internal Hom are the usual finite cochain constructions, and the dualizing object is $k$ concentrated in degree $0$ ([[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]], [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]]). (2) On the complex line with the open inclusion $j:\mathbb C^*\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ and the closed inclusion $i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$, there is a $k$-linear short exact sequence of sheaves
$$0\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to0,$$
and its associated exact triangle is the ordinary localization triangle of the constructible derived category.
items.strategy: (1) A sheaf on the point is its vector space of sections, so a bounded complex of $k$-sheaves on the point is a bounded complex of $k$-vector spaces, and the single-stratum stratification of the point makes constructibility exactly the condition of finite-dimensional cohomology; a bounded complex with finite-dimensional cohomology is isomorphic in the derived category to a bounded complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces (truncate outside the cohomological support and split the resulting finite complex), so $D_c^b(\operatorname{pt};k)\simeq D^b(k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}})$ via the injective derived model of [[lem-field-module-sheaves-have-injective-derived-models]]. The identity map is proper with exact inverse and direct images, so $f^*=f_*=\operatorname{id}$ and $f_!=f_*=\operatorname{id}$ on these categories, and dually $f^!$, being right adjoint to $f_!$, is also the identity; tensor and internal Hom are the signed total tensor and Hom complex of finite-dimensional complexes, and the dualizing object of the $0$-dimensional smooth point is $k$ in degree $0$ ([[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]], [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]]; these two interfaces are declared forward references, closed later in this run). (2) Specialize the published open/closed sequence to the constant sheaf $\mathcal F=k_{\mathbb C}$ ([[lem-extension-by-zero-short-exact-sequence]]): it reads $0\to j_!(k_{\mathbb C^*})\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*(k)\to0$, with $j_!$ the extension by zero of [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and with the sheaf supported at $0$ identified as a pushforward by [[lem-sheaf-supported-on-a-closed-subset-is-a-pushforward]]; exactness is the published stalk computation. The mapping cone of $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k$ is quasi-isomorphic to $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$ ([[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]), so rotating the cone triangle gives $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, the localization triangle of the derived category ([[thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure]]).
items.axiom_use: None beyond the assumptions of the cited suppliers: the point and line computations are finite or explicit.

items.title: Second-order Laplace-type operators on metric vector bundles
items.statement:
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary of dimension $n\ge2$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), let $\mu$ be a smooth positive density on $M$ ([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), and let $E\to M$ be a finite-rank smooth vector bundle ([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]) over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ carrying a smooth bundle metric $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]), Euclidean in the real case and Hermitian, linear in the first variable, in the complex case; in the complex case the fibres are complex vector spaces through a smooth complex structure on $E$ ([[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]). Write $\Gamma(E)$ for the smooth sections ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

A $\mathbb K$-linear map $P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(E)$ is a **linear differential operator of order at most two** on $E$ when, on every chart domain $\Omega$ of $M$ with coordinates $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ and in every local frame of $E$ over $\Omega$ in which a section is written $s\leftrightarrow u=(u^1,\ldots,u^r)$ and its image as $Ps\leftrightarrow((Ps)_1,\ldots,(Ps)_r)$,
$$(Ps)_\lambda=-\sum_{i,j=1}^na^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_ju^\mu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^nb^j_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_ju^\mu(x)+c_{\lambda\mu}(x)u^\mu(x),\qquad1\le\lambda\le r,$$
with smooth coefficient functions on $\Omega$ and summation over repeated indices $\mu$ (and over $i,j$); by the strategy below, verifying this on the members of one atlas of charts and frames already forces it everywhere. Such an operator is **Laplace type** when in addition, in every such chart and frame, its second-order coefficients are scalar multiples of the identity, $a^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}=a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, with $a^{ij}$ smooth real functions for which $(a^{ij}(x))$ is symmetric and positive definite at every $x\in\Omega$. Its **principal symbol** is the smooth section $\sigma_2(P)$ of $\mathrm{Sym}^2T^*M$ ([[def-smooth-tensor-field]]) given on such a chart by $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j$ for $\xi\in T_x^*M$; equivalently $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)\,\mathrm{id}_{E_x}$ for a smooth field of positive-definite quadratic forms $a_x$ on $T_x^*M$, so that $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)>0$ whenever $\xi\ne0$.

$P$ is **formally symmetric** for $(\mu,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ when
$$\int_M\langle Ps,t\rangle\,d\mu=\int_M\langle s,Pt\rangle\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $s,t\in\Gamma_c(E)$ ([[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]).
items.strategy: The definition is local. On a fixed chart and frame the displayed assignment is a $\mathbb K$-linear map on components with smooth coefficients, and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) computes the transition to another chart and frame on the overlap: the second-order coefficients transform by the symmetric tensor rule $a'^{kl}=a^{ij}\frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial x'^l}{\partial x^j}$ and by conjugation with the frame-change matrix, while the terms produced by the second derivatives of the coordinate change are absorbed into the first-order coefficients. Hence a single operator that admits a local expression on one cover admits a local expression on every chart and frame, and the two hypotheses placed on the leading coefficient are invariant: scalar-ness is preserved by frame conjugation and by the coordinate rule for a field of symmetric matrices, and symmetric positive definiteness is preserved by both. The principal symbol is therefore independent of the chart and frame (the order-two part is well defined because two local expressions of the same operator differ by an operator of order at most one), it is smooth in $(x,\xi)$ because the $a^{ij}$ are smooth, and it is positive on nonzero covectors exactly when $(a^{ij})$ is positive definite. Formal symmetry is an identity between integrals of compactly supported smooth sections and therefore depends only on the operator, the density and the metric. No choice is used and no existence of densities, metrics or partitions is asserted.
items.axiom_use: None: supplied data only, and all computations are finite chart calculations.
